# Front Cover and Spine

The manuscript is bound in a sturdy, dark brown leather cover, a testament to the durability of historical <term>bookbinding|the process of physically assembling a book from a stack of paper or parchment sheets</term>. The exterior is decorated with <term>blind-tooling|a decorative technique where patterns are pressed into the leather using heated metal tools without the application of gold or color</term>. 

The design features a large central diamond (rhombus) formed by triple-scored lines. This diamond is nested within a rectangular frame, also defined by triple lines, with additional lines extending from the points of the diamond to the corners of the frame, creating a balanced, geometric aesthetic common in early library collections.

The spine of the book, which would have faced outward on a scholar's shelf, features five <term>raised bands|horizontal ridges created by the cords used to sew the pages together, which are then covered by the leather of the spine</term>. These bands divide the spine into six compartments. 

In the second compartment from the top, there is a red leather label. While much of the gold-stamped lettering has been lost to time and wear, a few fragments of the original Latin title remain visible:

<insert>
<unclear>...</unclear>IS
<unclear>...</unclear>TE
<unclear>...</unclear>MAE <note>original: "MAE". Likely part of the word "Summae," referring to a "Summa" or a comprehensive summary of a specific subject, such as theology or law.</note>
</insert>

# THE EXCELLENT BOOK
## BY HUS ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH,

->Whose author perished at the<-
-><term>Council of Constance<note>original: "concilio Constantiensi" — A major 15th-century meeting of the Catholic Church (1414–1418) intended to end the Papal Schism. It is historically significant for condemning the reformer Jan Hus to death for heresy.</note></term>.<-

->(Jan Hus.)<-

->I ask you, kind reader, to attend not to who speaks, but<-
->to what is being said.<-

<summary>The title page for Jan Hus's seminal work "On the Unity of the Church," featuring a dedication to his martyrdom at the Council of Constance and an appeal for objective reading.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the main text of Jan Hus’s *De Ecclesia* (On the Church). It follows the alphabetical subject index provided in the front matter. Hus starts by defining the various meanings of the word "Church," moving from the physical building to the clergy, and finally to the universal assembly of all people.</meta>

JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH
B
<meta>catchword: great (original: "magna")</meta>

The Catholic Church of those in heaven and those on earth is one, obtaining various names from Holy Scripture according to its dignity.

## CHAPTER I

<image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial 'C'. Inside the curve of the 'C' is a circular frame containing a figure of a nude child or cherub holding a staff. The letter is surrounded by ornate floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

Since every <term>pilgrim<note>original: "viator" — literally "wayfarer"; in medieval theology, this refers to a person on their journey through life toward eternity, as opposed to those already in heaven.</note></term> ought to faithfully believe in the holy Catholic Church, just as they ought to love the Lord Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of that church, and the Church herself as His bride. But one does not love this spiritual mother unless they have at least known her through faith; therefore, one must know her through faith, and thus honor her as a preeminent mother. 

<margin>The "Church" is understood in many ways.</margin>
For some knowledge of it, therefore, it should be noted that "Church" first signifies the house of God, built for the purpose that in it the people may worship their God, as in First Corinthians 11. 

<margin><insert>Augustine</insert></margin>
> Do you not have houses for eating and drinking, etc.? Or do you despise the Church of God (according to <term>Augustine<note>original: "Augu." — Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose writings Hus frequently cites to support his arguments.</note></term>, that is, the house of prayer)? 

Second, "Church" signifies the ministers belonging to that house, and in this way the <term>clergy<note>original: "Clerici" — those ordained for religious service, such as priests and monks.</note></term> belonging to one physical church call themselves "the Church." But because "Church," according to the Greeks, is said to be a congregation held under one rule, as <term>Aristotle<note>Hus cites the ancient Greek philosopher to provide a logical and linguistic foundation for the definition of a "body" or "assembly."</note></term> teaches in the second book of the *Politics*, chapter seven, where he says: "moreover, all participate in the <note>original: "ἐκκλησίᾳ" (*ekklēsia*) — the Greek word from which "church" is derived; it originally referred to a public assembly of citizens.</note>assembly." Therefore, according to this meaning, the congregation of all people is called the Church. According to that passage in Matthew 25: 

> When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the seat of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him.

<summary>Jan Hus begins his treatise by defining the "Church," arguing that a believer must understand and love the Church as a spiritual mother. He distinguishes between the Church as a physical building, as the body of clergy, and as the universal assembly of all people.</summary>

->the great congregation of all humans under the governance of Christ the King.<- And because not all of that congregation is the holy Church, he therefore adds: "And he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats." <note>original: "Et separabit eos ab inuicem, sicut pastor segregat oues ab hædis." — Matthew 25:32.</note>

<margin>The Church of the sheep and the church of the goats.</margin>
<margin><unclear>Entia vum sub</unclear>
<unclear>Entia pumnu</unclear>

From which it is clear that one is the Church of the Sheep, and the other the church of the Goats; one is the church of the holy, and the other of the <term>reprobate<note>original: "reproborum" — those who are rejected by God and not destined for salvation, the opposite of the "predestined."</note></term>. Likewise, regarding the Church of the righteous, one is **Catholic**—that is, universal—which is not a part of another, and which will now be discussed. Another is **particular**, which is a part of the other, according to that saying of the Savior in Matthew 18: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." <note>original: "Vbi sunt duo uel tres congregati in noĩe meo, ibi sum in medio eorũ."</note> From this it is clear that two righteous people gathered in the name of Christ are, with Christ as their head, a particular holy Church; similarly three, four, and so on up to the number of all the predestined inclusive. And in this way "Church" is often understood in Scripture, as the Apostle says in First Corinthians 1: "To the Church which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus." Likewise in Acts 20: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as <term>Bishops<note>original: "Episcopos" — while modern readers think of a specific rank, Hus uses this in the biblical sense of an overseer or guardian of the community.</note></term>, to rule the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood." And in this way, the righteous now living under the governance of Christ in the Archdeaconry of Prague, and especially the predestined, are the holy Church of Prague. The same reasoning applies to other particular churches of the holy, of which <term>Ecclesiasticus<note>original: "Ecclesiast." — Hus is citing the Book of Sirach (Wisdom of Ben Sira). The citation numbers he uses (23 and 35) vary slightly from modern chapter numbering.</note></term> 23 says: "In the assemblies of the Most High she opened her mouth." And likewise in chapter 35: "All the assembly of the holy shall declare his alms."

<margin>The universal Church.</margin>

Moreover, the **holy Catholic Church**—that is, the universal Church—is the totality of all the predestined, which is to say, all the predestined of the past, present, and future. This opinion is clear from <term>Augustine<note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whom Hus cites as the primary authority for defining the Church as the "assembly of the predestined."</note></term> in his commentary on John; under his opinion in <term>Canon Law<note>original: "xxxij. q. iiij. Hus is using legal and patristic precedents to prove his definition is "orthodox" or traditional.</note></term>, it is held how that same Church of the predestined ran from the beginning of the world until the Apostles, and from then until the Day of Judgment. For he says: "The Church which brought forth Abel and Enoch and Noah and Abraham, the same brought forth Moses and the proph[ets]"

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s theological definition of the Church, building on his previous use of Saint Augustine’s writings. Here, he expands the definition of the "Holy Catholic Church" to include both the living on earth and the angels in heaven, explaining the Church's position in the Apostles' Creed.</meta>

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH
<meta>catchword: incor[rupt]</meta>

->Page 14<-

<margin>The Church is partly in heaven and partly on earth</margin>
[The Church] is not only composed of that part which journeys as a pilgrim <note>original: "peregrinatur" — Hus uses the metaphor of a pilgrimage to describe the "Church Militant," or Christians currently living on earth.</note> from the rising of the sun to its setting, praising the name of the Lord, and singing a new song after the captivity of its old age; it also includes that part which has always remained in heaven, joined to God ever since it was created, and has never experienced the evil of a fall. This part persists in blessedness among the holy angels and assists its pilgrim part as is fitting, because they shall be one in the fellowship of eternity, and are even now one by the bond of charity <note>original: "charitatis" — in a medieval context, this refers to divine, selfless love.</note>. The whole institution is established for the worship of God; therefore, neither the whole nor any part of it wishes to be worshiped in place of God. Thus says Augustine.

<margin>Why the Church is placed in the Creed immediately after the confession of the Trinity</margin>
This is the Holy Catholic Church which Christians confess immediately after their faith in the Holy Spirit. This placement is permanent: First, because according to Augustine (as noted above), the Church is the "supreme creature" <note>In medieval hierarchy, the Church is the highest of all created things, second only to the uncreated God.</note>. Therefore, it is placed immediately after the uncreated Trinity. Second, because by the love of the Holy Spirit, it is joined to Christ in a perpetual marriage. And third, because once the Trinity has been established, it is fitting for the Trinity to have a temple in which to dwell. <margin>Aug.</margin> Whence Augustine infers as follows, saying: "God therefore dwells in His temple—not only the Holy Spirit, but also the Father and the Son." This also includes His body <note>Referring to the Church as the "Body of Christ."</note>, through which He was made the head of the Church of God that exists among men, so that He might hold the preeminence in all things. He Himself said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will rebuild it." Thus says Augustine.

<margin>Angels are part of the Church</margin>
From these words it is gathered: first, that there is one universal Church, praising God from the beginning of the world until the end. Second, that the holy angels are part of the Holy Catholic Church. Third, that the pilgrim or militant <note>term: "militans" — the Church currently struggling on earth against sin and trial.</note> part of that Church is aided by the triumphant <note>term: "triumphante" — the part of the Church already in heaven.</note> Church. Fourth, that the militant and triumphant are united by the bond of charity. <margin>The Church does not want to be worshiped as God</margin> Fifth, that the entire Church and every part of it must worship God, and neither the Church herself nor any part of her wishes to be worshiped as God. From this it follows consequently that the faithful must not **believe in** the Church <note>original: "in Ecclesiam credere" — Hus makes a fine grammatical point common in medieval theology: one believes *in* God (absolute trust), but one believes *that* the Church exists as a holy institution. To "believe in" the Church as one does in God would be idolatry.</note>, since it is not God but the house of God, as Augustine says in his exposition of the Creed. <margin>The Church is a bride, not an adulteress.</margin> But they must believe the Holy Catholic Church to be the bride of the Lord Jesus Christ—a modest bride, I say...

<summary>Jan Hus defines the Church as a single entity spanning both heaven (angels) and earth (pilgrims), explaining its placement in the Apostles' Creed and emphasizing that while the Church is the "supreme creature," it must not be worshiped as God.</summary>

# CHAPTER I.

<margin>Cyprian</margin>
[The Church is] incorrupt, nor can it finally be corrupted <note>original: "adulterari" — here meaning to be made unfaithful or polluted by false doctrine</note>. For the blessed Cyprian, bishop and glorious martyr, says (in the legal collection *Case 23, Question 1, Chapter "Loquitur"*): "The Church is one, which is extended far and wide into a multitude by the increase of its fruitfulness." And he adds: "Yet there is one head, one origin, and one mother rich in fruitfulness. The bride of Christ cannot be unfaithful; she is incorrupt and modest. She knows but one Lord; she guards the sanctity of one bedchamber with chaste modesty." Thus he speaks. Therefore, that holy Church is the vineyard of the Father of the household, of which 
<margin>Gregory</margin>
Gregory says in a Sermon: "Our Creator has a vineyard, namely the universal Church, which has produced as many branches as it has brought forth saints, from the righteous Abel <note>Abel, the son of Adam, was considered by medieval theologians to be the first member of the Church.</note> even to the last elect person who shall be born at the end of the world." Ambrose speaks of her on his own (in *Case 23, Question 1*): "What house is more worthy of the entrance of Apostolic preaching than the Holy Church? <meta>This page continues Chapter I of Jan Hus’s treatise "On the Church." Building on the previous page's discussion of the Church's purity, Hus now addresses the specific relationship between Christ and the Church as his "mystical body," emphasizing that this body consists only of the holy and the elect.</meta>

# I. H: ON THE CHURCH

<margin>A sinner is not part of the church of Christ.</margin>
...[not] having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing <note>original: "maculã, neq; rugã" — a reference to the description of the Church in Ephesians 5:27</note>; therefore, he who is a sinner, or stained by any filth, cannot be called part of the Church of Christ.

<margin>The Church is the body of Christ.</margin>
Therefore, that same universal holy Church is the **mystical body of Christ** <term>mystical body: the spiritual union of all believers with Christ, functioning like the organs of a human body under one head</term>, as the Apostle says in Ephesians 1: *He gave him to be the head over all the Church, which is his body.* And in Colossians 1: *He is the head of the body, the Church.* And again: *For his body, which is the Church.* And in Ephesians 5: *Christ is the head of the church, and he is the savior of its body.* And further down: *Christ loved the church and gave himself up for it, so that he might sanctify it, cleansing it with the washing of water in the word of life, that he might present the church to himself in glory, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it should be holy and without blemish.* And the holy Doctors rely on this text.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine, in *On Christian Doctrine*: "Christ is the head of the church, which is his body, destined to be with him in the kingdom and eternal glory."

<margin>Gregory</margin>
Gregory, in the *Moralia*, Book 35, Chapter 9: "Because Christ and the Church are the same—head and body—they are one person." And in his *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 15: 

<margin>Bernard</margin>
"The Church is one substance with Christ its head." And Bernard, in his 12th *Sermon on the Song of Songs*, says: "The Church is the body of Christ, dearer [to him] than that [physical body] which he gave up to death."

<margin>Paschasius</margin>
And Paschasius, in his book *On the Sacrament of the Body of Christ*, says just as it is found in the holy scriptures: "The Church of Christ, or the bride of God, is called the body of Christ, certainly because the general Church of Christ is his body, and Christ is the head and all the elect <term>elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> are called members. From these, the one body of the Church is gathered into a perfect man, according to the measure of the fullness of Christ. Moreover, the body of Christ—namely the bride of God—is rightly called the church. This is according to what the Apostle says: *And they shall be two in one flesh.* This, he says, is a great mystery in Christ and the church. For if Christ and the Church are in one flesh, they are surely one body, one head, one bridegroom; yet the individual elect are members of one another." Thus says Paschasius. From these sayings of the saints, it is clearly drawn out that the ***holy universal Church is the number of all the predestined, and the mystical body of Christ*** (of which he himself...

## ticular parts. ->CHAPTER II<-

Having said what the universal holy Church is, and that it is only one—just as there is only one number of all the predestined <term>predestined: those chosen by God for salvation from the beginning of time</term>—and that it is spread throughout the world according to its members: it should be known that the holy Universal Church is divided into three parts, namely the Triumphant, Militant, and Sleeping Church.

<margin>The militant Church.</margin>
<insert>The threefold Church</insert>
The militant Church is the number of the predestined while they are journeying here toward their fatherland <note>original: "patriam" — a common medieval theological term for heaven, the true home of the soul</note>. And it is called "militant" because it carries out Christ’s warfare against the flesh, the world, and the devil.

<margin>The sleeping Church.</margin>
The sleeping Church is the number of the predestined suffering in purgatory <term>purgatory: in medieval theology, a place where souls are purified of lesser sins before entering heaven</term>. And it is called "sleeping" because, while existing there, it no longer earns blessedness, since it merited—through God’s preventing and helping grace—to be rewarded in the fatherland after the satisfaction of purgatory.

<margin>The triumphant Church.</margin>
The triumphant Church consists of the blessed resting in the fatherland who, holding fast to the warfare of Christ against Satan, have finally triumphed. However, there will be one great Church made up of all these on the Day of Judgment. And as a sign of this threefold part of the universal church,
<margin>Why the Eucharist is divided into three parts.</margin>
the Doctors <term>Doctors: high-ranking theologians whose teachings are authoritative in the Church</term> say that the sacrament of the Eucharist is divided into three parts. They say the first part, immersed in the liquid sacrament <note>The "liquid sacrament" refers to the consecrated wine, representing Christ's blood</note>, signifies the triumphant church, which is absorbed and inebriated by its dipping into the divine nature. As the Head of the Church says in the Song of Solomon 5 <note>original: "Cant. v." — Canticles or the Song of Solomon</note>, cheering his citizens and fellow-guests: "Drink deeply," <note>original: "Inebriamini"</note> he says, "my dearly beloved." ## CHAPTER II

Having stated what the universal holy Church is, and that it is only one—just as there is only one total number of all the predestined <term>predestined: those whom God has chosen from eternity for salvation</term>—and that it is spread throughout the world according to its members, it must be known that this holy Universal Church is divided into three parts: namely, the Church Triumphant, the Church Militant, and the Church Sleeping.

<margin>The Church Militant.</margin>
The Church Militant is the number of the predestined while they are on their journey here toward their homeland <note>The "homeland" (patria) refers to Heaven.</note>. It is called "militant" because it carries out Christ's warfare against the flesh, the world, and the devil.

<margin>The Church Sleeping. <insert>The triple Church</insert></margin>
The Church Sleeping is the number of the predestined suffering in purgatory. It is called "sleeping" because, while existing there, it no longer earns merit for blessedness; rather, by God’s preceding and helping grace, its members earned merit in the present life so that they might be rewarded in the homeland after the satisfaction of purgatory.

<margin>The Church Triumphant.</margin>
The Church Triumphant consists of the blessed resting in their homeland, who, having maintained Christ’s warfare against Satan, have finally triumphed. However, there is one great Church made up of all these on the Day of Judgment. As a sign of this threefold division of the universal Church, the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" are the authoritative theologians of the medieval Church, such as Thomas Aquinas or Peter Lombard.</note> say that the sacrament of the Eucharist is divided into <margin>Why the Eucharist is divided in three ways.</margin> three parts. But in the Incarnation, he celebrated a second wedding, creating a certain queenly part of the whole Church, which by a certain distinction is called the Christian Church. For then our familiar leader and law-giver, addressing his bride—as the Apostle says in Hebrews 1—takes up our armor <note>original: "inducit arma nostra"; a metaphor for Christ taking on human nature as a weapon against sin</note> through the assumption of humanity. Therefore, all Christian doctrine stands upon that prayer of the Church, in which we ask the groom, through his coming in the flesh, to teach us to despise earthly things and love heavenly ones. To despise <note>original: "despicere"</note> means to set them aside in our affection, and to love Christ the groom above all things.

<margin>The Apostolic Church.</margin>
From these things, it is clear that the universal holy Church is the unique bride of Christ, a virgin who is ultimately most chaste, whom the Son of God joined to himself in marriage out of eternal love and the grace of adoption. This is the Church we firmly believe in when we say in the Creed, "I believe in one holy Catholic Church" <note>original: "Credo unam sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam"</note>, and to which is added in the second creed <note>The Nicene Creed.</note>, "and Apostolic." It is called "Apostolic" because the apostles are full members, purified in the Spirit, of that same Mother Church, which they themselves planted with the doctrine of Christ and their own blood. By their doctrine and the authority of their <term>Vicars: earthly representatives or successors, specifically the bishops and popes</term>, they now rule this young maiden as she seeks the groom of the Church. And thus the Decretals <note>A collection of canon laws; here referencing Gratian’s Decretum, C. 23, q. 1.</note> speak. Pope Leo, it says, warns us to seek a privilege wherever a judgment is brought from his own equity. For he himself resides in heaven, seeing and providing that which God binds and looses. Hence Boniface VIII, in the <term>Extravagant: a decree added to the official body of canon law</term> decree, says: "One is compelled by the urgency of faith to believe in and to hold to one holy Catholic Church, and she herself Apostolic" <note>A reference to the famous 1302 bull "Unam Sanctam" regarding the unity of the Church.</note>.

### Objection: that every Christian, even the foreknown or those finally to be damned, is a part of the church. An elegant solution to this objection through notable points. CHAPTER III

<margin>Matthew 13. Gregory: The Church as a Drag-net.</margin>
But against what has already been said, it is first objected that if that opinion stands, no <term>foreknown person</term> <note>original: "praescitus"; a technical theological term for someone whom God knows will ultimately reject salvation and be damned</note> would be a part of the holy mother universal Church. This consequence is seen as false, since every Christian is part of that Church, according to Matthew 13: *The kingdom of heaven is like a net thrown into the sea, which gathers fish of every kind.* Regarding this, the Blessed Gregory says in his Homilies: "The holy Church is compared to a net thrown into the sea because it is committed to fishers, and through it, everyone is drawn from the waves of the present age toward the eternal kingdom, lest they be submerged in the depths of eternal death."

**Why Christ is called and is the head of the church.**

Furthermore, it should be noted that Christ is called the "Head of the Church" because he is the most noble person of the human race, bestowing <term>motion and sense</term> <note>In medieval biology, the head was thought to "flow" life-force and sensation into the rest of the body; Hus uses this as a metaphor for spiritual grace</note> upon all its members. Without his influence, it cannot live or feel. ### CHAPTER III B

<meta>catchword: unt</meta>

...for grace to precede, which is the principle of ministering among the clergy and of working among the laity. The Spirit, moreover, gives grace, the Lord receives the ministry, and God requires that ministry. To one, he says, is given through the Spirit the **word of wisdom**; to another, indeed, the **word of knowledge** according to the same Spirit. To another, **faith** in the same Spirit; to another, the **grace of healing** in the one Spirit; to another, the **working of miracles**; to another, **prophecy**; to another, the **discernment of spirits**; to another, **kinds of tongues**; to another, the **interpretation of speeches**. And these nine the Apostle seems to express consequently in their order among the men who receive those gifts. "God," he says, "has placed some in the church: first **apostles**, second **prophets**, third **teachers**, then **miracles**, thereafter the **graces of healing**, **helps**, **administrations**, **kinds of tongues**, and **interpretations of speeches**," <note>original: "interpretationes sermonum"</note> which nine roles seem to be adapted to the nine gifts mentioned previously. And in that same place, making a comparison between the body of the Church and its members to the natural body of a man, the Apostle says: "For just as the body is one and has many members, but all the members of the body, though they are many, are one body, so also is Christ."

<margin>**The conformity and difference of the human body to the mystical body of Christ.** <insert>Beyond the part of the body, it speaks to us.</insert></margin>

Moreover, a threefold correspondence and a threefold difference between the members of the <term>mystical body</term> <note>The "Mystical Body" (Corpus Mysticum) is the theological term for the Church as a spiritual organism united to Christ</note> and the human body is to be noted. First, just as members constitute one body to which the soul is joined. And again: just as every member is necessary to every other, since they help each other reciprocally in their duties, so it is with the members of the church, by the power of communion and the bond of charity. Thirdly, indeed, just as the members conduct themselves in their own governance, so also do the members of the Church. Since, according to <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>Referring to the *Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum*, a widely read commentary in the Middle Ages attributed to St. John Chrysostom, though modern scholars believe it was written by an anonymous Arian author</note> in the *Incomplete Work*, "man is a certain book in which the whole Christian religion is inscribed." Just as, therefore, there is an affinity of the head to the feet, so reason and affection are connected.

<margin>**Without contention over superiority.**</margin>

Just as also every member, noble or ignoble, serves the spirit without contention. So every member of the church serves Christ without contention over superiority and obedience. And just as the preeminent members do not boast of their nobility, but act...

<summary>Hus uses St. Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians to argue that the Church functions like a human body, where different spiritual gifts (like wisdom, healing, or prophecy) correspond to different roles (like apostles or teachers). # I. HUS ON THE CHURCH

...the Son of God, whom the Roman leaders condemned to a most shameful death. <note>original: "filius dei, Roma. pri. morte turpissima condemnarunt." Hus is likely drawing a parallel between the institutional condemnation of Christ and the institutional pressures of the 15th-century Church.</note>

<margin>
We are made members of the church not by human election, but by divine predestination.
</margin>
It must be noted further that no physical place or human election makes one a member of the holy universal Church; rather, it is divine predestination, with respect to anyone who perseveringly follows Christ in love. <margin><insert>What predestination is</insert></margin> According to Augustine in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, predestination is the "election of the divine will through grace." <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD) was a foundational North African theologian. Hus relies heavily on Augustine’s view that God chooses the "elect" by His own sovereign will.</note> Or, as is commonly said: Predestination is the preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future. <margin><insert>Two types of predestination</insert></margin> Moreover, it is stated in the *Treatise on Penance* <term>Treatise on Penance: *De Poenitentia*, a section of the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard collection of canon law in the Middle Ages</term>, distinction 4, in the section "Hence the Prophet," that there is a two-fold predestination. The first is that by which someone is pre-ordained here to righteousness and to receive the remission of sins, but not to obtain the life of glory; the second definition mentioned above does not apply to this type of predestination. The other type is the predestination by which someone is predestined to obtain eternal life in the future. The first type follows from this second type, but not the other way around. For if anyone is predestined to eternal life, it follows by consequence that they are predestined to righteousness. And if they achieve eternal life, they have consequently achieved righteousness—but the reverse is not true. For many become participants of righteousness in the present, but because of a failure of perseverance, they do not become participants of eternal life. Hence, in the *Treatise on Penance*, distinction 4, in the section "These things therefore," it is said: "Many seem predestined by the merit of their present righteousness, but they are not predestined to eternal radiance." Gratian <note>Gratian was a 12th-century legal scholar known as the father of Canon Law.</note> founds this position on the word of the Apostle in Ephesians 1: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavens in Christ. Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love; who predestined us to be adopted as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace, by which he has made us accepted in his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood and the remission of sins." <note>Hus quotes Ephesians 1:3–7 to support his claim that the true Church is composed of those "chosen... before the foundation of the world," rather than those chosen by human officials.</note>

<summary>Jan Hus argues that membership in the true Church is determined solely by God’s eternal predestination rather than human appointment or institutional status. He distinguishes between those who are temporarily righteous and those who are eternally chosen for salvation.</summary>

### CHAPTER III

<margin>There are two ways humans belong to the church.</margin>
It appears further that there are two ways humans can be of the holy mother Church: first, according to predestination <term>predestination: the theological concept that God has ordained from eternity who will be saved</term> to eternal life, which is how all who are finally holy belong to the holy mother Church; or second, according to predestination only to present righteousness <note>original: "iustitiam"</note>, as is the case for all who receive the grace of the remission of sins but do not ultimately persevere.

<margin>Two kinds of grace.</margin>
It appears further that there are two kinds of grace. First is the grace of predestination to eternal life, from which one who is pre-ordained cannot finally fall away. The other is grace according to present righteousness, which is present now and absent at another time, for it is sometimes gained and sometimes lost. This first grace makes one a child of the holy universal Church and makes a person, in a sense, infinitely more perfect than the second, because it bestows an infinite good to be enjoyed forever, whereas the second does not. The first makes one an heir to an eternal inheritance, while the second makes one an official accepted by God for a time.

<margin><insert>Paul</insert></margin>
Therefore, it seems probable that just as Paul was at once a blasphemer <note>original: "blasphemus"</note> according to his present injustice and yet a member of the holy mother Church—and with this, faithful and in grace according to his predestination to eternal life—so too Iscariot <note>original: "Scarioth"</note> was at once in grace according to <margin>How Judas was of the church</margin> present righteousness and yet never a member of the holy mother Church according to predestination to eternal life. Since he lacked that predestination, Iscariot, although he was an apostle or a bishop chosen by Christ—which is a name of an office <note>Hus argues that holding a high office like Bishop or Apostle does not guarantee one is a true member of the spiritual Church.</note>—was nevertheless never a part of the holy universal Church. Similarly, Paul was never a member of the devil, even though he performed certain acts similar to the acts of the church of the malignant. <margin><insert>Peter</insert></margin> Likewise Peter, who fell into a grave perjury <note>This refers to Peter's denial of Christ three times.</note> by the Lord's permission so that he might rise up stronger; for in such sins, as Augustine says, it is beneficial for the predestined to fall. <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD) was a foundational Church Father whose views on grace and predestination Hus follows closely.</note>

<margin>A two-fold division from the church</margin>
It appears from these things that there is a two-fold division from the holy Church. The first is permanent <note>original: "indeperdibilis," literally "not to be lost"</note>, which is how all the foreknown <term>foreknown: *præsciti*, those whom God knows will ultimately reject Him and who are not predestined for heaven</term> are divided from the Church. The second is temporary <note>original: "deperdibilis"</note>, which is how some heretics are divided from that same holy Church through a sin that can be lost.

<unclear>Christ the principal head</unclear>

From the points already noted, it is first concluded that Christ alone is the head of the universal Church, who is not merely a part in relation to another part. This is evident because if anyone is the head of that universal church, then he has been made better than the angels and every created blessed spirit—a status that belongs to Christ alone. <note>original: "solũ Christo competit"</note> According to Hebrews 1: It is necessary for Him to be the firstborn among many brothers. Also, according to Colossians 1, He must consequently be the captain by the dignity of the right of the firstborn. This deduction is clear through the Apostle in Colossians 1 <note>The author attributes this quote to Colossians, though it contains elements from Ephesians 1:20–23.</note> where he says: That God worked in Christ, raising Him from the dead, and seating Him at His right hand in the heavens above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age, but also in the one to come; and He put all things under His feet, and gave Him as head over the whole church, which is His body. 

From this it is clear that if any Christian were to be the head of the universal church along with Christ (since the church <margin>The church cannot be two-headed.</margin> cannot be a monster having two heads of equal status, as is stated in the *Extravagantes* of Boniface VIII, <note>A collection of canon law; specifically referring to the famous papal bull *Unam Sanctam* (1302) which asserted papal supremacy.</note> beginning "Unam Sanctam." Therefore, he says, "of the one church, there is one body and one head, not two heads like a monster") then one would have to grant that the Christian who was the head of that Church was actually Christ. Or, alternatively, one would have to grant that Christ would be inferior to him and a humble member of him. Since this is impossible, the conclusion is evident. 

Whence the holy Apostles harmoniously confessed themselves to be servants of this Head and humble ministers of the Church, His bride. <margin><unclear>The Apostles are servants of the church of Christ</unclear></margin> For never did any of the Apostles presume to assert that he was the head or the bridegroom of the said Church, because this would be to commit adultery with [the queen...] <note>original: "adulterari cum [regina]"</note>

<summary>Jan Hus argues that Christ is the sole, singular head of the universal Church, citing scripture and canon law to demonstrate that a "two-headed" church would be a monstrosity. He emphasizes that the Apostles viewed themselves as servants, not heads, of the Church.</summary>

...queen of heaven, and to assume the title of dignity and office. Of dignity, regarding eternal predestination, and of office, because by eternal decree God appointed Christ to supremely rule his bride <note>The "bride" here refers to the Church, a common biblical metaphor.</note>. This is also clear through the blessed Augustine in his *Letter to Dardanus*. For he says: "She [the Church] has only one head, namely the one who rules her, who is excellent and provides the example for all, both in spiritual and secular governance."

<margin>
The internal and external head of the church
</margin>
Thus, the "head of the church" can be understood in two ways: either *internal* or *external*. The *internal* head is the principal person of that church, and this functions in two ways: either by presiding over the physical goods of that church, or by ruling over its spiritual goods. The external head is a person presiding over subjects of their own nature, but standing outside their number; when they rule by exerting influence over them, they are called their head. In this way, Christ is the extrinsic head of any particular church and of the universal church according to his divinity; and He is the intrinsic head of the universal church according to his humanity. These two natures—divinity and humanity—are the one Christ, who is the unique head of his bride, the universal church, which is the <term>totality of the predestined</term> <note>Hus defines the true Church not as the visible institution, but as the "praedestinatorum uniuersitas"—all those God has chosen for salvation desde eternity.</note>.

<margin>
John 3
</margin>
For she is the "man who descends from heaven and ascends into heaven," as is said in John 3. This is not said of the whole body itself, but according to its head, whose descent was not a movement from place to place, but rather the incarnation or <term>emptying</term> <note>original: "inanitio." This refers to *kenosis*, the theological concept of Christ "emptying himself" to become human as described in Philippians 2:7.</note>. And the ascent was a local movement, by which He draws the other parts of his body with Him.

<margin>
A particular church can have many subordinate heads.
</margin>
From this it is clear that it is not contradictory for a particular church to have several heads. For it can have three heads: namely, the divinity, the humanity of Christ, and a <term>Captain</term> <note>original: "Capitaneum." Here Hus refers to a human leader, such as a bishop or prelate, who serves as a subordinate head.</note> ordained for its governance by God. But those heads are subordinated: the divinity is the supreme, the humanity of Christ is the middle, and the Captain is the lowest. The universal church, however, as has been said, has two heads: one extrinsic, which is the divinity, and the other intrinsic, which is the humanity.

<summary>Hus distinguishes between Christ's role as the divine (external) and human (internal) head of the Church, defining the true Church as the collective of those predestined for salvation. He argues that while a local church may have a human leader (a "Captain"), the Universal Church has only one head: Christ.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Christ as the external and internal head.</margin>
And it further appears from these points that Christ, from the very beginning of the world, was the external head of the church according to his divinity until the incarnation. From the incarnation, however, he is the internal head of the Church according to his humanity. In this way, the entire holy catholic Church has always had and still has Christ as its head, from whom it cannot fall away, since the Church is a bride bound to her head by perpetual love. For in Jeremiah 31:3, the bridegroom says to the church itself: *I have loved you with a perpetual love, and therefore, pitying you, I have drawn you to myself.* <note>original: "In charitate perpetua dilexi te, & ideo attraxi te miserans."</note> Therefore, the bridegroom was always present to the whole church from the beginning according to his divinity, he who was yet to come for the holy fathers <note>The "holy fathers" refers to the Old Testament patriarchs and prophets.</note> according to his humanity.

queen of heaven, and to assume the title of dignity and of office. Dignity, in respect to eternal predestination; and office, to which by eternal ordination God appointed Christ to rule his bride <note>The "bride" is a traditional metaphor for the Church.</note> with supreme authority.

<margin>Augustine on the One Head</margin>
This is also clear through the blessed Augustine in his letter to Dardanus. For she herself <note>the Church</note>, he says, has only one head, namely the one ruling her, who is supreme and provides the pattern for all, in both spiritual and secular government.

<margin>The internal and external head of the church</margin>
Whence the head of the church can be understood in two ways: either internal or external. **Internal**, as the chief person of that same church, and this in two ways: either that he presides over the bodily goods of the same church, or over the spiritual goods in his governing. The **external head** is a person presiding over subjects of his own nature, but who is outside their number; since he rules them by flowing into them <note>This "flowing" refers to the theological concept of "influx," where grace flows from Christ to the believers.</note>, he is called their head. And so Christ is the external head of every particular church and of the universal church according to his divinity, and he is the internal head of the universal church according to his humanity. These two natures, divinity and humanity, are the one Christ, who is the unique head of his bride, the universal church, which is the university <note>The "university" here means the "totality" or "whole assembly."</note> of the predestined.

<margin><unclear>What the speech...</unclear></margin>
For it is he who is the man who descends from heaven and ascends into heaven, as stated in John 3. <note>original: "Ioan. iij." Referring to John 3:13.</note> This is not according to the whole of himself but according to the head, whose descent was not a change of location, but rather the incarnation or the "emptying out" <note>Hus uses the term "inanitio," referring to the *kenosis* or Christ emptying himself to take on human form.</note>. And the ascent was a change of location, by which he draws the other parts of the body with him.

<margin>A particular church can have many subordinate heads.</margin>
Whence it is clear that it is not contradictory for a particular church to have several heads. For it can have three heads: namely, the divinity, the humanity of Christ, and a **Captain** <note>Hus uses "Capitaneus" to refer to a human leader or prelate like a bishop or the Pope.</note> ordained for it by God for its governance. But those heads are subordinate, because the divinity is the highest, the humanity of Christ is the middle, and the Captain is the lowest. However, the universal church, as has been said, has two heads: one external, which is the divinity, and another internal, which is the humanity.

<summary>Jan Hus defines Christ as the sole head of the universal Church, distinguishing between his divine role as an external ruler and his human role as an internal head. He argues that while local churches may have human leaders ("Captains"), these are always subordinate to Christ's dual-natured headship.</summary>

<margin>Christ as the external and internal head.</margin>

...[Christ] proves that no creature will be able to separate them from the love which is in Christ Jesus, binding his members together inseparably, since the love of predestination never fails; that is, 1 Corinthians 13. Whereupon in Romans 8, the Apostle says: "But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if indeed the spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he is not of him," and he understands this to mean that such a person is not a part of his body.

<margin>An objection concerning a foreknown person existing in grace.</margin>
And if it is objected through these points that a foreknown person <note>The "foreknown" (praesciti) are those who, though they may currently live righteously, are known by God to be headed for eventual damnation.</note> existing in temporal charity possesses this bond, and consequently has a union with Christ; and likewise, a predestined person existing in a state of crime <note>That is, a mortal sin.</note> lacks this bond, and consequently lacks union with Christ. It is clear that just as in the human body there is both "flowing moisture" and "radical moisture," <note>Hus uses medieval medical terminology here. "Radical moisture" (humidum radicale) was thought to be the innate, life-sustaining fluid of an organism, while "flowing moisture" (humidum fluens) was temporary nourishment.</note> so in the mystical body of Christ there is grace according to present righteousness, and there is consummated grace. Whereupon, just as abscesses are attached to the body through flowing moisture but are not truly part of its continuous nature because of their different essence, so it is with the members of the devil, even though for a time they are attached [to the Church] according to present righteousness.

<margin>The predestined possess radical grace.</margin>
The predestined, however, although they may be deprived of flowing grace for a time, nevertheless possess radical grace from which they cannot fall away. And thus the predestined who are currently righteous, possessing a double grace, are bound by a double bond.

<margin>An objection.</margin>
But an objection is raised against these things. For it follows from what has been said that one must concede that the same person is at one and the same time both righteous and unrighteous, faithful and unfaithful, a true Christian and a heretic, in chief grace and **graceless**, <note>original: "ἄχαρις" (acharis). Hus uses the Greek term for someone without grace or favor.</note> and so on regarding other contrary designations, from which a manifest contradiction follows.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
To this it is said that it must be conceded that the same person is at one and the same time righteous and unrighteous, but it is a contradiction for them to be righteous and unrighteous at one and the same time *in the same respect*. Just as it is a contradiction for opposites to exist in the same thing at the same time in the same respect; and thus the aforementioned designations are not contrary because of their equivocation <note>Hus is using a logic term here: "equivocation" means using the same word to mean two different things.</note>, since according to **the Philosopher** <note>This refers to Aristotle, the primary authority on logic in the Middle Ages.</note> only one thing is the opposite of one thing. And so the same...

<summary>Jan Hus uses a medical analogy of "radical" versus "flowing" moisture to explain how the predestined remain part of the Church even when they sin, while the damned are only superficially attached to it. He argues that theological terms like "righteous" can be used in different senses without creating a logical contradiction.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV

<margin>Peter was both righteous and unrighteous at once.</margin>
A man is righteous through the grace of predestination <note>In Hus’s theology, this refers to God’s eternal and unchangeable choice of who will be saved.</note>, and unrighteous from a depraving vice—such as Peter was when he denied Christ, and Paul when he persecuted him. For at that time, they had not fallen away from the love of predestination. Consequently, according to that love, they were in grace and thus righteous; but because they were then in a state of crime <note>A serious or "mortal" sin.</note>, they were deprived of flowing temporal grace <note>The temporary state of being in God's favor, which Hus distinguishes from eternal predestination.</note>, and thus they were unrighteous. And if it is then inferred, "Therefore they were not righteous, and consequently they were [simply] not righteous," this is answered by denying the first conclusion. For a logical move from a specific lack to a total negation is not valid without limitation; as in this case, it follows that Peter and Paul were unrighteous, therefore they were not righteous according to *present* grace, and that conclusion is true. Thus it is truly granted that they were righteous according to the grace of predestination, and they were not righteous according to present grace. Similarly, Paul was faithful according to predestination and unfaithful according to his persecution [of the Church]; he was an Israelite according to predestination and a blasphemer according to present justice; he was in the love of predestination and <term>ἀχάρις</term> <note>original: "acharis", meaning "without grace" or "unpleasant."</note>, that is, without the love of present justice.

<margin>The "not beloved" became "beloved."</margin>
And to confirm this point, Paul’s citation of Hosea in Romans 9 is useful, where it says: "I will call 'not my people' 'my people,' and 'her who was not beloved' 'my beloved,' and 'her who had not obtained mercy' 'one who has obtained mercy.' And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called sons of the living God." Whereupon, they do not understand this scripture and others like it unless they know that there is no contradiction unless opposites are present in the same thing, in the same way, and at the same moment.

<margin>Christ was both dead and alive.</margin>
Therefore, those who know how to examine this matter grant that Christ, during the holy three days <note>The "Triduum," the period between Christ's death on Good Friday and his resurrection on Easter Sunday.</note>, was both dead and alive. Indeed, as Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), a highly influential Bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church.</note> says, he was dying and not dying, because he lived in the spirit and was dead in the flesh; he was dying as a man, and not dying as God. And the Apostle in 1 Timothy 5 says that a widow living in luxury is dead while she lives, because she lives in the flesh but does not live in the spirit; thus it is clear that neither contraries nor contradictions follow [from these statements]. From what has now been said, it is finally clear that

### CHAPTER V: Response to the authorities cited above in the objection.

<margin>What predestination is</margin>
Predestination <term>predestination: God's eternal "blueprint" or decision on who will be saved</term> is the preparation of grace in the present and glory in the future; it is not a position of dignity, nor human election, nor any sensible sign. For no one is a member of that Church unless he is, in his own time, "without spot or wrinkle," <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27, describing the purity of the true Church.</note> and no one should assert without fear or revelation that he is predestined and holy, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore, this is the conclusion.

Do we ever believe that they are without the "spot" of mortal sin or the "wrinkle" of venial sin? <margin>Objection that every cleric is a part of the Church</margin>
But an objection is raised against these points. First, by this: that whoever is a cleric, marked with a "character" <term>character: a spiritual mark believed to be imprinted on the soul during ordination</term> or a sensible sign by a prelate in the reputation of the church, is a part of the Holy Mother Church. For if that whole body is the most principal Bride of Christ, then it is the Church that is "antonomastically" holy, since she is the "one dove" and the "queen standing at the king's right hand," to whom the young virgins shall be brought.

Therefore, just as in the time of the sojourn of the clergy with whom Christ conversed—that same clergy, the high priests, priests, and Pharisees, with their ranks of the priesthood and their observance of traditions which they themselves established, along with their claim that they have God as their father and that they are the seed of Abraham and have never served anyone—even with the high regard of the people, all these things did not make that clergy the "Holy Church" spoken of antonomastically in truth. For Christ said of them in Matthew 15 that the disciples should let them be offended, because "they are blind and leaders of the blind." Thus it stands that a particular multitude of clergy is not the "Holy Church," spoken of antonomastically, simply because that multitude affirms itself to be that Holy Church. And such subtleties are understood by considering what it means to be *in* the church, and what it means to be a *member* or *part* of the church, and that predestination makes one a member of the holy catholic church.

<margin>What predestination is</margin>
Predestination is the preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future; it is not a position of dignity, nor a human election, nor any perceptible sign. Since the devil [Judas] Iscariot—notwithstanding Christ's election and the temporary spiritual gifts <note>original: *charismatibus temporaneis*</note> given to him for the Apostleship or Bishopric, and despite the reputation among the people that he was a true disciple of Christ—was not a true disciple but a wolf covered in sheep's skin, as Augustine says. Consequently, he was not predestined, and thus not a part of the church, the bride of Christ.

From this it is clear that it would be a great presumption to assert, without a revelation or [holy] fear, that one is a member of that holy church. For no one except the predestined is, in his own time, a member of that church "without spot or wrinkle" <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27, describing the purity of the Church.</note>. No one, without fear or revelation, would assert that he himself is predestined and holy, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore, this is the conclusion.

Hence it is truly remarkable with what boldness those most devoted to the world—living more secularly and lawlessly, distanced from the way of life of Christ, and more barren in fulfilling Christ's counsel and commandment <term>counsel and commandment: Hus distinguishes between the basic laws all Christians must follow (commandments) and the higher spiritual path of the clergy (evangelical counsels)</term>—would assert without fear that they are the heads, or the body, or the principal members of the church, the bride of Christ. Do we really believe that they are without the spot of mortal sin <term>mortal sin: a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul</term>, or without the wrinkle of venial sin <term>venial sin: a lesser sin that does not result in complete separation from God</term>, when their abandonment of Christ's counsel, their idleness in holy office, and their works teach us to perceive the opposite? For the Bridegroom of the church says: "By their fruits you shall know them." Matthew 7.

<margin>Objection that every cleric is a part of the church.</margin>
But an objection is raised against these points. First: that any <term>cleric</term> <note>A member of the clergy, such as a priest or bishop.</note> who is marked with a sensible <term>character</term> <note>The "sacramental character" is a theological concept referring to an indelible spiritual mark impressed on the soul during ordination.</note> or sign by a prelate, and is held in the reputation of the church, is a part of the holy mother church; and only the multitude of such clerics is called the church <term>antonomatice</term> <note>original: *κατὰ ἀντονομασίαν* / *antonomatice*. It is argued that we must honor this specific multitude, for otherwise it would follow that Christians would not know their own mother. Indeed, if she were unknown, they would not pay what is corporally due to her, such as offerings and tithes, and a very great confusion would follow in the <term>Church Militant</term> <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christian community currently living on earth, who are "at war" against sin and the devil.</note>.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The response here is made by denying the first part of the argument. For an example is given in Judas, who was elected to the ministry of the Bishopric by Christ—who could not err. Yet he himself, being <term>foreknown</term> <note>original: *praescitus*. In Hus's theology, this refers to those God knows will ultimately be lost/damned, as opposed to the "predestined" who will be saved.</note>, was never a true disciple of Christ, as **Augustine** proves. Rather, he was a wolf covered in sheep’s skin, and was always <term>chaff</term> <note>Refers to the biblical metaphor of wheat and chaff; the chaff is the worthless part of the grain that is discarded.</note>, and a seed of tares or weeds. Similarly, the second part of the argument is denied. For the church "in the truest sense" is the **Bride of Christ**, which is the <term>entirety of the predestined</term>, as has been said. If that entire body is the most principal Bride of Christ, then that body is the church which is holy in the truest sense, since she is the "unique dove" and the "queen standing at the king’s right hand," to whom the young virgins shall be led. 

Therefore, consider the time of the pilgrimage of the clergy with whom Christ lived. That clergy—the high priests, priests, and Pharisees—held the ranks of the priesthood and observed the traditions which they themselves established. They affirmed that they had God as their Father, that they were the seed of Abraham, and that they had never served anyone; this was also the opinion of the people. Yet all these things did not mean that that clergy was the holy church "in the truest sense." For Christ, in Matthew 15, said of them (when the disciples asked if they should be offended) that they are **blind and leaders of the blind.** Thus it stands that a particular multitude of clergy does not become the holy church in the truest sense simply because that multitude affirms itself to be that holy church.

This is evident, because no one is bound to believe anything unless God moves him to believe it. But God does not move a man to believe what is false. For although good may sometimes come from a false faith by occasion, and God may move toward the sustaining of the act [of believing], nevertheless God does not move a man in such a way that he is deceived. If a layman believed of his prelate that he is a holy member of the church, and it were not so, his faith or his belief would be false. ### Just as Christ is the Head of the Elect, so the Synagogue of the Wicked has Satan as its Head — CHAPTER VI

<margin>The Devil is the Head of those who do evil.</margin>
Having spoken of the holy catholic Church, which is the mystical body of Christ, of which He Himself is the head, we must now speak briefly of the "church of the wicked" <note>original: *Ecclesia malignantium*. # CHAPTER VI

Since it is manifest that a thing is not a member or a head except in relation to an entire, whole body, it is clear that there is one body of the devil. However, where the body of Christ is called a "mystical body" <note>original: *corpus mysticum*</note> because of the mystery of the heavenly marriage between Christ and the church, the body of the devil is not "mystical" in this way, but "dark" <note>original: *obscurum*. Hus contrasts the hidden, divine light of the Church's union with the shadowy, chaotic gathering of the wicked.</note>, since being joined to the devil does not suggest a "mystery" directly, but rather a scourge. Thus, that body of the devil has a "natural existence," since according to Augustine in his book *On the Nature of the Good*: "Every evil must be founded in a good." Therefore, every moral evil is founded in the good of nature. And besides this natural existence, that body of the devil has an "existence of vice," just as Christ’s mystical body has an "existence of virtue." For this reason, the Blessed Augustine denies in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 32, that there is one single body composed of the members of Christ and the members of the devil.

And if it is asked: What "form" unites the members of the devil in that body? It is said that there is an "extrinsic form" and an "intrinsic deformity." The <term>extrinsic form</term> <note>The "outer" shaping principle.</note> is the eternal <term>foreknowledge</term> <note>original: *praescientia*. Hus uses this specifically for God's knowledge of those who will ultimately be lost, distinguishing it from "predestination" for the saved.</note> of God, who knows and ordains that all those foreknown as members of that diabolical body shall be bound together for perpetual punishment. The <term>intrinsic deformity</term> <note>The "inner" lack of proper shape or alignment with God.</note>, however, is final disobedience or pride, which the saints call the fault of "final impenitence," or the "sin against the Holy Spirit." And thus, this same sin both joins them together and sets them apart. For it joins the members of the devil together, binding them in <term>Tartarus</term> <note>A classical term for the deepest pit of Hell, frequently used by medieval writers.</note> in their own malice, and it separates them from the company of the blessed. It is just as heat, when dissolving a mixture, gathers together <note>original: τῶ ὁμογενῆ (*to homogene*)</note> **those of the same kind**, because it causes every element of the dissolved mixture to seek its own place. But it separates <note>original: τῶ ἑτερογενῆ (*to heterogene*)</note> **those of a different kind**, because it destroys the harmonious balance, resolving the parts of the mixture into their own separate, simple natures. For on the day of judgment, it must be that because of the opposition between the coldness of the devil's body and the heat of the charity of Christ's body—according to the law of the "ultimate form"—the twofold body will be dissolved. Then the light parts will fly up with their head, which is a consuming fire, to their natural dwellings among the saints. The leaden parts, however, by their affection <note>original: *affectione*. Here meaning the "weight" or "disposition" of their desires.</note>

<margin>Solution.</margin>

From these things it is clear how Christ is the head of all men and how he is the head of the predestined. It is also clear how it is not contradictory even to call the body of the devil (which is the **synagogue of Satan**) the "church of Christ" by reason of his creation, beneficence, and preservation of them, but *not* by reason of a union in charity. In this latter way it is called the Church of Christ "which he loved, so that he might present her to himself as a bride without spot," to be embraced forever. However, which group is more numerous—the Church of Christ or the synagogue of Satan, among men or even among angels—we shall only know after the Lord Christ has performed the final judgment.

### CHAPTER VII

<margin>The question is asked whether the Roman church is the Catholic church.</margin>

Because it has been stated that Christ alone is the head of the holy universal Church, and that all the predestined—past and future—are his mystical body, and each of them is a member of that same body, it remains to be seen briefly if the Roman church is that universal holy church, the bride of Christ. And it seems that it is, because there is only one holy Catholic Apostolic church, and that is none other than the Roman; therefore, the doubt appears true. The first part is made clear by Pope Boniface, who in the *Extravagante* <note>Hus refers to the collection of "Extravagantes," specific papal decrees not originally included in the main body of Canon Law. Here he cites the famous Bull *Unam Sanctam* issued by Pope Boniface VIII in 1302.</note> says: "We are compelled by faith to believe and to hold that there is one holy Catholic church, and it is also Apostolic." And the second part is likewise made clear by the same **Decretal** <term>decretalis - a papal letter or decree used as a legal precedent in Church law</term>, where it is said: "Of the one and only church, there is one body and one head, not two heads like a monster; namely, Christ and Christ’s **vicar** <term>vicarius - one who acts in the place of another</term>, Peter, and the successor of Peter, for the Lord said to Peter: 'Feed my sheep' <note>original: *Pasce oues meas*, from John 21:17.</note>," he said.

[...committed them] generally, not specifically to these or those individuals. It is clear that he is understood to have committed all to him. Whether therefore the Greeks or others claim that they have not been committed to Peter and his successors, they must necessarily confess that they are not among the sheep of Christ; as the Lord says in the Gospel of John, "There shall be one fold and one shepherd." <note>John 10:16. Hus is citing the standard medieval argument for papal jurisdiction over all Christians, including the Eastern Orthodox ("Greeks").</note> Behold, from these points it appears that the holy Roman church is that universal holy Church, because all the sheep of Christ are one fold under one shepherd. And this is the intent of the aforementioned Decretal <note>A "Decretal" is a papal law. Hus is specifically referencing *Unam Sanctam* (1302) by Pope Boniface VIII, which asserted absolute papal authority over all people.</note>, which concludes thus: "Furthermore, we declare, say, and define that it is absolutely necessary for the salvation of every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff." <note>original: *Porro subesse Romano Pontifici omni humanae creaturae declaramus, dicimus & diffinimus omnino esse de necessitate salutis.*</note> If, therefore, every person is by necessity subject to the Roman Pontiff by this definition, it follows that the proposed statement would be true.

To the contrary, the argument is made: the Roman church is the church of which the Pope is the head and the Cardinals are the body, together constituting that church. But *that* church is not the holy Catholic and apostolic church; therefore, the claim is false. The first part is clear through the sayings of certain doctors, among which it is posited that the Pope is the head of the Roman church, and the college of Cardinals is the body. And the second part is manifest from this: that the Pope with the Cardinals is not the "universality of all the predestined." <note>This is a core pillar of Hus's theology: he defines the true "Church" only as the total number of those chosen by God for salvation ("the predestined"), rather than as the visible institutional hierarchy of the Pope and Cardinals.</note>

For the understanding of the present matter, that Gospel must be weighed where Simon Peter said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And Jesus, responding, said to him: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Matthew 16. <note>Matthew 16:16–19. This passage, known as the "Petrine Commission," is the biblical foundation for the authority of the Pope. Hus will proceed to interpret "the rock" not as Peter himself, but as Peter's faith or Christ himself.</note> In this Gospel, the church of Christ, its faith, its foundation, and its power are made known. The Church is noted there: "I will build my church." The Faith is noted there: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
<margin>The Church. Faith.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Chapter VII of Jan Hus’s *De Ecclesia*. On the previous page, Hus presented arguments for the Roman Church’s claim to universal authority. ### CHAPTER VII

G ij

<margin>Foundation. Power.</margin>
...three. The Foundation is found in the passage, "upon this rock I will build." <note>Matthew 16:18: "And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church."</note> The Power is found there: "I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." <note>Matthew 16:19.</note> And concerning these four—namely the Church, Faith, the Foundation, and the Power of the church—we shall briefly touch upon them.

<margin>The Church is spoken of in three ways: first, in the plain sense.</margin>
Regarding the first point, it can be assumed from what was declared above that, besides the church so-called by reputation or by name, the "church" is spoken of in three ways. First, there is a certain congregation or calling together of the faithful in a qualified sense, or for a time, or plainly according to "present righteousness." <note>original: *secundum præsentem iustitiam*. This refers to people who are currently living uprightly and are in a state of grace, regardless of their ultimate salvation or damnation.</note> In this way, the <term>foreknown</term> <note>original: *præsciti*. In Hus's theology, these are people God knows will ultimately be lost, even if they appear holy now.</note> belong to the church for the time they are in grace. However, that church is not the <term>mystical body of Christ</term>, nor the holy Catholic church, nor a part of it.

<margin>Second, in a mixed sense.</margin>
Second, the church is understood in a mixed sense, comprising both the predestined and the foreknown, while they are in grace according to present righteousness. This church communicates in part, but not in its entirety, with the holy church of God. This church is called "mixed," containing both <note>original: *granum & palea, frumentũ & çiçania*</note> grain and chaff, wheat and weeds, the "kingdom of heaven" like a net cast into the sea gathering every kind of fish, and the "kingdom of heaven" like ten virgins, of whom five were foolish and five were wise, as was said above. <note>Hus is referencing various parables from Matthew 13 and 25 to show that the visible church on earth is a mixture of the saved and the lost.</note> Tyconius <note>A 4th-century North African theologian.</note> erroneously called this the "bipartite body of the Lord," as is seen in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 32. <note>Hus is citing St. Augustine's *De Doctrina Christiana*, where Augustine critiques Tyconius's view.</note> For the foreknown are not the body of the Lord, nor a part of it.

<margin>Third, for the predestined; this is the truly Catholic church, an article of faith.</margin>
But in the third way, the church is understood as the calling together of the <term>predestined</term>, <note>original: *prædestinatorum*. Those whom God has eternally chosen for salvation.</note> whether they are currently in grace according to present righteousness or not. In this way, the church is an "article of faith," of which the Apostle speaks in Ephesians 5, saying: "Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish." <note>original: *Christus dilexit ecclesiã...* Ephesians 5:25-27.</note>

<margin>The Church of Christ.</margin>
And the Savior calls this Church *His* church in the cited Gospel, when he says: "Upon this rock I will build my church."

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

<summary>Hus defines three levels of the "Church": the temporary gathering of those currently in grace, the "mixed" visible church of both the saved and lost, and the true "Holy Catholic Church" consisting solely of the predestined.</summary>

->I. H. ON THE CHURCH<-

<margin>The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</margin>
That this <note>Referring to the rock or the foundation mentioned on the previous page.</note> marks out the church is immediately clear from the words that follow: "And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." <note>Matthew 16:18.</note> Since Christ is the rock and the foundation of that church, in whom it is founded according to **predestination** <note>God’s eternal decision on who will be saved.</note>, the church cannot be finally overcome by the gates of hell—that is, by the powers or the assaults of persecuting tyrants or of evil spirits. For Christ, the King of Heaven and the groom of that church, is more powerful than the "prince of this world" <note>The devil.</note>. Therefore, to show His power, foreknowledge, and predestination—by which He powerfully builds, protects, foreknows, and predestines His church—and to give His church hope for perseverance, He added: *And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.*

<margin>Lyra.</margin>
Regarding this, **Lyra** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), an influential Franciscan scholar whose literal biblical commentary was widely respected.</note> says: "From this it is clear that the church does not consist of men by reason of ecclesiastical or secular power or dignity, because many princes and Supreme Pontiffs <note>Popes.</note> and others of lower rank have been found to have apostatized from the faith." Thus he says. This statement is partially evidenced in the apostle and bishop Judas Iscariot, who was also present when Christ said, "Upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against her." For he himself was not built upon Christ the rock according to predestination; therefore the gates of hell finally prevailed against him.

<margin>Peter represented the person of the universal church.</margin>
It seems, moreover, from the aforementioned words of the Lord, that the "church" is understood above all in a special way as all those who, after His resurrection, were to be built up in Him through faith and through "consuming grace" <note>Grace that completes or perfects the believer.</note>. For to Peter—who was representing the person <note>original: *personā*. Acting as a representative or symbol for the whole group.</note> of the universal church and confessing this faith, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"—the Lord spoke in praise: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah." This praise applies to Peter and to the entire holy church, which is "blessed in its journey" <note>original: *beata in uia*. In medieval theology, humans on earth are "wayfarers" (*uiatores*) on a journey to God.</note> at its beginning, by confessing humbly, obediently, courageously, and constantly that Christ is the Son of the living God. Moreover, "flesh"—that is, worldly wisdom—and "blood"—that is, pure philosophical knowledge—did not reveal that faith concerning such a hidden **article of faith**, but...

He uses Judas Iscariot as an example of a high-ranking church official who was not part of the true Church because he was not "built on the rock" of predestination.</summary>
