### CHAPTER VII.

->**G iij**<-

...but uniquely God the Father. Therefore, because of such a clear and firm confession, the Rock <note>Referring to Christ as the "true Rock."</note> said to Peter: "And I say to you, that you are Peter"—that is, the confessor of the true Rock, which is Christ—"and upon this rock which you have confessed, that is, upon me, I will build," through firm faith and through perfecting grace, "my church"—that is, the gathering of the predestined, who after their labor are ordained to glory. Therefore, "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."

Furthermore, it is gathered from the Savior's words that the church is **one** (from the singular word "church"); second, that it is **Christ’s** (from the word "my"); third, that it is **holy** (from the phrase "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it"). From this it is concluded that there is one holy church of Christ, which is called *catholic* <note>original Greek: *καθολικὴ*</note> in Greek (meaning "universal" in Latin) and *apostolic* <note>original Greek: *ἀποστολικὴ*</note> (meaning "pertaining to the Apostles"), because it was strengthened and founded upon the rock of Christ by the words and deeds of the Apostles, as Jerome says in the prologue to his commentary on the Apocalypse. From this I assume that it is called the Holy Roman Church. 

For the Decree <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Canon Law for the medieval Church.</note> (Distinction 21) says: "Although the one bridal chamber of Christ is the universal <term>catholic</term> <note>From the Greek word for universal.</note> Church throughout the world, nevertheless the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church has been placed above other churches by many synodal decrees," which it proves by that passage from Matthew 16: "You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." 

<margin>The church having no stain is not the pope with the cardinals.</margin>

And that church it later calls the Roman Church, the primary seat of the Apostle, "not having stain or wrinkle." <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:27, often used to describe the purity of the true Church.</note> This church cannot be understood as *this* Pope with *these* Cardinals and his household. Thus, the gloss <note>The "Ordinary Gloss," a standard commentary used by medieval law students and theologians.</note> on this text says: "The argument is," it says, "that wherever there are good people, there is the Roman Church." And this argument would give full confidence to the faithful in knowing where the Roman Church is. And so the Decree (Cause 24, Question 1, *A recta*) is understood. There, the canon speaks of the Roman Church in this way: "This is the holy and apostolic mother of all churches, Christ's church, which by the grace of God Almighty is proven never to have wandered from the path of apostolic tradition, nor [yielded] to heretical novelties—"

# JAN HUS ON THE CHURCH

<margin>
The Pope can err
</margin>
...succumbed to being corrupted. Where it is noted, this cannot be understood of any Pope and his household; therefore, the <term>gloss</term> <note>The "Ordinary Gloss" was the standard legal commentary written in the margins of Canon Law books to explain the text.</note> speaks. I ask, therefore, which church do you understand as the one that cannot err? For it is certain that the Pope can err, as seen in <note>original Latin: "xix. d. Anastasius, & .xl. d. Si Papa"</note> Distinction 19, *Anastasius*, and Distinction 40, *Si Papa*. Therefore, neither he nor his family is that church of which it is said here that it cannot err. Hence the gloss says: "The congregation of the faithful itself is called this church." And this will also be understood as the saying of Blessed Jerome placed in <note>original Latin: "xxiiij. q. i. Hæc est fides"</note> Question 24, Case 1, *This is the Faith*. "The Roman Church is holy," he says, "which has always remained immaculate, the Lord providing and the Blessed Apostle Peter bringing help; it will remain in the future without any insult from heretics, and will persist as the first and immovable through all time." This cannot be understood as referring to any Pope with his college of Cardinals. For they are more often stained by wicked deception and sin, as in—

<margin>
A woman was Pope. In the year of our Lord 858.
</margin>
—the time of Pope John, an English woman, who was called Agnes <note>original: "Hagna." Hus is referring to the medieval legend of Pope Joan, which was widely accepted as historical fact in the 15th century.</note>. How then did that Roman Church—that Agnes, Pope John, with her college—always remain immaculate, she who gave birth? And the reasoning is the same for other Popes who were heretics and were deposed on account of multiple enormities.

<margin>
The Roman Church has primacy, but it is not the whole mother and universal church.
</margin>
Since, therefore, according to the Decrees, the Roman Church has primacy and dignity before God over all others, it is clear that she is the total <term>militant church</term> <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the body of Christian believers currently alive on earth, as opposed to those in heaven or purgatory.</note>, which God loves more than any of its parts. And so it follows clearly from the faith that not that college [of Cardinals], but the whole mother dispersed among every nation and language is that holy Roman Church of which the Laws speak along with the holy doctors. Hence, to impress this sentiment upon us through the blessed Augustine and Ambrose, this song was ordained for the church: "The holy church throughout all the world <note>original: "Te per orbem terrarum sancta confitetur ecclesia"</note> confesses you" <note>A line from the *Te Deum*, one of the most famous hymns in the Western Church.</note>. And in the <term>Canon of the Mass</term> <note>The central and most sacred prayer of the Eucharistic liturgy.</note> we offer first and principally for the "holy catholic Church," that God may deign to pacify, guard, and unite it throughout the whole world. Hence there is no doubt that prayer is offered for the most principal militant church, which he supposes...

### CHAPTER VII

<meta>catchword: was.</meta>

<margin>
The Pope with his college is the principal part of the church in dignity.
</margin>
...to be the Roman Church. However, among its parts, in a comparison of greatness, the Pope and his college <note>The "college" refers to the College of Cardinals.</note> are the principal part in dignity, provided that they follow Christ more closely; and by abandoning pride and the ambition of primacy, they serve their mother <note>The Church</note> more effectively and humbly. For by doing the opposite, they are turned into an idol of desolation <note>original Latin: "desolationis idolum." This is a biblical reference to the "abomination of desolation," signifying a corrupting or pagan presence within a holy place.</note>, and into a college contrary to the humble college of the apostles and of the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>
The Roman, Antiochian, Alexandrian, and Constantinopolitan Churches.
</margin>
It should be noted, however, that the Roman Church was properly called the congregation of Christ's faithful existing under the obedience of the Roman Bishop. Just as the Antiochian church was called the congregation of Christ's faithful under the bishop of Antioch. And likewise concerning the Alexandrian and the Constantinopolitan churches. In that way, Peter, the Apostle of Christ and Roman bishop, names the church in the last part of 1 Peter, saying to the faithful of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia: "The church which is gathered in Babylon greets you." <note>original Latin: "Salutat uos ecclesia quæ in Babylone collecta est." Hus follows the common medieval interpretation that "Babylon" in 1 Peter 5:13 was a code name for Rome.</note> Look, there "Church" is taken to mean the faithful of Christ who were in Rome with the blessed Peter. Hence also the Apostle <note>Paul</note> called particular churches in that way; for instance, writing from Corinth to the Romans in the last chapter, he says: "All the churches of Christ greet you." And later: "I, Tertius, who wrote this epistle, greet you in the Lord. Gaius, my host, and the whole church greets you." <note>original Latin: "Salutat uos Gaius hospes meus & uniuersa ecclesia." Romans 16:23.</note> There, "the whole church" is understood as all the faithful of Christ who were serving with Paul in Corinth. Likewise, in the first chapter of 1 Corinthians: "To the church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus." And in the first chapter of 1 Thessalonians, Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy say: "To the church of the Thessalonians." And often elsewhere. Thus they are properly called particular churches, each of which is a part of the universal church, which is the Church of Jesus Christ.

<margin>
The Church began in Judea.
</margin>
Moreover, the Christian church took its origin from Judea, and the first was called the Jerusalem church. Hence, in Acts 8 it is said: "And on that day a great persecution arose against the church which was..." <note>The sentence concludes on the following page: "...in Jerusalem."</note>

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument in Chapter VII of "De Ecclesia" (On the Church). # I. H. ON THE CHURCH

<meta>catchword: tic</meta>

...was in Jerusalem, and all were dispersed throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria except for the Apostles. <note>original Latin: "erat Hierofolymis, & omnes difperfi funt per regiones Iudææ & Samariæ præter Apoftolos." This refers to the persecution following the death of Stephen in Acts 8:1.</note>

<margin>The second church of Antioch.</margin>
The second church was the Antiochian church, in which Peter the apostle resided, and there that name, "Christian," first became known. Previously, the faithful were called "disciples" and "brethren," but later they were called Christians. For we read in Acts 11: "Now the apostles and brethren who were in Judea..." <note>original Latin: "Fuerunt autẽ Apoftoli & fratres qui erant in Iudæa."</note> And at the end of the chapter it describes how Barnabas brought Paul to Antioch, and for a whole year they moved within the church and taught a great crowd, so that in Antioch the disciples were first given the name "Christians."

In a second way, the term "Roman Church" is taken to mean whatever Pope exists along with whatever Cardinals there may be, regardless of where they might live, or whether they live well or poorly.

And in a third way, it is used to refer to the Pope alone. However, these two latter definitions have been wrested from scholars <note>Hus is arguing that defining the "Church" as just the Pope or the College of Cardinals is a forced, modern interpretation not found in ancient scripture.</note>. For there is no good reason to call our mother the "Roman Church" on account of pride, or to please the Emperor who endowed the church <note>A reference to the "Donation of Constantine," a document (later proved a forgery) that claimed the Emperor Constantine gave vast lands and secular authority to the Pope.</note>, nor because of the haughtiness of a Pope making a show of imperial power based on his primacy or lordship. Nor, thirdly, should it be used to suggest that every Christian must recur to him, and acknowledge him as the head and most holy father out of necessity for salvation—rather, the term should be used for other reasons.

Since the "Roman Church" is a term instituted beyond what is founded in Holy Scripture, it is enough to have a probable reason for it. <margin>See how much the author has granted to the Roman Church.</margin> For the holy church of Christ flourished first in Jerusalem during the time when the Apostles journeyed and lived with Christ, and afterward in Antioch, and afterward in Rome during the time of the preaching and passion <note>The term "passion" here refers to the martyrdom or suffering and death of the saints.</note> of Peter and Paul. And thus will be understood the saying of the Savior in Matthew 12: "Truly the kingdom of God has come upon you." <note>original Latin: "Profecto peruenit in uos regnũ dei."</note> And that in Luke 17: "The kingdom of God is within you," <note>original Latin: "Regnum dei intra uos est."</note> for wherever the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered.

For although every Christian church began in Judea, and the head of the church, Christ, was martyred in Jerusalem, nevertheless...

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument in Chapter VII of "De Ecclesia" (On the Church). On the previous page, Hus was discussing the different ways the term "Roman Church" is used. He concluded by noting that the Church of Christ is "reasonably" called the Roman Church for specific historical and theological reasons. The text here provides those three reasons.</meta>

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Three reasons why the Church of Christ is called the Roman Church.</margin>
...sonably, the Church of Christ is called the Roman Church according to a certain preeminence, for three reasons. First, because Christ knew that the Gentiles under the Roman Empire were to be brought in to take the place of the Jews who unfaithfully disbelieved, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> says in Romans 9. The second reason is because a greater multitude of martyrs triumphed there than in any other city. For just as a person takes their name from where they are born from the womb and triumph gloriously, so it is here. Since the holy Church was born in Rome according to many of its parts, gathered out of the womb of the Synagogue, and there it triumphed while growing among the Gentiles, it was therefore fitting that it should take its name from the metropolitan city of the Gentiles, which is Rome. Hence in Distinction 22 <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law; the specific canon is *Sacrosancta*.</note>, it is said that Peter and Paul consecrated the holy Roman Church on one and the same day, and they preferred it above all other cities in the whole world both by their presence and by their venerable triumph. The third reason is to make it known that it is not location or antiquity, but <term>formed faith</term> <note>original: "fides formata"; in medieval theology, this refers to faith made complete by love or charity.</note> that founds the Church of Christ. For in regards to persons and time, the Church of Christ existed earlier in prior seats <note>That is, earlier locations like Jerusalem or Antioch.</note>. And in this sense it is said in 2 Maccabees 5: "The Lord did not choose the people for the sake of the place, but the place for the sake of the people." <note>original Latin: "Non propter locum gentem, sed propter gentem locum dominus elegit."</note> 

<margin>The Church of Christ takes names according to various locations.</margin>
And from this, I believe it is permitted to call Christ's Church by the name of whatever place the righteous faithful inhabit. Just as Christ is called a Nazarene because of his conception which took place in Nazareth, and can be called a Bethlehemite because of his birth, and a Capernaumite because of the working of miracles which he performed in Capernaum, and a Jerusalemite because of his most glorious passion.

<margin>A responsive conclusion.</margin>
From what has been said, it is clear what should be said regarding the doubt raised at the beginning of this chapter. For it must be conceded that the Roman Church is the holy mother Catholic Church, the bride of Christ.

<margin>To the argument on the opposite side.</margin>
To the argument on the opposite side—which argues that the Roman Church is the church of which the Pope is the head and the Cardinals the body—it is said in concession, taking "church" in the second sense, namely for...

H
<meta>catchword: ...which [original: "licun"]</meta>

<summary>Hus provides three historical and theological reasons why the "Roman Church" became the preeminent name for the Church of Christ, emphasizing that the Church is defined by faith rather than geography. He concludes that while the Roman Church is the "bride of Christ," this does not strictly limit the definition of "church" to the Pope and Cardinals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument from Chapter VII of "De Ecclesia," where he challenges the idea that the physical institution of the Roman Church (the Pope and his inner circle) is identical to the "Holy Catholic Church" mentioned in the Apostles' Creed. He is responding to a logical argument about whether the presence of a Pope and Cardinals automatically constitutes the true Church.</meta>

-># BOOK IV. ON THE CHURCH<-

...the Pope, along with whatever Cardinals, wherever they may reside. But it is denied that that specific church is the holy catholic and apostolic church. And thus, even if both parts of the argument are granted, the logical consequence is denied. And if it is said: "I posit that the Pope is holy, along with all twelve Cardinals living with him." For regarding the first, that word of Christ is verified: *The gates of hell shall not prevail against it* <note>Matthew 16:18</note>. <margin>Christ, not the Pope, is the head of the church.</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII.

Concerning common faith, one believes implicitly whatever is individually contained under the authority of holy mother church. Similarly, by believing whatever Christ wished to be believed about himself, and by not believing about Christ what he did not wish to be believed about himself, a person in this way believes every article—whether affirmative or negative—that is believable concerning Christ. <meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter VIII regarding the nature of faith. It transitions from the previous discussion on "implicit faith" to defining the specific properties and requirements of faith, as well as how mortal sin represents a fundamental failure of faith.</meta>

# J. H. ON THE CHURCH

<margin>Faith is of the truth.</margin>
For something to be truly believed, two things are necessary for faith. First, truth, which illuminates the mind. Second, authority, which strengthens the soul. From this, we gain one property of faith: that it is concerned only with truth, to the exclusion of falsehood; the believer must defend this truth even unto death.

<margin>Faith is of obscure things.</margin>
The second property of faith is that, lacking direct demonstration and specific knowledge, it is obscure <note>original: *obscura*</note> for the believer, since we do not say we "believe" that which we see with our own eyes. Furthermore, the saints in the fatherland <note>A theological term for Heaven, the final destination of the soul</note> who clearly see those articles of faith which we know only obscurely are not said to "believe" them, but rather to see them. In the place of faith, they possess clear vision, and in the place of hope, they possess perpetual enjoyment.

<margin>Faith is the foundation.</margin>
The third property of faith is that it is the foundation for the <term>wayfarer</term> <note>Latin: *viator*; a common medieval term for a human being currently living on earth, traveling toward eternity</note> to reach the quiet habitation of things to be believed. Therefore, the Apostle says in Hebrews 11: "Faith is the substance"—that is, the foundation—"of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen," namely, to the senses. For we hope for our blessedness and we believe in it, but we do not see it with carnal eyes. And because "without faith it is impossible to please God" (Hebrews 11), it is necessary that everyone who is to be saved must first of all be a believer. Now, a believer is one who possesses faith infused by God, without any contrary trepidation or doubt being mixed into their faith.

<margin>All those in a state of crime are unfaithful.</margin>
Furthermore, all those in a state of crime <note>Those living in "mortal" or serious sin</note> are, according to present justice, unfaithful, since it is impossible for anyone to sin mortally except insofar as they fail in faith. For if a person were to consider the punishment to be inflicted on those so sinning, and fully believed and had faith in divine knowledge—specifically, how God clearly knows all things and is present even then with those sinning—then they would undoubtedly not sin in that way.

<margin>One fails in faith in three ways.</margin>
Moreover, a person can fail in faith in three ways. In the first way, through weakness; and in this way, he fails who wavers in believing and does not persevere until death in the defense of the faith. In the second way, one fails in faith because, while he firmly believes many things that ought to be believed, in many other things to be believed—as if through gaps...

# CHAPTER VIII

...whoever fails in faith, and thus has a shield of faith full of holes <note>original: *scutum fidei foraminosum*</note>.

In the third way, someone fails in faith in the application of that shield. And this happens in this way: that though one may possess a firm habit regarding the articles to be believed, they fail in the act of meritorious work because of a disordered life. Hence, in Titus 1, it is said of them: "They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny Him." Therefore, whoever fails in faith in any of these ways lacks the firmness of faith.

<margin>Faith differs from hope in three ways</margin>
And it must be considered that faith differs from hope. First in this: that hope is only regarding a future reward to be obtained. Faith, however, is about the past—such as that God created the world, that Christ was incarnated, and so forth for other things. It is about the present—such as that God exists, that the saints are in the fatherland <note>Theologians used this term to describe Heaven as the true home of the soul</note>, and that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. It is about the future—such as that Christ will come to judge, that all who have not yet risen will rise on the Day of Judgment, and that God will finally reward with blessedness all the saints who finish this life in grace. Second, hope does not reach the same degree of knowledge as faith regarding that which it hopes for, but rests in a certain middle act between doubt and belief. Hence, many things are to be proposed to the faithful which, setting aside distinctions, they should neither doubt, concede, nor deny, but rather hope for.
<margin>Many things are hoped for which are not to be conceded, denied, or even doubted.</margin>
As if it is proposed to me: "You shall be saved"; I ought not concede it, because I do not know if it is true, nor should I deny it, because I do not know if it is false, nor should I doubt it, but I should hope. Third in this: that hope is only about a present good that is possible for the one so hoping, while faith is about both evil and good. For we believe in the remission of sins, which is a great good for all who are to be saved, and we believe that the sin of blasphemy <note>This refers to the "unforgivable sin" against the Holy Spirit mentioned in the Gospels</note> shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the one to come.

<margin>What it is to believe.</margin>
And because "to believe" is the act of faith, which is to trust, know therefore that to believe—which is necessary for a person's blessedness—is to adhere firmly and without hesitation to the truth as if spoken by God. For the sake of this truth, by reason of its certainty, a person ought to expose their life to the danger of death. And in this way everyone is bound...

# CHAPTER VIII

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s theological treatise "De Ecclesia" (On the Church). The previous page concluded a comparison between faith and hope, establishing that while hope looks to the future, faith encompasses the past, present, and future. This page transitions into a critique of human authority versus divine scripture.</meta>

# JAN HUS ON THE CHURCH

<margin>To what extent one should believe the word of a man.</margin>
A Christian must believe, either explicitly or implicitly, every truth that the Holy Spirit has placed in the Scriptures. In this way, a person is not bound to the sayings of the saints outside of Scripture, nor is one bound to believe papal Bulls <note>Bulls: formal proclamations or edicts issued by the Pope, named after the lead seal (*bulla*) attached to them.</note>, except for what they might say from Scripture, or what is founded implicitly in Scripture. However, a person may believe Bulls as a matter of opinion, because both the Pope and his Curia <note>Curia: the administrative body and court of the Roman Catholic Church in Rome.</note> can be mistaken due to ignorance of the truth. For it is proven of such a court that it deceives and is deceived. Greed deceives the Pope, and he is deceived due to ignorance. Experience, which is the mistress of all things, teaches us how much trust should be placed in the letters of princes, the legal instruments of Notaries, and the stories of men. For experience itself teaches that these things often fail.

<margin>One believes God in one way, and the Pope in another.</margin>
Therefore, one believes God, who can neither be deceived nor deceive, in one way. One believes the Pope, who can both be deceived and deceive, in another way. Thus, one believes the Holy Scriptures in one way, and humanly devised Bulls in another. For it is not permitted to disbelieve or contradict the Holy Scriptures. But it is sometimes permitted both to disbelieve and to contradict Bulls—specifically when they recommend or promote unworthy people, when they savor of greed, when they glorify the unjust and oppress the innocent, or when they implicitly contradict the commands or counsels of God.

From what has already been said, it is clear what kind of faith is the foundation of the Church, in which it is founded and built upon the rock of Christ Jesus: it is that faith which the Church confesses—that Christ is the Son of the living God. For Peter spoke on behalf of all the faithful: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" <note>original Latin: *Tu es Christus filius dei uiui* (Matthew 16:16).</note>. This, says John in the first [letter] of John, chapter 5, is "the victory that overcomes the world: our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?" <note>original Latin: *uictoria quæ uincit mūdum fides nostra...* (1 John 5:4-5).</note>.

### How Christ is the foundation of the church and how the apostles are also its foundations. Also, praise of Peter for his extraordinary virtues, which his vicars ought to imitate.

->CHAPTER IX<-

<meta>catchword: Fun- (Foundation)</meta>

### CHAPTER IX

The foundation, which was the third point in our proposal, was touched upon in that passage: **"Upon this rock I will build my church."** <note>original: "Super hanc petram ædificabo eccleſiam meam." This quote from Matthew 16:18 is the traditional biblical basis for the authority of the Pope as the successor of St. Peter.</note> And because the Popes most frequently use this saying of Christ in their own decrees, wishing to conclude that they themselves are the rock or the foundation upon which the Church stands—just as it was said to Peter, to whom it was spoken: *You are Peter*—therefore, for the understanding of the Lord's word, it must be noted that the foundation of the Church *by whom* it is founded is touched upon in the phrase: **"I will build."** And the foundation *in which* it is founded is touched upon in the phrase: **"Upon this rock."** And the foundation *whereby* the Church is founded is touched upon in the phrase: **"You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."**
<margin>The foundation of the Church: by whom, in what, and through what.</margin>
The foundation by which first and in which first the holy catholic Church is founded is Jesus Christ; and the foundation whereby it is founded is faith, which works through love <note>Galatians 5:6</note>, which Peter set forth, saying: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Christ, therefore, is the foundation of the Church, who says in John 15: "Without me you can do nothing." <note>original: "Sine me nihil poteſtis facere."</note> That is, without me as the first and most principal foundation.
<margin>Christ builds the church upon himself as the rock.</margin>
Moreover, Christ founds and builds his Church upon himself, the rock, while he disposes her to hear and do his words; for then the gates of hell shall not prevail against her. Hence, in Luke 6, Christ says: "Everyone who comes to me, and hears my words, and does them, I will show you to whom he is like. He is like a man building a house deep, who laid the foundation upon rock. And when a flood arose, the river broke against that house, and could not shake it, for it was founded upon rock." And the Apostle Paul shows this foundation in 1 Corinthians 3, saying: "No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." And in 1 Corinthians 10, he says: "And the rock was Christ." <note>original: "Petra autem erat Chriſtus."</note> In this foundation, therefore, and on this rock, and by this rock, the holy Church is founded, because he says: "Upon this rock I will build my church."

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument from Chapter IX of "De Ecclesia." Having established that Christ is the primary foundation of the Church, Hus now uses the writings of the Apostle Paul and St. Augustine to prove that the "rock" mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew refers to Christ himself, or the faith in Christ, rather than the person of St. Peter or his successors.</meta>

# I. M. ON THE CHURCH

<margin>The Apostles built churches upon Christ.</margin>
The Apostles built [the Church] of Christ. For they did not call the people to themselves, but to Christ, who is the first necessary and most effective foundation. Therefore, the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> says: **"No one can lay another foundation."** <note>original: "fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere" — 1 Corinthians 3:11</note> Wherefore the Apostle himself, seeing the Corinthians erring concerning the foundation, rebukes them in the first [letter] to the Corinthians, chapter 1, saying: **"Each of you says, 'I am of Paul,' 'I am of Apollos,' <note>Apollos was a contemporary of Paul and a prominent preacher in the early Church.</note> 'I am of Cephas,' <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for Peter, meaning 'rock'.</note> or 'I am of Christ.' Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?"** As if to say: no. Therefore, neither Peter, nor Paul, nor any other person besides Christ is the principal foundation or head of the Church. Therefore, subsequently in 1 Corinthians 3, the holy Apostle says: **"What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are his ministers in whom you believed, and to each as the Lord gave them to serve the Church. I,"** he said, **"planted,"** namely through preaching, **"Apollos watered,"** namely through baptism, **"but God gave the growth,"** namely through the foundation of faith, hope, and charity. So neither he who plants, like Paul, nor he who waters, like Apollos, is anything—that is, anything upon which the Church could be founded—but he who gives the growth, God himself, is the foundation of the Church. And it follows: **"But let each one see how he builds upon it, for no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus."**

<margin>The Rock.</margin>
Moreover, this foundation is the <term>rock of justice</term> <note>original: "petra iustitiae" — a theological term referring to the unchanging and righteous nature of Christ as the Church's base.</note> of which Christ speaks in the Gospel, saying to Blessed Peter: **"You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church."** Upon which Blessed Augustine, in his 13th sermon on the words of the Lord, says thus: "Our Lord Jesus Christ said to Peter: **'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.'** Upon this rock which you have confessed, upon this rock which you have recognized, saying, **'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,'** I will build my church—that is, upon myself, the Son of the living God, I will build my church; I will build you upon me, not me upon you." For men wishing to be built upon men used to say, "I am of Paul, I [am of] Apollos..."

I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...that the immovable rock might hold together the structure and mass of the entire work of Christ. These are the words of Ambrose, showing that Peter is called the rock <note>original: "petra"</note> [in a secondary sense].

<margin>The Resolution.</margin>
Here I say that the interpretation of Augustine, that most excellent interpreter of Scripture, seems to be—and indeed is—more effective. This is because it is founded on the explicit Scripture which says that Christ is the rock, the cornerstone, and the most effective foundation. However, it is nowhere read explicitly in Scripture that Peter is the rock. Nor did Christ—who could easily have said it—say: "You are the rock, and upon you, the rock, I will build my church." Instead, He said: "You are Peter" <note>original: "Tu es Petrus." Hus is highlighting the distinction between the masculine name *Petrus* and the feminine noun *petra* (rock) used in the Latin Vulgate of Matthew 16:18.</note>—that is, the confessor of the true rock. "And upon this rock which you have confessed, I will build my church."

<margin>The church is built upon Christ through faith, hope, and charity.</margin>
Moreover, Christ builds the church upon Himself through faith, hope, and charity. Therefore, we believe and hope in Christ, and not in Peter; and we ought to have greater charity or love toward Christ than toward Peter. For in this way, the fathers of the Old Testament did not believe or hope in a future Peter, but in the Rock. Similarly, the saints of the New Testament do not believe or hope in Peter, but in Christ, who is the objective focus of our faith and our hope.

<margin>The Apostles are foundations of the church, but in a different way than Christ.</margin>
It must nevertheless be granted that the Apostles are foundations of the church, but not in the same way that Christ is the foundation. For He Himself is the "foundation of foundations," just as He is the "Holy of Holies." Therefore, the blessed Augustine, commenting on that Psalm, *His foundations are in the holy mountains* <note>Psalm 87:1 (Vulgate 86:1).</note>, shows that Christ is the principal foundation and cornerstone of the city of the New Jerusalem—the city of Zion—and the mountains are the Prophets and Apostles in whom the foundations of the Church are found. He says: "You should know that Christ is the foundation, both the first and the greatest." The Apostle says, "For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ." <note>1 Corinthians 3:11.</note> How then are the Prophets and Apostles foundations, and how is Jesus Christ the foundation, beyond whom there is nothing further? How do we think of this? For just as He is openly called the Holy of Holies, so figuratively...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter IX from the previous page, further developing Hus’s argument that Christ is the primary foundation of the Church, while the Apostles and Prophets serve as secondary foundations through their faith and testimony.</meta>

### CHAPTER IX

->The Foundation of Foundations.<- Therefore, if you consider the sacraments, Christ is the Holy of Holies <note>original: "Sanctus Sanctorum"</note>. If you consider the flock placed under him, Christ is the Shepherd of shepherds. If you consider the building, Christ is the Foundation of foundations. And afterwards, showing the reason why the Prophets and Apostles are called the foundations of the structure of the city of Jerusalem: why are the Prophets and Apostles foundations? It is because their authority carries our weakness. Why are they the gates? Because we enter through them, and we enter through Christ, for He himself is the door <note>original: "ianua"</note>. And the twelve gates of Jerusalem are spoken of, and Christ is the one gate; and the twelve gates are Christ, because Christ is in the twelve gates. This is what Augustine says. 

And the gloss <note>A "gloss" is a standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> on that word in Revelation 21: "The wall of the city having twelve foundations," says this refers to the prophets, in whose faith the Apostles were founded; for faith followed from the prophets into the Apostles, and the same preaching of the Apostles drew its credibility from the prophets, who said the same thing. Or, let us understand the foundations to be the Apostles, in whom the entire defense of the church is founded. Also in the same place: "The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone, and the first foundation was jasper." The gloss says: the foundations—that is, the prophets or Apostles—were adorned within themselves with every kind of virtue.

<margin>How Christ is the foundation of the church, and how the apostles are foundations.</margin>

Behold, from these points it is clear how Christ is the foundation of the church, and how the Apostles are foundations. Christ is the foundation by authority, who begins from Himself, and in Him the constitution of the church is finished, and through Him it is completed. But the Prophets and Apostles are foundations because their authority carries our weakness. And Ambrose also intends this meaning in his saying: That Peter is called the rock <note>original: "petra"</note> for this reason: that he was the first to lay the foundations for the imitators of the faith; and like an immovable stone—meaning by his final constancy—he holds together the structure and the mass of the entire work of Christ. But the foundation upon which the church is founded in Christ is the faith which Peter confessed, saying: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And of this foundation, Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 3.

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

According to the grace which has been given to me, as a wise architect I have laid the foundation, namely teaching the faith of Christ. And it follows: *But another builds upon it*, that is, he performs good works upon the foundation of faith. *But let each one see how he builds upon it*, namely the spiritual life in Christ. For *no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus.* But if anyone builds upon this foundation **gold**, that is, the doctrine of the deity and of heavenly things; **silver**, that is, the doctrine of humanity and of created things; **precious stones**, that is, the virtues adorning the soul and its powers—he is without doubt founded in Christ Jesus. The Apostles built in this way: while fervently and clearly teaching the doctrine of the deity, humanity, and the virtues, and living in the flesh, they planted the church of Christ with their blood. However, which of them might have built more upon Christ, or more fully planted the church in Christ, we shall without doubt only know when, by the Lord’s grace, we come to the fatherland <note>original: "patriam," a common medieval term for heaven, the true home of the soul</note>. It is granted, however, that Peter received his humility, poverty, firmness of faith, and consequently his blessedness from the Rock <note>original: "petra"</note> of the church, which is Christ.

But regarding that word of the Gospel, *Upon this rock I will build my church* <note>Matthew 16:18</note>, the idea that Christ intended to build the entire militant church <term>militant church: the community of believers currently living on earth, as opposed to those in heaven</term> upon the person of Peter is contradicted by the faith of the Gospel, the explanations of Augustine, and by reason. For it was upon the Rock—which is Christ, from whom Peter received his firmness—that Christ was going to build his church, since Christ is the head and foundation of the whole church, and not Peter.

<margin>Peter is not the head of the church, but the captain of the apostles.</margin>
Assuming what we have said in chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4—that there is only one holy universal church, which consists of all those predestined to be saved, and that Christ alone is the head of that church, just as He alone is the most worthy person in that church, granting movement and feeling for the life of grace to it and its members—then it is manifest that Peter was not, nor is he, the head of the holy catholic church. And the statement of the Blessed Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> is true: that Peter was the "captain" among the Apostles and was a foundation of the churches, as was said recently regarding the Apostles. And Augustine's statement is also true, that Peter was the first among the Apostles according to a certain prerogative. And Marcellus's statement is true, that Peter was the "head" of the entire church, which he ruled by doctrine and example. He was not, however, a person more worthy than the mother of Christ, nor was he equal to Christ, nor was he appointed the ruler of the angels, who at that time constituted the triumphant church. <term>triumphant church: the assembly of the saved and the angels in heaven, as opposed to the "militant church" on earth.</term>

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

<margin>Peter did not dare to assert himself as head of the church.</margin>
Hence, there is no doubt for the simple believer that Peter did not dare to assert that he was the head of the holy catholic church, for the reason that he did not rule the whole of it, nor did he surpass it so far in dignity, nor was he the spouse of that same catholic church. John the Baptist—of whom the Truth <note>original: "ueritatis"; a common medieval way to refer to Christ, who is "the Way, the Truth, and the Life."</note> testified in Matthew 11, saying: "Among those born of women there has not risen one greater"—did not dare to call himself the spouse of the church, but instead humbly confessed himself to be a friend. Hence, in John 3, when his disciples were zealous on his behalf and said: "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him." John answered and said: "A man can receive nothing unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear witness to me that I said, 'I am not the Christ,' but that I have been sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom. It is enough for me that I am the friend of the bridegroom, standing and hearing with joy the voice of the bridegroom," which says in John 15: "You are my friends if you do what I command you." And it is clear that it would be an excess of presumption and folly for any man other than Christ to call himself the head or the spouse of the holy catholic church.

<margin>Three virtues excelled in Peter.</margin>
<margin>The first: Faith.</margin>
Furthermore, the reason why Christ established Peter as the captain and pastor after himself was the preeminence of the virtues required to rule the church. For otherwise, the Wisdom of the Father <note>original: "sapientia patris"; a title used for Christ as the second person of the Trinity.</note> would have acted unwisely in establishing him as the bishop of his church. And since all moral virtues are generally connected, it is clear that Peter possessed a certain preeminence in every kind of virtue. However, there were three virtues in which Peter especially excelled: Faith, humility, and charity. Faith, which must be the foundation of the church, excelled first in Peter, for which reason the best Teacher <note>original: "magister optimus"; referring to Christ.</note> ordained in Matthew 16 that, in response to the question he asked concerning himself—"Who do people say the Son of Man is?"—Peter should answer on behalf of all. He said: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." In this, he confessed the humanity in Christ, by which he signified

Peter was more prepared to suffer martyrdom because of his denial of the Master; and especially because, recognizing his own weakness from that denial, he had a fresher memory of his own fragility. <margin>The Vicar of Peter ought to walk in the ways of Peter.</margin>
If the one called the Vicar of Peter walks in these aforementioned paths of virtue, we believe that he is his true vicar and the chief Bishop of the church which he rules. But if he walks in contrary ways, then he is the messenger of Antichrist, contrary to Peter and the Lord Jesus Christ.

This saint knew that Pope Eugenius ought to be a vicar in poverty and humility, not in pride, but in the feeding of the sheep, following Peter. For he is a true vicar of that man whose place he takes, and from whom he legitimately receives the power of a proxy.

<margin>He who truly acts in the place of Christ</margin>

But no one truly and acceptably to Christ acts in the place of Christ or of Peter, unless he follows him in character, since no other following is relevant; nor does he receive the power of a proxy from God under any other condition. And therefore, for such an office of 

<margin><unclear>True Christ[ian]</unclear> <unclear>...</unclear></margin>

vicar, both conformity of character and the authority of the institutor are required. And to this, the Savior, commending the institution of the venerable Sacrament at the Last Supper and appointing the disciples as vicars for this purpose—that they should do this in his memory—said in John 13: "I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you should do likewise." And in Matthew 5: <note>The OCR says "Matth. xj" (Matthew 11), but the quote "He who does and teaches" is from Matthew 5:19.</note> "He who does and teaches, this man shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." Wherefore, regarding this, St. Jerome says to Heliodorus—and it is placed in the *Decretum*, distinction 40: <note>The "Decretum Gratiani" is a collection of Canon Law compiled in the 12th century, which became a standard legal textbook.</note> "It is not easy to hold the seat of the saints Peter and Paul, who reign with Christ, because it is said to this man: They are not the sons of the saints who hold the places of the saints, but those who practice their works." And St. Gregory says the same: "Neither places nor ranks make us close to our Creator, but either our good merits join us to him, or our bad ones separate us."

# CHAPTER IX

<margin>
Many are priests in name, but few in deed.
</margin>

Likewise, Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> says: Many are priests, and yet few are priests; many in name, but few in deed. See to it, therefore, how you sit upon the seat <note>original: "cathedra" — the official chair or throne of a bishop or teacher, symbolizing authority.</note>, for it is not the seat that makes the priest, but the priest who makes the seat; the place does not sanctify the man, but the man sanctifies the place. Not every priest is holy, but every holy person is a priest. He who sits well upon the seat brings honor to the seat; he who sits poorly does injury to the seat. Therefore, a bad priest acquires a crime from his priesthood, not a dignity. So says he.

Likewise, in the same place, from the acts of the martyr Boniface <note>This refers to a famous and controversial passage in Canon Law (Decretum Gratiani, Dist. 40, c. 6) attributed to Saint Boniface, which argues that a Pope can be judged if he deviates from the faith or neglects his duties.</note>, it is said: If the Pope, negligent of his own and his brothers’ salvation, is found useless and slack in his works, and moreover silent—which is most harmful to himself and his sheep—he nonetheless leads innumerable people in crowds with himself to the chief domain of Gehenna <note>original: "geennæ" — a term for Hell.</note>, where they shall be beaten with many stripes for eternity along with him. Nor is it necessary to cite many saints, since the High Priest of priests <note>Referring to Jesus Christ.</note> says in John 10: "All as many as came [before me] are thieves and robbers." And in Matthew 5, he says to the disciples: "You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its flavor, with what shall it be salted? It is then good for nothing, except to be cast out and trampled underfoot by men." And in Luke 14, he says: "Salt is good; but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what shall it be seasoned? It is useful neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, but it shall be cast out." And wishing to impress this sentiment upon the minds of men, the most pious Savior and best teacher immediately added: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

Therefore, let every priest see to it if he has entered well, remaining clean from crime, with a sincere intention for the honor of God and the benefit of the church; and if he conducts himself worthily, disregarding worldly honors and the profit of the age. For otherwise he is a liar and an Antichrist <note>original: "Antichristus" — in this context, the author uses the term to describe anyone who acts in opposition to Christ’s teachings, especially those in high office.</note>, and the higher his office, the greater an Antichrist he is. Let the humble traveler look to Christ, who says in John 14: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Behold, he who wishes to go has a way, because Christ is the way. To where he wishes to go, Christ is the truth. And where he wishes to remain, Christ is the life.

E. H. ON THE CHURCH

### On the manifold power of men, and what kind of power was conferred upon Peter and all priests in these words: "Whatever you bind on earth," etc. CHAPTER X

Now we must speak of the power of Christ, which was handed down by him to his **Vicars** <note>original: "Vicarijs" — those who act as representatives or deputies of Christ, specifically the Pope and the clergy.</note>. This is touched upon in the passage: *I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven*, which is to say, the power of binding and loosing sins, as Augustine says in the final question on John. The effect of this power is demonstrated when Christ adds: *And whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.*

<margin>Spiritual power.</margin>
And because the aforementioned power is a **spiritual power**, it should be noted that spiritual power is the power of the spirit, ordered by itself immediately so that a rational creature may be directed according to the **goods of grace** <note>Spiritual gifts or virtues that come from God, rather than through nature.</note>. Moreover, every man is a spirit, since he consists of two natures, as the Savior says in Luke 9, speaking to his disciples: *You do not know of what spirit you are.* And in the first epistle of John, chapter 4, it is said: *Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God.* <note>original: "Omnis spiritus qui soluit Iesum" — This is a Latin Vulgate reading of 1 John 4:3, often interpreted as referring to heretics who "divide" Christ's humanity from his divinity.</note> In that passage, "spirit" refers to a subtle heretic who denies that Jesus is true God and true man. Thus it is clear that—whether power is related by analogy to God and rational creatures, or restricted to the powers of men and angels—it is true that every spiritual power is the power of a spirit. And although a man does not give grace himself, he nevertheless administers the **sacraments**, so that the subject may be directed according to the goods of grace.

<margin>Corporal power.</margin>
**Corporal power** <note>Physical or earthly authority.</note>, however, although it exists for the sake of the goods of grace, is nevertheless immediately concerned with ordering God’s creature according to **natural goods** or the **goods of fortune** <note>Refers to physical health and life (natural goods) or wealth and social status (goods of fortune).</note>. And so every man seems to have...

...to possess a twofold power, since every man ought to have power over the actions of his members, and for that reason has the power of walking in grace. Therefore, **spiritual power** admits a manifold subdivision, since some is of **Order**, and some is **Common**.
<margin>Spiritual power is manifold.</margin>

The **power of order** is called that spiritual power which a **Cleric** <note>A member of the clergy, such as a priest or deacon.</note> possesses for administering the **Sacraments** of the church, so that he may spiritually benefit himself and the laity; such as the power of consecrating, absolving, and administering other sacramentals. For the power of consecrating is ordered in itself and immediately so that the priest may consecrate, just as the habits of moral virtue are ordered for the sake of better actions; and since the priest is directed according to the **goods of grace** so that he may consecrate worthily, the above definition is clear.

However, **common spiritual power** is the power which any **parishioner** <note>original: "plebanus" — while sometimes meaning a parish priest, Hus here uses it to refer to the common member of the Christian community.</note> possesses in performing spiritual works, in himself and in others, which this verse mentions: <term>Teach, counsel, chastise, console, forgive, bear, pray</term> <note>original: "Doc. consul. castig. solare remitte fer ora" — a mnemonic verse for the Seven Spiritual Works of Mercy: teaching the ignorant, counseling the doubtful, admonishing sinners, comforting the sorrowful, forgiving offenses, bearing wrongs patiently, and praying for others.</note>. For as many as received Christ through faith, he gave them the power to become the sons of God, so that it might be permitted for them to direct themselves and their brothers in the way of their father, Christ, and by correcting them charitably, as is clear in Matthew 18. *If your brother sins against you,* says Christ, *reproach him between you and him alone.*

<margin>Secular power is twofold.</margin>
**Secular power** is twofold: namely, **civil** and **common**. Authoritative civil power belongs only to a civil lord. But vicarious civil power belongs to officials or ministers. However, **common secular power** is the power by which a man can, according to the goods of nature and fortune, direct himself and his own; and just as a man cannot be whole without a soul and a body, nor an adopted son of God without the goods of nature and grace, so it is not possible for a **pilgrim** <note>original: "viatorem" — literally a "wayfarer," referring to a human being currently living on earth, traveling toward the afterlife.</note> to exist unless he possesses both common secular and spiritual power, even if in infants and the dead it is bound <note>Meaning the power exists but cannot be exercised due to age or state of being.</note>.

<margin>Spiritual power is everywhere more perfect.</margin>
But **spiritual power** is everywhere more perfect, and the **priestly power** itself exceeds the **royal power** in terms of dignity, because...

<margin>Note on royal and priestly power</margin>...according to the Apostle in **Hebrews 7**: "The one who blesses is greater, and the one who is blessed is lesser." <note>Hebrews 7:7, a standard text used in the Middle Ages to argue for the superiority of the clergy over secular rulers.</note> Hence, **spiritual priestly power** exceeds **royal power** in antiquity, dignity, and utility. 

It exceeds in **antiquity** because the priesthood was instituted by God’s command first, as is clear in **Exodus 28**. Afterward, royal power was instituted through the priesthood by God's command, as seen in **Deuteronomy 17** and **1 Samuel 13**. <note>The Latin text cites "1 Kings 13," which in the Vulgate Bible refers to what modern English Bibles call 1 Samuel.</note> 

It exceeds in **dignity**, as has been said, because the priest, as the superior, blesses, consecrates, and anoints the king. 

Its **utility** is evident as being greater because spiritual power is sufficient in itself for ruling the people, as is clear from the example of **Israel** up until the time of **Saul**, which was managed wholesomely without royal power. Therefore, since spiritual power concerns the highest and most self-sufficient goods, it exceeds earthly power, as the latter is worth nothing without spiritual power principally regulating it. 

But on the contrary, spiritual power can be sufficient by itself without the earthly; and for this reason, priests who abuse such a high power through pride or other crimes fall deeper into **Gehenna** <note>A term for Hell or eternal punishment.</note> with the devil, according to the rule of **Saint Gregory** and other saints: *The higher the status, the heavier the fall.* <note>original: "Quanto status altior, tanto casus grauior." A common medieval proverb reminding the clergy that their high office brought greater moral risk.</note>

And it should be noted that "power" sometimes refers absolutely to the capacity for ruling, and at other times it refers collectively to such capacity along with an authentic notification or proclamation.

<margin><term>All power is from God.</term></margin>And it is clear that there is no contradiction in saying that power exists only from God, and yet it is another thing for a person to be given power by God—that is, through an authentic proclamation in the face of the church—so that a created person may hold this kind of power from God. Such a "collective" power <note>Referring to the combination of God's authority and the Church's public recognition of it.</note> is indeed given by man, but only if God principally authorizes it.

<margin>...</margin>And from this, it can be further understood that power is not loosened or tightened, increased or diminished, regarding its **essence**, but rather regarding the **execution** of the work that proceeds from it; and this is permitted to be done, but only if a reasonable cause is present.

And it is clear that there is no contradiction in saying that power comes from nowhere but God, and yet someone other than God may "give" power—that is, the authentic proclamation before the Church that a created person has received this kind of power from God. This collective whole <note>The combination of the inner power and the public office.</note> is granted in part by man, but only if God primarily authorizes it.

From this, it can further be understood that power is not loosened or tightened, nor increased or diminished, in regard to its essence, but only in regard to the **execution of the work** which proceeds from it. And it is permitted to do this, but only if a rational cause is present...

### CHAPTER 10

...in relation to God. And Canon 23, question 1, *Miramur* <note>original: "Miramur." This refers to a specific section in Gratian’s Decree, the collection of canon law used in the Middle Ages.</note> explains this sense. It says: "The power of office is one thing, its execution is another." <margin>The power of an office and its execution are different.</margin> Most often, the power of office is retained by monks and others, even as in those who are suspended; to them, administration is forbidden, but the power is not taken away. In a similar sense, it is granted that natural power—which is **free will**—can sometimes be loosened by grace and sometimes restricted. Thus are resolved the apparent disagreements of the doctors <note>The "doctors" refer to established authoritative theologians of the Church.</note>, of whom some, like **Anselm** <note>Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), a philosopher and theologian.</note>, say that free will cannot be lost, increased, or diminished. Others, however, like **Augustine** in his *Enchiridion* <note>A "handbook" or manual on Christian teachings written by St. Augustine around 420 AD.</note>, say that free will can be lost through sin and increased through grace.

<margin>A dispute exists regarding the granting and restriction of power.</margin>
Regarding the granting, subtraction, or restriction of power, there is a great dispute in the church. However, it is well known that when God and reason compel it for the benefit of the church—so that it is carried out through a human agent—then, and only otherwise, God gives, removes, or restricts this power. Hence, when Christ says to Peter, "I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" <note>Matthew 16:19.</note>—the power of binding and loosing sins—he spoke in the person of Peter to the whole **Church Militant** <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christian community on earth, currently "at war" against sin and the devil, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven.</note>. This does not mean that every individual person in that church possesses those keys indiscriminately, but that the whole church possesses them through its individual parts that are suited for this purpose.

<margin>What the keys of the church are.</margin>
These keys are not material objects, but spiritual power and the knowledge of **Gospel science**. Because of this power and knowledge, it is believed that Christ names the "keys" in the plural. Hence the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose book *The Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the medieval university.</note> says in Book 4, Distinction 18, Chapter 2: "He says 'keys' in the plural because one is not enough. These keys are the science of discerning and the power of judging, by which the judge ought to receive the worthy and exclude the unworthy from the ecclesiastical kingdom."

<margin>Spiritual power is held differently from God, from the humanity of Christ, and from the prelates of the church.</margin>
And it should be noted that although the Trinity alone possesses this sort of authentic and principal power, and the humanity of Christ alone has this sort of sub-authentic and intrinsic principal power (since Christ is simultaneously God and man), nevertheless the **prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops.</note> of the church have...

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...[they] have committed to themselves an **instrumental** <note>In medieval theology, "instrumental power" means the priest acts as a tool through which God works, rather than being the primary source of the miracle or grace.</note> or **ministerial power**, which is a **judicial power** <term>potestas iudiciaria: the legal right to hear cases and pass judgment within the church</term>, consisting principally in two things: namely, in the power of discretionary inquiry <note>original: *arbitrarie cognoscendi* - the power to investigate the facts of a case or a confession</note>, and in the power of judicial sentencing. 

The first of these, in the "forum of penance" <note>The private setting of confession where a priest hears a person's sins.</note>, is called the **key of conscience** <term>clauis conscientiæ: the intellectual capacity or authority to discern the spiritual state of a person</term>, serving as a preparation for the second, more principal power. For no one rightfully holds the power of issuing a definitive sentence unless they first have the power of knowing the case in which they are said to be judging. Therefore, the first "key" is not simply the act or habit of knowing, but the power of such preliminary inquiry.

Therefore, every power of the priestly order to instrumentally open the door—which is **Christ**—to a human being, or to close said kingdom to a subject, is the **key of the church** <term>clauis ecclesiæ</term> given to Peter and to the others. This is clear from Matthew 18, where the Savior says: "Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." <note>original Latin: *Amen dico uobis, quæcũq; alligaueritis super terram, erũt ligata & in cœlo...*</note> And in John 20: "Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained." And in Matthew 16, it was said to Peter and the church through him: "Whatever you bind," etc. Because of a lack of understanding, these words terrify many Christians, causing them to fear in a servile way, while others are deceived by them, presuming upon a **fullness of power** <term>plenitudo potestatis: a term often used to claim that the Pope has absolute authority over all matters</term>.

Therefore, it must first be understood that the Savior’s statement is necessarily true in its literal sense <note>original: *de uirtute sermonis*</note>, because it is impossible for a priest to loose or bind anything unless that loosing or binding is also in the heavens. This does not merely refer to the "celestial body" <note>The physical stars and planets which medieval thinkers believed influenced the world below.</note> that contains the sublunary world and everything within it, but refers to the approval of God and the angelic nature, which are the true "heavens."

Here it should be noted that in the soul of one who sins mortally, guilt is created, and grace is seized or ceases to exist. Because of this, the person sinning mortally is bound by the debt of eternal damnation if they do not repent. While persisting in this guilt, they are separated from the company of those traveling in grace...

# CHAPTER X

<margin>Penance is the remedy for sin</margin>
...separates. However, one can have a remedy through **penance**, by which guilt is deleted, grace is conferred, the chain of damnation is broken, and a person is reunited with the church. This penance is perfected through **contrition**, **confession**, and **satisfaction** <term>the three traditional "parts" of penance: sorrow for sin, verbalizing it to a priest, and performing acts to repair the damage done</term>. Contrition, which is a sadness or full grief for the sin committed, must include a displeasure toward the sin—both for what was committed and for what might be committed—and in a moment of necessity, this alone would suffice for a person’s salvation. Thus, the Savior, recognizing the mind of the adulteress was in sorrow in John 7 <note>The text cites John 7, though the story of the woman caught in adultery is traditionally found in John 8:1–11</note>, enjoined upon her the second part, saying: "Go, and sin no more." On this point, Saints Augustine, Ambrose, and Gregory say in harmony that "to repent is to bewail the evils committed, and to not commit again those things which must be bewailed."

<margin>Infinite power is required for the justification of the wicked.</margin>
Secondly, it must be noted that for the **justification of the wicked** <term>iustificationem impij: the theological process by which a sinner is moved from a state of sin to a state of grace</term>, an infinite power is required, by which God purges the soul of its stain and grants grace. Secondly, God’s mercy is required, by which He releases the offense against His majesty and the eternal punishment which would be due as a debt if the person did not repent. Because of this, the Church frequently prays thus: "Almighty and merciful God" <note>original: *Omnipotens & misericors deus*</note>, wherein are suggested God’s infinite power and His mercy. That infinite power is required for the justification of the wicked is clear because, according to Augustine, "It is easier to create the world than to justify the wicked." Since the former requires infinite power, so does the latter. The reason is that in the justification of the wicked, the active giving of the **Holy Spirit** is required, which can belong to no one but God, as Augustine proves in many places (as I have set forth in the discussion on Indulgences). And the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1100–1160), whose book of "Sentences" was the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note> in Book I, Distinction 14, concludes from Augustine's words: "Therefore, men, however holy they may be, cannot give the Holy Spirit." The same reasoning applies to the active remission of sins.

<margin>Man does not forgive sins, but God.</margin>
Hence, John the Baptist said uniquely of Christ in John 1: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold Him who takes away the sins of the world" <note>original: *Ecce agnus dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mūdī*</note>. Regarding this, Augustine says in his 4th Homily on John: "Let no man claim for himself and say that he himself takes away the sins of the world." Now pay attention...

<margin>What it is to truly repent.</margin>

And what is it to **retain sins**, if not to refuse to absolve those who are not truly repentant? For many of those confessing seek absolution, yet they do not wish to abandon their crimes entirely. Many promise caution for the future, but do not wish to make **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the performance of penitential acts to make amends for the harm caused by sin</term>. All such people, because they do not truly repent, undoubtedly ought not to be absolved. For this is to truly repent: to grieve for past transgression with a firm purpose of confessing, making satisfaction, and taking every care to avoid it in the future. Those repenting in this manner deserve to be absolved; otherwise, they are sent away without absolution, and this is what it means to **retain sins** <note>the act of a priest refusing to grant forgiveness if the sinner is not sincere</note>.

### ON THE CHURCH

[Christ's] Vicar is able to absolve or bind sins, to remit or retain them, only if God has first done so; this is evident through that passage in John 15:
> He says, "Without me, you can do nothing." <note>original: "Sine me inquit, nihil potestis facere."</note>

The **vessel of election** <note>A traditional title for St. Paul, referring to Acts 9:15</note> knew this, and therefore says in 2 Corinthians 3: that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. If, therefore, we are not sufficient even to think unless God has produced that thought, how are we sufficient to bind or loose unless He Himself has first bound or loosed? Even the philosophers recognize this, saying that a **secondary cause** <term>causa secunda: in medieval philosophy, a created thing that acts as a cause, but only because it is empowered by God</term> can do nothing without the cooperation of the **first cause** <term>causa prima: God, the ultimate source of all action and existence</term>. And it is further evident that a person cannot be loosed from sin, nor receive the remission of sins, unless God has loosed them or granted them remission. Hence, John the Baptist said in John 3:
> "A man can receive nothing unless it has been given to him from heaven." <note>original: "Nõ potest hõ accipere quicquã, niſi fuerit ei datũ de cœlo."</note>

Just as the eternal Lord first dismisses the sin committed against Him within the soul before He allows this to be proclaimed by Himself or through another, so it is necessary for God to act.

<margin>The priest binds or looses nothing unless Christ has first bound or loosed.</margin>
Therefore, those priests are madly insane who think or say that they loose or bind according to their own will without the prior absolution or binding of Jesus Christ. For the binding or loosing by God is simply first. Therefore, the Gospel says that what is bound on earth shall be bound in heaven, but it does not say that it is bound in heaven *afterward*, and not before. <note>Hus is arguing against a contemporary view that the priest's action on earth forces God to act in heaven; he argues God must move first.</note> Thus, the ignorant think that the priest binds and looses first in time or in the moment, and God follows after him; it is foolishness to judge it so. 

<margin>A twofold priority.</margin> 
But Logicians know well that there is a **twofold priority**: namely, the **Priority of Origin** <term>prioritas originis: the relationship between a cause and its effect</term>, taken from the material cause, and the **Priority of Dignity** <term>prioritas dignitatis: a ranking based on importance or perfection</term>, taken from the final cause. These two priorities commonly run together in time, and thus the binding or loosing of the **Church Militant** <note>The Church on earth, currently struggling against sin</note> is, in a certain way, prior to the binding or loosing of the **Church Triumphant** <note>The Church in heaven</note>, and vice versa. But the binding or loosing of God is simply first. ### CHAPTER X

<margin>Christ does not always bind or loose what the Pope binds or looses.</margin>
Therefore, the faithful person must beware of this saying: that if the Pope or another claims to loose or bind by any sign, then by that very act the person is loosed or bound. For anyone conceding this must consequently concede that the Pope is **impeccable** <term>impeccabilis: unable to sin or, in this context, unable to make a mistake in judgment</term>, and thus a god; otherwise he could err and act in a way different from the **key of Christ** <note>original: "claui Christi," referring to the "power of the keys" granted to the apostles to forgive sins.</note>. And it is clear that just as it is impossible for the shape of a material key to open something if its substance is missing, so it is impossible for Christ’s vicar to open or close unless he is conformed to the key of Christ, who is the one opening or closing first.

For just as Christ—the firstborn among many brothers and the firstfruits of those who sleep—was the first to enter the kingdom, so He alone could, as the Head, merit the spiritual kingdom. This kingdom was universally closed by the transgression of our first parents until His time, and the same must be said regarding every specific opening or closing in relation to the **heavenly homeland** <note>original: "patriam," a standard theological term for heaven, our true home.</note>. This is also evident in those things which concern the faith and the keys of the church, as those who study the **Chronicles** <note>historical records of the church and the lives of the popes</note> know, since even Peter, Christ's first vicar, sinned in this way.

Likewise, it is God alone who cannot be ignorant of to whom sin should be forgiven, and He alone is the one who cannot be moved by a perverse affection and judge unjustly. But any vicar can be ignorant of to whom sin should be forgiven, and can be moved by a perverse affection to bind or loose. Therefore, if he refused to grant absolution to one who is truly repentant and confessing, being moved by anger or greed, he would not by that very act bind that person in guilt. Therefore, the Vicars of Christ <term>Vicarii Christi: those acting in the place of Christ on earth, specifically the Pope and the clergy</term> must take care that they do not presume rashly to loose or bind <note>In church law, "binding and loosing" refers to the authority to impose or lift spiritual penalties like excommunication, or to forgive sins.</note> whatever they wish.

<margin>An objection.</margin>
But an objection is raised through the Canon *Solitæ* <note>A significant decree by Pope Innocent III regarding the relationship between papal and secular authority</note>, concerning seniority and obedience, where Pope Innocent says: The Lord said to Peter, and in Peter he said to his successors, "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven." <note>Matthew 16:19</note> Innocent claims that by saying "Whatever," he excluded nothing.

<margin>The solution: Peter was unable to loose many things.</margin>
On this point it must be noted that even after that statement, "Whatever you loose," Peter could not loose the Scripture, because Christ Jesus our Savior said in John 10: "The Scripture cannot be broken." <note>original: "Non potest solui scriptura." Here, "broken" or "loosed" means the divine truth cannot be undone.</note> Second, he could not loose one who is unwilling to repent, and thus he said to Simon <note>Simon Magus, who tried to buy spiritual power</note> in Acts 8: "Repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps it may be forgiven." Third, he could not loose a marriage, because the Savior said in Matthew 19: "What God has joined, let no man separate." Fourth, he could not loose Judas from sin, because the Savior said: "None of them has perished except the son of perdition, that the Scripture might be fulfilled." <note>John 17:12</note> If Peter, therefore, through that saying of Christ—"Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven"—had claimed he could loose those four things mentioned above, would it have been so loosed in heaven? Certainly not. For the will of God would stand in the way regarding the Scripture, the marriage, and Judas; and in the case of another person who is unwilling to repent, their own stubbornness and the will of God would stand in the way.

It does not follow, then: "This vicar thinks he looses or binds whomever he wishes, therefore he does so." And regarding this, Blessed Augustine, in his work *On True and False Repentance*, speaks thus: God brought Lazarus, whom he had already raised from the dead from the tomb, to his disciples to be unbound, <note>Referring to John 11, where Jesus raises Lazarus but tells the onlookers to "untie him."</note> demonstrating by this the power of loosing granted to priests. He said, "Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven," which means: I, God, and all the ranks of the heavenly army, and all the saints praising in that glory, confirm with us those whom you bind and loose. He did not say, "those whom you *think* you bind and loose," but those upon whom you exercise the works of justice or mer—
