# JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH
## CHAPTER X (Continued)

...[works of] mercy, but your other works against sinners I do not know. <note>original Latin: "ricordiæ, alia autē opera uestra in peccatores nō cognofco." This concludes a quote likely from Augustine's commentary on the limits of clerical judgment.</note>

Augustine says this, cutting off the false self-importance of clerics in the matter of loosing or binding. Likewise, Richard <note>Richard of Saint Victor (died 1173), a prominent mystical theologian often cited by Hus.</note> in his book *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*, speaks as follows: "But you still persist and say: 'If I cannot bind and equally absolve whatever I wish, remitting the sins of whoever or retaining them, what does it mean when it is said generally to Peter: *Whatever you bind, whatever you loose*? <note>Matthew 16:19</note> Just as it is proposed generally, which is said to all the apostles in common: *Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them; whose sins you retain, they are retained.* <note>John 20:23</note>'"

"This question would rightly trouble you if the Lord had said to Peter: 'Whatever you *want* to bind will be bound, and whatever you *want* to loose will be loosed.' But He did not say this, nor did He wish it to be understood that way. If someone wanted to bind what he cannot bind, would it therefore be bound? Who would say such a thing? Therefore, He does not say 'whoever you want to bind,' but 'whatever you bind' will be bound in heaven."

"Indeed, he is truly bound who, according to the character of his confession, is held by a just debt of satisfaction <term>satisfactio: the outward act of penance or restitution performed to demonstrate true repentance for sin</term>. He is truly absolved by the priestly office whose sin is justly remitted for adequate satisfaction. Thus, he [the priest] binds and absolves those who, by the priest’s sentence, deserve to be justly absolved. But the sins of those are undoubtedly retained—not those to whom the absolution of sins is denied unjustly, but those to whom it is denied justly."

"Therefore, what the Lord says to Peter is as much as if He were saying in other words: 'What has been bound and loosed by you, will be bound and loosed with Me.' He who is constrained by you through the imposition of a required satisfaction, is held by Me as a debtor of that same satisfaction. And he who has earned from you the required absolution of his sins, by My judgment cannot be further restricted in this regard."

"In this same way, we must also understand what He says to all the apostles: *Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained.* For truly, the sins of those who offend the Lord will be remitted or retained, which through His ministers—the priests—have been justly either remitted or retained. Both of these acts are truly done by them when they carry them out..."

# CHAPTER X

...while he proceeds in Canonical order; but they can do neither according to their own wish, but according to merit and the instituted order. Thus says Richard.
<margin>
There is a difference between "whatever you loose" and "whatever you wish to loose."
</margin>
And it is clear from the declaration of Augustine and Richard himself that it does not follow <note>Hus is pointing out a logical fallacy here: just because a priest has the power to loose, it does not mean his personal desire to loose someone makes it spiritually valid.</note> that because Christ said to Peter, or to any of his vicars, "Whatever you loose on earth (that is, in the church militant <note>church militant: the Christian community living on earth, struggling against sin.</note>), will be loosed also in heaven (that is, the church triumphant <note>church triumphant: the community of the saved in heaven.</note>)," that it therefore follows: "Whatever you *want* to loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven." And it is clear that in that statement, the distribution <note>distribution: a logical term referring to the scope or application of a universal statement.</note> applies to anyone who is truly repenting. And in the phrase, "Whatever you bind," the distribution applies to the unrepentant; for to any truly repentant person belongs the loosing (absolution), and to the unrepentant, the binding. And the logic is the same regarding the power to retain and remit sins.

Therefore, a disciple of Christ must beware of the fallacy of the Antichrist <note>Hus frequently uses "Antichrist" to describe a corrupt institutional church or a Pope who acts against the Gospel.</note> when he argues in this way: "Whatever the vicar of Christ binds on earth will be bound also in heaven; but he binds this faithful layman on earth because the man is unwilling to give him money for absolution; therefore he is bound in heaven." Similarly, when he argues: "Whatever the vicar of Christ looses on earth will be loosed also in heaven; but he looses this unrepentant man on earth because the man is willing to give money; therefore he is loosed also in heaven." Similarly, if he argues: "Whatever the vicar of Christ looses on earth will be loosed also in heaven; but he looses this man (indicating one who is foreknown <term>foreknown: *praescitus*, a technical term in Hus's theology for someone God knows is ultimately destined for damnation, regardless of their current status in the church.</term>) on earth in the throes of death; therefore he is loosed also in heaven." 

In those arguments, the minor premise <note>minor: the second step in a formal logical argument (syllogism).</note> is flawed in its substance; for unless the said man in the minor premise has bound himself by an evil will, or loosed himself through true contrition, the minor premise is false. And according to Richard, the argument should be corrected thus: "Whatever the vicar of Christ binds *justly* on earth will be bound also in heaven. But he binds this faithful layman on earth for refusing to give money." Behold, the minor premise is false <note>The argument fails because the priest's act of binding is "unjust" and therefore does not trigger the heavenly response.</note>. In the same way, the other arguments are corrected.

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...[it follows] that we ought to believe he <note>Referring to the priest or the Pope as Christ's vicar.</note> only then binds or looses when he ministers according to the rules of the law of Christ. When he deviates from these rules, he merely *claims* to bind or loose, but he does not actually do so. 

Then, regarding the saying of Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216), who strongly asserted papal authority.</note>: "The Lord said to Peter, excepting nothing: 'Whatever...'" <note>original: "Dominus dixit ad Petrũ nihil excipiẽs, Quodcunqꝫ"</note> If Innocent understands the "distribution" <note>distribution: a logical term referring to the scope or range of a statement.</note> to mean "whatever Peter or his vicar *claims* to bind," then Innocent’s meaning would be false. For then, by logical subsumption <note>subsumption: the process of taking a specific case and applying a general rule to it.</note>, an absurdity would follow, arguing thus: 

"Whatever Peter or his vicar binds on earth shall be bound in heaven. But the vicar claims to bind this holy man on earth; therefore, this man is bound in heaven." 

The conclusion is false and impossible. Since the "minor premise" <note>The claim that the vicar is attempting to bind a holy/innocent person.</note> is true, or could be true, then the "major premise" <note>The general rule that the Pope's actions are always mirrored in heaven.</note> according to Innocent's opinion would have to be false. 

If, however, Innocent—along with Richard, Augustine, and Gregory—conceives of the "distribution" as applying to that which is *rightfully* loosed or bound, then it is true what the Lord says: "Whatever," excluding nothing. For this logic holds: "Whatever truly repentant person you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven." Similarly: "Whatever unrepentant person you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven." 

And this is hinted at by the glosses of the Decretals <note>Decretals: collections of papal decrees that formed the basis of Canon Law.</note>, which say: "The key not erring" <note>original: "Claue non errante." This legal principle states that a priest's judgment is only valid if he makes no error in judgment or procedure.</note>, and consequently, as long as the act was holy on earth, it will be confirmed in heaven. For whatever man, rightly repenting, is loosed on earth by Christ’s vicar on earth, is also loosed in heaven. 

This is just like the scripture: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved." This refers to one who believes with charity until the end. For "to believe" is understood there in the same way as in John 3: "He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life." 

From this, one might argue: "Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life; and every Christian believes in the Son of God; therefore every Christian has eternal life." Or again: "Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but this <term>foreknown one</term> <note>original: "praescitus." In Hus's theology, a "foreknown" person is someone God knows will ultimately be damned, even if they currently appear to be in a state of grace or hold office in the Church.</note>, who is currently in a state of grace, believes in the Son of God; therefore this foreknown one, who is in grace, has eternal life," the consequence is [false]...

Therefore, true Christians <term>Christicolæ</term><note>Literally "Christ-worshippers"; those who truly follow the teachings of Christ.</note>, wishing to attain that power, ought to resist any pretended power that strives to remove them from the imitation of Christ, whether by force or by deceit. For by resisting such power, one does not resist God's ordinance, but rather the abuse of power. And the Simoniacs <margin>Simoniacs.</margin> exercise that abuse regarding the power of the keys <term>power of the keys</term><note>The authority claimed by the Church to forgive sins or exclude members, based on the keys given to St. Peter.</note>; they pretend to either condemn the innocent or release the guilty, and they do this because of a refusal of their feigned obedience, or for the sake of their own profit. Concerning these, the Lord says in Ezekiel 13:

> They profaned me among my people for a handful of barley and a piece of bread, to kill souls that should not die, and to keep alive souls that should not live, by lying to my people who believe in lies. <note>original: "Violabant me ad populu meum, propter pugillum ordei uel fragmen panis..."</note>

Concerning this, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, a foundational figure for medieval theology.</note> says (and it is held in canon law, 11th Question, 3rd Part, in the section beginning "To many"): "Rightly," he says, "it is said through the prophet: they put to death souls that do not die and give life to souls that do not live. For he kills one who is not dying who condemns a righteous person; and he strives to give life to one who is not alive who attempts to release a guilty person from punishment." Those exercise the abuse <margin>Selling bishoprics.</margin> of power who sell and buy holy orders; who acquire and sell Bishoprics, Canonries, and Parsonages <term>Plebania</term><note>The office or jurisdiction of a parish priest (plebanus).</note> through simony; who demand payment for the sacraments; who, living greedily, luxuriously, lustfully, or in any criminal way, pollute the power of the priesthood. For although they confess they know God, they deny Him by their deeds (as in Titus 1). Consequently, they do not believe in God, and thus, like unfaithful sons, they think faithlessly about the seven sacraments of the church, about the keys, offices, censures <term>censures</term><note>Ecclesiastical penalties, such as excommunication or interdict.</note>, morals, ceremonies, and the sacred things of the church, the veneration of relics, indulgences, and orders. This is evident because such people <margin>The greed of priests is rebuked.</margin> despise the name of God. Hence it is said in the first chapter of Malachi:

> "But you, O priests, who despise my name, and you said, 'In what have we despised your name?' You offer polluted bread upon my altar. Who is there among you who will shut the doors, and kindle [fire]..." <note>original: "At uos o sacerdotes, qui despicitis nomen meum..."</note>

Thus he says.

How then are the greedy, the simoniacs <note>Those who buy or sell church offices or sacraments.</note>, the lustful, and those [stained] by other crimes...

...in all [things] of the matter, <note>original: "nibus rei", completing the word "omnibus" from the previous page.</note> they think of the Lord and his sacraments in a good way: when they unfaithfully despise the name of God, pollute his bread, crucify the Son of God Jesus Christ for themselves and hold him up to contempt, act impiously against the law of God, and despise and blaspheme his authority. And it is clear that such people are the **pestilential clergy** <note>original: "Clerus pestifer". Hus uses this strong term to describe clergy whose corrupt lives and teachings act like a plague upon the faithful.</note>, thinking unfaithfully about the seven sacraments of the church, and about the keys <term>keys</term><note>The "Power of the Keys" refers to the authority to forgive or retain sins, based on Matthew 16:19. And it is clear that the statement of the Doctors—whose leader at that time was **Stephen Paletz** <note>A former friend and colleague of Hus who became one of his most bitter enemies and accusers at the Council of Constance.</note> together with Stanislaus [of Znaim], dragging after them Peter of Ikoyma, John Helias, Andrew Bioda, John Hildesen, Matthew the monk, Herman the Hermit, George Bota, and Simon Vuenda—which was set forth as the matter of dissent, is verifiable in the clergy who live criminally. For they say at the beginning of their writing: *The matter of this dissension, on the part of certain ones from the pestilential clergy, is manifest.*

<margin>Behold the articles falsely imposed upon the Hussite by the heretical Inquisitors of heretics.</margin>

Because Christ’s priests preached against the crimes of the pestilential clergy, dissension arose for this reason: the clergy, bringing the plague of scandal upon the people and unwilling to endure preaching contrary to their plague, rose up against those preaching the Gospel and wishing to heal their plague through the word of the Lord, maliciously wanting to extinguish the preaching. But it was the intention of the said Doctors that those evangelizing against the malice of the pestilential clergy should be thought to hold heretical views regarding the keys of the Church—which, with the Lord's help, they will not prove during the span of their lives.

To the honor of the Lord Jesus Christ—whom these aforementioned doctors did not name anywhere in their writing, neither as "Honor" nor as "Christ"—this conclusion is proven: **To be subject to the Roman Pontiff is for every human creature a necessity of salvation.** <note>original: "Subesse Romano pontifici, omni humanæ creaturæ est de necessitate salutis." This is a direct quote from the Papal Bull *Unam Sanctam* (1302) by Pope Boniface VIII, which asserted absolute papal authority. Hus is cleverly subverting the claim.</note> This is clear from the fact that no one can be saved unless they are meritoriously subject to Jesus Christ. But Christ himself is the **Roman Pontiff** <term>Roman Pontiff</term><note>While this title usually refers to the Pope in Rome, Hus argues that Christ is the true "High Priest" (Pontifex) and the rightful head of the Roman Church and the universal Church.</note>, just as he is the head of the universal Church and of every particular church; therefore, the conclusion is true. The logic is clear regarding the major premise, and the minor premise is clear from what was said above, and through that passage in 1 Peter 2: *For you were once like sheep going astray, but you have now returned to the shepherd and bishop of your souls.* And in Hebrews 7: *Jesus has become the guarantor of a much better covenant.* There were indeed many other priests according to the law, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office. But this one, because he remains forever, has a perpetual priesthood; therefore, he is also able to save forever those who approach God through him, since he is always living to make intercession for us. For it was fitting that we should have such a **Pontiff** <note>original: "Pontifex". Translated here as High Priest in many English Bibles.</note>: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. He does not need to offer sacrifices daily, as those priests did, first for his own sins and then for the people's; for he did this once and for all by offering himself. Behold, this is the most holy and supreme Roman Bishop and Pontiff, standing before God the Father and remaining with us, as he says in the last chapter of Matthew: *Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.*

Christ, the true pontiff, administers the sacraments.

### CHAPTER XII

You have taken care to imprint the word of address, calling me **"Universal Pope,"** <note>original: "Vniuerfalem me Papam"</note> which I ask that your sweetest holiness <note>Gregory was writing to Eulogius, the Patriarch of Alexandria, who had addressed him with this exalted title.</note> no longer do to me; for that which is given to another more than reason requires is taken away from us. I do not seek to prosper in words, but in conduct; nor do I consider a man to be honored in a way that I know causes my brothers to lose their own honor. For my honor is the honor of the **universal church**; <term>universal church</term> <note>The whole body of Christian believers throughout the world.</note> my honor is the solid vigor of my brothers. I am then truly honored when the honor due to each individual is not denied. For if your holiness calls me the **Universal Pope**, you deny that you yourself are what you admit me to be in my entirety. <note>original: "negat se hoc esse, q me fateť uniuerfum." Gregory argues that if one bishop is "Universal," then all other bishops cease to be true bishops in their own right.</note> But let this be far from us; let these words recede which puff up vanity and wound charity.

<margin>Modern Pontiffs do not imitate Saint Gregory.</margin>

From the words of this holy Pope, it is gathered how easily one is puffed up who, while perhaps existing in a state of sin, is called **"Most Holy Father,"** and the one who addresses him is struck by the greed of flattery or lies out of ignorance. Whence Gregory notably says: **"I do not seek to prosper in words, but in conduct."** But alas, the **Modern Pontiffs** <note>Hus's contemporaries in the early 15th century, during the Great Western Schism.</note> do not seek it thus; they glory in the naked name alone, without the conduct of virtue, pretending that by reason of their office or ecclesiastical dignity, the name of "holiness" belongs to them. But if this reasoning were sound, then even **Judas** should have been called a "holy apostle." But blessed be the Lord, who, to remove such false cover, said to His disciples in the sixth chapter of John: **"Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?"** <note>original: "Nonne ego uos duodecim elegi, & unus ex uobis diabolus eft." John 6:70.</note> and He said these things before **Iscariot** <note>Judas Iscariot.</note> had even betrayed his Master.

Wherefore, the more holy men are praised by others, the more they humble themselves, and they weigh down their minds with fear, lest praise should cast them down from a more worthy merit. Whence in the **Acts of the Apostles**, Peter, the apostle of Christ, having been called by messengers, went humbly to **Cornelius** the Gentile; and when he had come to Cornelius, the latter came to meet him...

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

<margin>The mountains are touched. <note>original: "Tanguntur montes." A biblical allusion to Psalm 104:32, "He touches the mountains and they smoke," often interpreted by medieval theologians as God humbling the proud or the "high" figures of the world.</note></margin>
Cornelius, having been assured by an angel of Peter's holiness, prostrated himself at Peter’s feet. And Peter, having been taught by God regarding Cornelius and certain of his own blessedness through revelation, did not permit Cornelius to lie down at his feet, as **modern Pontiffs** do. In these men, not a spark of holiness is discerned; rather, perhaps suspecting their own inner crimes, they make a great show of the veneration exhibited to them. Indeed, if the title of their pompousness is omitted, they are immediately shaken with anger. 

Wishing to extinguish that pride, the **African Council** <note>The Council of Carthage (c. 397 AD), whose canons were later incorporated into medieval law.</note> in *Distinction 99* states: *The Bishop of the first see shall not be called the prince of priests, or the highest priest, or anything of this sort, but only the Bishop of the First See. Moreover, not even the Roman Pontiff should be called "Universal."* <note>original: "Vniuerfalis autem nec Romanus pontifex appelletur."</note> All these titles have now been prescribed out of pomp, flattery, and greed, and among the simple, out of blind deception. 

Returning, therefore, to our most humble **High Priest**, Jesus Christ, who in Luke 14 commands that one invited to a wedding should recline in the lowest place, let us confess to Him according to His own command in Luke 17 that we are **unprofitable servants**. For He says: *When you have done all that was commanded of you, say: We are unprofitable servants.* For when we have humbled our souls before the High Priest Himself by fulfilling His commands—even granted it were possible that our Pontiffs be "thieves and robbers"—He Himself, the **Bishop of our souls**, will not fail us in things necessary for salvation. Instead, being the truly good shepherd, He will feed, guard, and nourish His sheep.

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument from Chapter XIII, where he challenges the claim that the institutional Roman Church (the Pope and Cardinals) is the sole and infallible head of the universal Church. # I. H. ON THE CHURCH

This is clear, for **Constantine II** was an unlearned layman, who, having been suddenly ordained a priest, was made Pope through ambition; he was later deposed, and everything he had ordained was "un-ordained" <note>original: "exordinata." This refers to the historical act of declaring all his religious appointments and sacraments null and void.</note> around the year of our Lord 707. <note>While the text says 707, the antipope Constantine II actually reigned from 767–768 AD.</note> The same is clear regarding **Gregory**, who, being unlearned in letters, consecrated another to serve with him. When this act displeased the people, a third Pope was brought in; while these three were arguing among themselves, the Emperor came to Rome, deposed them all, and ordained one other alone.

<margin>A woman was Pope for two years.</margin>
Regarding a female [pope], it is clear in the case of **Agnes**, who was called **John English** <note>This refers to the legend of "Pope Joan," which was widely accepted as historical fact in the Middle Ages.</note>, of whom the **Monk of Chester** <note>original: "Cestrensis." Refers to Ranulf Higden (c. 1280–1364), a Benedictine chronicler whose work, the *Polychronicon*, was a standard history text.</note> writes in Book 5, chapter 3: A certain woman sat in the papacy for two years and five months after Leo. She is said to have been a girl called Agnes, born in **Mainz** <note>original: "Mogūtina."</note>, who was brought to Athens by her lover in male clothing and named John English. She progressed so far in various sciences that, upon coming to Rome, she had great masters as her students and lectured on the **trivium** <note>The three basic liberal arts: grammar, logic, and rhetoric.</note>. Finally, having been elected Pope, she was impregnated by her lover. While she was proceeding from St. Peter’s Church to the Lateran, she was overcome by the pains of childbirth and gave birth between the Colosseum and St. Clement’s church; she died and was buried there. Because of this, it is said that the Pope commonly avoids this route, and for this reason, she is not placed in the catalog of Popes.

<margin>[Chester] Book 4.</margin>
Regarding a heretic, it is clear in **Pope Liberius**, of whom the Monk of Chester writes in Book 4: that by order of Constantine <note>Specifically Constantius II, the son of Constantine the Great.</note> he was exiled for three years because he refused to favor the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arianism, a belief that Jesus was a created being and not fully God, which was the major heresy of the 4th century.</note>. Meanwhile, the Roman clergy ordained **Felix** as Pope, who, having held a council, condemned and cast out two Arian priests, **Ursacius** and **Valens**. Hearing this, Liberius was recalled from exile. Overcome by the long duration of his banishment and cheered by the prospect of recovering the papacy, he consented to heretical depravity. Having cast out Felix, he held the churches of Peter, Paul, and Lawrence by force, so that the clerics and priests who favored Felix were slaughtered in the church without Liberius forbidding it, and Felix was martyred.

### CHAPTER XIII

<margin>A perverse Pope is the Antichrist.</margin>
And then regarding the **Antichrist**, it is clear: because every Pope who lives contrary to Christ—just like any other perverse person—is commonly called an "Antichrist," according to that passage in **1 John 2**: *Many Antichrists have arisen.* Nor will a faithful person dare to stubbornly deny that it is possible for the "man of sin" to sit in the holy place. The Savior prophesied this in **Matthew 24**, saying: *When you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place,* etc. Likewise, the Apostle in **2 Thessalonians 2** <note>original: "ij. ad Thessalonicen. v." refers to chapter 2.</note> says: *Let no one deceive you in any way, for that day will not come unless the rebellion <note>original: "discessio," often translated as "apostasy" or "falling away."</note> comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God.*

<margin>Whence the name "Pope" took its origin.</margin>
And it is clear through the **Chronicles** how the Papal dignity grew into its current form. For the Emperor **Constantine**, around the year of our Lord 301 <note>Hus’s dating follows medieval tradition; Constantine’s reign actually began in 306 AD and the Edict of Milan was in 313 AD.</note>, commanded that the Supreme Bishop should be called "Pope" by everyone, and that name increased further through the **Endowment** <note>original: "dotatione." Refers to the "Donation of Constantine," a document (later proven to be a forgery) claiming Constantine gave the Pope authority over the Western Roman Empire.</note>. The Emperor **Phocas** also, around the year of our Lord 600, confirmed this same thing at the insistence of the clergy, as is read in his annals. Hence, the **Monk of Chester** <note>Ranulf Higden, author of the *Polychronicon*.</note> recounts in Book 4, chapter 14: How the excellence of the Roman Empire assisted the Papacy of its bishop above others. He says that the **Council of Nicaea** conferred this privilege upon the Roman Pontiff: that just as **Augustus** was held above other kings, so the Roman Pontiff should be held as the [Supreme] Bishop, and be called "Pope," the principal father. The origin of that name and excellence, however, was in the **Endowment of the Church**, as specified in the **Decretum** <note>The standard collection of Canon Law.</note>, distinction 96, [chapter] *Constantinus*.

Having noted these things to prevent any withdrawal [from my argument], I suppose that the doctors <note>Referring to the university theologians Hus was debating.</note> note in their writing that by the "Roman Church," they mean that church of which the Savior said to Peter: *Upon this rock I will build my church.* For in this way, as was said in Chapter 7, the Saints and the **Decrees** call it the holy Roman Church, as in Distinction 22, the chapter *Quamuis*; and Distinction 23, question 1, the chapter *A recta*; and Distinction 23, question 1, the chapter *Hæc est fides*; and in the **Clementines** <note>A collection of decrees by Pope Clement V.</note> regarding the Oath, it is said that the Roman princes...

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s critique of the institutional claims of the Roman Catholic Church. ->### JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH<-

...professors of the orthodox faith, who venerate the most holy Roman Church—of which the head is Christ our redeemer—and the Roman Pontiff, who is the Vicar of that same redeemer, with the fervor of faith and the promptness of clear devotion. And in the *Sext* <note>original: "in sexto," referring to the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a major collection of Canon Law published in 1298.</note>: "Our nurturing mother the Church." And in the *Extravagant* of Boniface VIII <note>original: "Extrauagante Bonifacij. viij.," referring to the famous papal bull *Unam Sanctam* (1302), which claimed that subjection to the Roman Pontiff was necessary for salvation.</note>: "The Holy Roman Church," and other such sayings located elsewhere and cited above.

<margin>What the [unlearned] doctors feel about the Roman Church.</margin>
Regarding these things, therefore, in the trifles <note>original: "nugis," implying the arguments are frivolous or nonsensical.</note> of the doctors, I perceive these specific points: 
1. **First**, the Pope is the head of the holy Roman Church. 
2. **Second**, the college of Cardinals is the body of the holy Roman Church. 
3. **Third**, the Pope is the true successor of Peter, the prince of the Apostles. 
4. **Fourth**, the Cardinals are the true successors of the college of Christ’s other Apostles. 
5. **Fifth**, for the governance of the Church throughout the entire world, it is necessary that such manifest and true successors always remain in the office of Peter, the prince of the apostles, and Christ’s other apostles. 
6. **Sixth**, no other such successors can be found or granted on earth except for the existing Pope as the head and the college of Cardinals as the body of the Roman Church.

<margin>An argument against the aforementioned points.</margin>
Against all six points now set forth, it is argued in brief: Every truth in the religion of Christ that is to be followed is either a truth known by the bodily senses, or discovered by an infallible intellect, or known through revelation, or set forth in the Divine Scripture. But none of these six points is a truth known by the bodily senses, nor discovered by an infallible intellect, nor known through revelation, nor set forth in the Divine Scripture. Therefore, none of these six points is a truth to be followed in the religion of Christ. 

The major premise is made evident by the blessed **Augustine** in his *Enchiridion*, chapter 3 <note>A handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love written around 420 AD.</note>, where he speaks thus: *For these things are to be followed above all—indeed almost alone—in religion; whoever contradicts these is either entirely a stranger to the name of Christ, or a heretic.* And it follows: *These things are to be defended by reason, whether starting from the senses of the body or from the [intellect...]*

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s critique of the theological faculty at the University of Prague. On the previous page, Hus began listing six specific claims (the "six points") made by the "doctors" regarding the absolute authority of the Pope and the Cardinals. He now uses the authority of St. Augustine to argue that these points are not divinely inspired and therefore do not demand absolute belief from the faithful.</meta>

### CHAPTER XIII

...intelligence found by the mind. However, regarding those things which we have neither experienced through bodily sense nor been able—or are now able—to grasp with the mind, we must without doubt believe those witnesses by whom that scripture, which has already deserved to be called "divine," was composed. These witnesses, whether through the body or through the soul, were divinely aided and were able to see, or even to foresee, these truths. These are the words of Blessed Augustine. 

Furthermore, the Doctors cannot disprove the minor premise <note>original: "Minorem," referring to the secondary part of a logical syllogism in Hus's argument.</note>, nor has any of their **six points** been divinely revealed to them. For those points are not evident from bodily sense, nor from reason, nor from divine scripture. On the contrary, by putting forward those points as an authority to be believed, the Doctors seem to be <term>anathema</term> <note>From the Greek "anathema," meaning something dedicated to evil or formally cursed and excommunicated by the Church.</note> according to that very authority of Augustine which they themselves cite in their own writing. 

"If anyone should venerate any writings—or hand them down as holding authority—other than those which the Catholic Church has received, let him be **Anathema**." This is clear because they themselves have handed down their own writings as an authority to be believed, and the Catholic Church has not received those writings, since they are placed neither in divine law nor in Canon Law. Therefore, it follows that the doctors themselves are, in this way, anathema. It is also clear that <term>religious faith</term> <note>original: "fides religiosa," the highest level of belief required for truths revealed by God.</note> is not to be granted to them regarding those points, unless they have proved them evidently, or founded them in sacred scripture, or by vigorous reason, as Augustine says to Jerome in a letter:

<margin>How authors ought to be read.</margin>

"I have learned to yield this honor and fear only to those writers who are now called 'Canonical,' so that I dare not believe any of them to have erred in writing. But others I read in such a way that, no matter how much they may excel in holiness or doctrine, I do not therefore think a thing is true because they themselves felt it to be so, but because they were able to persuade me through the Canonical authors or probable reasons that do not shrink from the truth." This is found in the <term>Decrees, Distinction 9</term> <note>original: "Dist. ix. Ego solū," referring to a specific section of the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Canon Law.</note>, in the chapter beginning "I only."

# JAN HUS ON THE CHURCH

<margin>That the Pope is not the head of the church.</margin>
Then, in a similar way, regarding the point that the Pope is the head of the Roman Church—while always maintaining uniformly that the Roman Church is the bride of Christ built upon Christ, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail <note>A reference to Matthew 16:18, where Jesus promises that his church will endure.</note>—it is argued thus: no Pope is the most worthy person of the Catholic Church except Christ; therefore, no Pope is the head of that Catholic Church except Christ. It follows that no one, without a special revelation, should reasonably assert of himself or another that he is the head of the holy power of the church, although by living well he ought to hope that he is a member of the holy Catholic Church, the bride of Christ. Therefore, concerning this, we should not argue about the essential fact—that whoever is living and interacting with us is the head of a particular holy church—but rather we should assume based on their works that if he is a superior ruling a holy particular church, then he is the superior in that specific church. This should be assumed of the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> unless his works contradict it, because the Savior said: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; by their fruits you shall know them." (Matthew 7 and John 10 says: "Believe the works"). Likewise, it is not necessary to believe that whoever is the Roman Pontiff is the head of any particular holy church unless God has predestined him. This is clear, because otherwise the Christian faith would be forced to be deceived and a Christian would be forced to confess a lie, since the Church was deceived in the case of **Agnes** <note>Hus refers to the medieval legend of "Pope Joan," here called Agnes, a woman who allegedly disguised herself as a man and was elected Pope. Hus uses this common historical belief of his time to prove that the institutional Church can make mistakes in its leadership.</note>. Without doubt, God allowed this for the sake of his own people for the better, so that one who is elected Pope is not immediately considered holy, or held to be exactly as he is presented, without any fear or caution.

For this reason, I would wish that the doctors would teach the people publicly whether—at that time when the entire clergy then living estimated they had a true Pope—Agnes herself was actually the head of the Roman Church. Or if the church was then **headless** <term>headless</term> <note>original Greek: ακεφαλος [akephalos]</note>, while the name of the Pope existed in the **militant church** <note>The "church militant" refers to the living Christians on earth who are still struggling or "fighting" against sin, as opposed to those in heaven.</note> for two years and five months. From this, the faithful can understand that just as it is not an essential part of the **universal** <term>universal</term> <note>original Greek: καθολικης [katholikēs]</note> faith to believe explicitly that this Liberius, John, Boniface, Clement, or Urban is predestined <note>Chosen by God for salvation.</note>, or a member of the holy mother church according to the opinion stated above. So also, it is not a matter of necessity.

# CHAPTER XIV.

...since he received vicarious power <term>vicarious power (vicaria potestas); the authority to act as a representative or deputy for a superior</term>, it is necessary that he be more immediately conformed in his works to the one whose place he takes; for otherwise, the power in him would be frustrated. From this, an argument is formed: A man is the Vicar of the one whose place he takes and from whom he legitimately receives procuratorial power. But no one truly takes the place of Christ or Peter unless he follows him in his character, since no other following is more pertinent; nor does he otherwise receive procuratorial power from God. 

<margin>Note that the Pope must act such that he is a true successor of St. Peter.</margin>

Therefore, both a conformity of character and the authority of the one instituting the office are required for that vicarious office. If, therefore, the Pope is a most humble man, valuing little the honors and worldly gain of this age; if he is a shepherd drawing his name from the "pasturing" of the Word of God—concerning which pasture the Lord said to Peter in John 21: *Feed my sheep* <note>original: "pasce oues meas"</note>; if he feeds the sheep by the Word and by the example of his virtues, having been made "a pattern for the flock from the heart," as Peter teaches in 1 Peter 5; if he is mild, patient, chaste, and laboring anxiously and solicitously in the ministry of the church, considering all the temporal things of the world as dung—then, without a doubt, he is a true Vicar of Jesus Christ, manifest to God and to men, at least according to external, sensory judgment. 

If, however, he lives in a manner contrary to these virtues—since there is no "fellowship of Christ with Belial" <note>original: "Christi cõmuni catio ad Belial"; quoting 2 Corinthians 6:15, where Belial represents personified wickedness or the devil</note>—and as Christ says in Matthew 12: "He who is not with me is against me," then how is he a true Vicar of Christ or Peter? 

<margin>An evil Pope is a Vicar of Antichrist.</margin>

Is he not rather a Vicar of Antichrist, as he opposes Christ in his character and in his life? Thus Christ called Peter "Satan"—which means "adversary"—in Matthew 16, when Peter was contrary to Him in will and words, even after the promise of the giving of the keys. Christ said: *Get behind me, Satan, you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not savor the things that are of God, but the things that are of men.* <note>original: "Vade post me Sathana, scandalum mihi es, quia nõ sa pis ea quae dei sunt sed ea quae hominum."</note> 

If, therefore, Peter—the first Vicar of Christ, chosen by Him and spiritually deputized for the church—was called "Satan" by Christ because, out of an affection of fleshly love, he tried to dissuade Him from undergoing the punishment of death, why should another person, who is even more contrary to Christ in his life, not truly be called "Satan," and consequently the Vicar or chief minister of Antichrist?

Hence the Blessed Bernard says regarding the *Song of Songs*: "Iniquity has gone forth from your senior judges, O Lord, who seem to rule your people" <note>original: "Egressa est iniquitas a senioribus iudicibus tuis domine, qui uidentur regere populum tuum." Likewise, all are friends and all are enemies, all are necessary and all are adversaries, all are members of the household and none are peacemakers, all seek what is their own; they are ministers of Christ, and they serve Antichrist. Likewise, Augustine, in his commentary on John, showing those who are not true shepherds but hirelings <term>hireling (mercenarius); a person who works only for pay, specifically a "shepherd" who abandons the sheep at the first sign of trouble</term>, says and proves in the *Decretum* <note>original: "viij. q. j." refers to the Decretum Gratiani, Case 8, Question 1, a foundational collection of canon law</note>: There are certain leaders in the church, the apostle Paul says, who seek their own things, and not those which belong to Jesus Christ. What is it then to "seek one's own"? It is to not love Christ freely, not to seek God for his own sake, to pursue temporal advantages, to gasp after profits, and to desire honors from men. When these things are loved by a leader, and God is served for this reason, whoever is such a person is a hireling; let him not count himself among the sons of God. For concerning such people the Lord also says, "Amen, amen, I say to you, they have received their reward" <note>original: "Amen amen dico uobis receperũt mercedem suã." A reference to Matthew 6:2.</note>.

<margin>Peter is the type of the good, Judas of the evil.</margin>
Hence Augustine himself says that just as the apostle Peter carried the type <term>type (typus); a person or thing in the Bible believed to foreshadow or represent a later reality or a specific class of people</term> of all the good, and especially of Bishops, so Judas carried the figure of all the evil and especially of Priests. Hence, in his commentary on John regarding that word in John 12: "For the poor you will always have with you, but me you will not always have," <note>original: "Pauperes enim semper habebitis uobiscum, me aut̃ non semper habebitis"</note> he says: What does he mean? How is this to be understood: "me you will not always have"? Do not be afraid; this was said to Judas. Why then did he not say "you [singular] have," but "you [plural] have"? Because there is not just one Judas, not just one evil person; he signifies the whole body of the evil, just as Peter signifies the body of the good. Below: In the person of Peter are signified the good in the church; in the person of Judas are signified the evil in the church. To them it was said, "but me not always..."

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument from Chapter XIV, focusing on the distinction between the outward signs of faith and the inner reality of a righteous life. ### CHAPTER XIV

...you will always have. What does "not always" mean, and what does "always" mean? <note>Hus is quoting Augustine's commentary on John 12:8: "The poor you always have with you, but me you do not always have."</note> If you are good, if you belong to the body which Peter represents, you have Christ both in the present and in the future. In the present through faith, in the present through the sign <note>The "sign" often refers to the sign of the cross or the outward profession of faith.</note>, in the present through the sacrament of baptism, and in the present through the food and drink of the altar <term>food and drink of the altar; the bread and wine of the Eucharist or Holy Communion</term>. You have Christ in the present, and you have Him always, because when you depart from this life, you will come to Him who said to the thief: "Today you will be with me in Paradise." But if you live wickedly, you may seem to have Christ in the present because you enter the church, you sign yourself with the sign of Christ, you are baptized with the baptism of Christ, and you mingle with the members of Christ; in the present you have Christ, but by living wickedly you will not always have Him. 

Thus says Augustine, showing that the true Vicars of Peter <term>Vicar of Peter; a title for the Pope, implying he stands in the place of the Apostle Peter</term> are the righteous, while the evil ones are Vicars of Judas Iscariot—especially greedy, hypocritical, and blasphemous priests. And he shows the same regarding that Psalm: "O God, do not be silent regarding my praise" <note>Psalm 109:1 (108 in the Vulgate), which was traditionally interpreted as referring to Judas.</note>. And Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> says in the final question of [the Decretum] Case 22: "Beware, brothers, of a lie; for it is a lie to call oneself a Christian and not do the works of Christ." For it is a lie to profess oneself a bishop, a priest, or a cleric, and to act contrary to this order. According to Case 2, Question 1: "All prelates [who act thus] are not considered prelates. For the name does not make a Bishop, but the life." And in Distinction 4, under the Rubric: "He is not truly a priest who is only named a priest." And Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), Archbishop of Constantinople, famous for his preaching.</note> [says]: "There are many priests, and yet few priests."

<margin>A greedy Pope is the vicar of Judas.</margin>
Behold, from these and other points mentioned, it is shown that a Pope is not the manifest and true successor of Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, if he lives in a manner contrary to the character of Peter; and if he seeks greed, then he is the vicar of Judas Iscariot, who loved the reward of iniquity, selling Jesus Christ.

# [JAN HUS] ON THE CHURCH

...in the name <note>The Latin text begins with "ni," the suffix of "nomini" (to the name), completing the phrase "in the name of Jesus Christ."</note> of Jesus Christ. For the Apostles traveled on foot in humble clothing through cities, towns, and villages, evangelizing the kingdom of God.

### CHAPTER XIV

...[Acts] chapter 7; because devoted contrition and the healing and washing of the feet of Christ—that is, the poor—blot out the crimes of the traveler <note>original: "uiatoris"; a theological term for a human being on their earthly journey toward the afterlife</note>. Regarding the one being kissed, the Pope is entirely blameworthy, because he cannot be made equal to Christ so as to receive such great honor.

But the Apostles held in memory the word of Christ in Luke 14: 
> When you are invited to a wedding, do not sit down in the first place, lest perhaps someone more honorable than you has been invited by him; and he who invited you and him comes and says to you, "Friend, give place to this man," and then you begin with shame to take the lowest place. 

It is clear from the sayings of the saints that Christ is speaking of a spiritual calling, placing, and dining, not a physical one, since by the wedding is understood the betrothal of Christ and the Church, which will be completed in eternity at the final supper. To these weddings many are indeed called, but few are chosen, as Christ speaks in Matthew 22. <margin>To recline in the lowest place.</margin> However, he reclines in the lowest place who piously considers himself the least of the chosen, just like the Apostle of Christ <note>Saint Paul, who described himself as the "least of the apostles" in 1 Corinthians 15:9</note>, who saw secrets that a man is not permitted to speak, yet considers himself the least Apostle. <margin>The Pope cannot be "most holy."</margin> If, therefore, the Pope considers himself the "most holy father," or pleasingly receives that adjective from his subjects, how is he not presumptuously choosing the first place? 

Hence, if there were humility in him, as in Blessed Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (the Great), who rejected exalted titles and called himself "Servant of the servants of God"</note>, he would very quickly destroy, or desire to destroy, that style of address. But if he follows Christ in humility, patience, and labor, out of a great bond of charity, then he is holy. But far be it that he should be "most holy," because then he would be God Almighty, and consequently he would not exist <note>Hus argues that the superlative "most holy" belongs to God alone; for a man to claim it is a theological impossibility and a sign of pride</note>.

# CHAPTER XV

[...unless you] become <note>original: "efficiamini"</note> like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. And lest they should, through pride, cause those believing in Christ to stumble, he added:
> Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a heavy millstone <note>original: "mola asinaria"; literally a millstone turned by a donkey, representing worldly labor.</note> hung around his neck, and be drowned in the depth of the sea.

Discussing this word, Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), known as Gregory the Great, whose book *Pastoral Care* was the standard manual for bishops in the Middle Ages.</note> says in the second chapter of his *Pastoral Care*:
> Pastors who are perverse in their conduct, he says, destroy by their actions what they preach with words. Thus it happens that when the pastor walks over cliffs, the flock follows him to the precipice; for when laypeople learn the sayings of the <term>Prelates</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note>, they are perverted by their deeds.

<margin>Evil Prelates are a stumbling block for the people.</margin>
Hence it is written by the prophet: "Evil priests are the cause of the people's ruin." Concerning whom the Lord says through the prophet: "They have become a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel." Indeed, no one harms the church more than one who acts perversely yet holds the name or rank of holiness; for no one dares to rebuke such a person when they fall into sin, and the example of their fault spreads widely when the sinner is honored out of reverence for their rank. Surely those who are unworthy would flee the dangers of such heavy responsibility if they carefully considered the sentence of truth:

> Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a heavy millstone hung around his neck, and be drowned in the depth of the sea.

<margin>The heavy millstone.</margin>
Indeed, by the "heavy millstone" is expressed the circularity and pain of a worldly life, and by the "depth of the sea" is designated final damnation.

Therefore, for one who has been brought to the appearance of holiness, yet destroys others by word or example, it would certainly have been better if his earthly deeds had bound him to death under a secular garment; for the sacred offices show him to be a person whose faults change others, whereas if he had fallen alone, a more tolerable punishment in hell would surely have tormented him. That holy Pope [Gregory] knew the conditions and dangers surrounding a <term>Prelate</term>, and especially the <term>Roman Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope.</note>, since the sin of his commission or omission would be a scandal to the entire Christian people. For it is said in <term>Distinction 4</term> <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of Canon Law; "Distinction 4" specifically discusses the qualities required of the Pope.</note>: The goodness of the Pope...

JAN HUS ON THE CHURCH

[...as if he] were the Vicar of Jesus Christ, who refused to allow a woman to kiss his feet after his resurrection—when they were immortal and undoubtedly blessed—precisely to remove blasphemous presumption from those wretched men who sometimes falsely pretend to be Christ’s Vicars. For the feet of Christ, and of those who ascend with Christ, are blessed; they are not food for worms, a rotten limb, or the stinking sweat of worldly passions. From these things, one can be convinced whether that fourth point—that the cardinals are the manifest and true successors of Christ’s apostles—holds the truth. For a tree is known by the fruit it bears.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>
The Church was ruled for three hundred years without Cardinals.

The fifth point is this: for the governance of the church throughout the entire world, there must always remain such a sort—namely, cardinals—as manifest and true successors to the office of Peter, the prince of the apostles, and of the other apostles of Christ. In this point, the word "must" <note>original: "oportet"</note> does not imply a necessity on the part of God who rules the church—who can rule the church dispersed throughout the whole world without such successors—nor does it imply a necessity on the part of the church, which can be ruled just as well by holy priests, even if those twelve "hinges" <term>hinges</term> <note>Hus is punning on the etymology of *cardinal*, which comes from the Latin *cardo* (hinge); he suggests the church can turn without these specific "hinges."</note> were removed. This was the case for three hundred years and more after the ascension of Christ. This is said lest someone claim, perhaps, that the word "must" implies a necessity of the kind the Savior noted in Matthew 18, saying: "It is necessary <note>original: "necesse est"</note> that scandals come, but woe to that man through whom the scandal comes." # I. H. ON THE CHURCH

<meta>catchword: niuit</meta>

...is, as it were, the salvation of all, and his perversity results in the damnation of innumerable persons <note>original: "Dist.xl. Si papa"; a reference to the Canon Law decree stating that a Pope can be judged if he deviates from the faith</note>. If, therefore, the Pope and Cardinals—through pompous processions on horseback, glittering garments, exquisite and wondrous trappings, through excessive care in amassing benefices <note>church offices that provided an income</note> or money, and through manifest ambition for honor more than secular laypeople—should cause those believing in Christ to stumble, how could they necessarily always remain as manifest and true successors in the office of Peter the Apostle and the other apostles of Christ for the governance of the universal church?

<margin>Note the office of the Apostles.</margin>
Never was the office of the apostles anything other than following Christ in conduct: to teach the church, to baptize people, to heal the sick, to cast out demons, to offer the sacrifice of Christ’s body, and to exercise the power enjoined upon them for the progress of the church on every side. If, therefore, the Pope with his cardinals exercises this office, he holds Peter’s office. If he, along with the cardinals, turns away from this, who can doubt that he turns away from the true Vicarship <term>Vicarship: the office of acting as a representative or deputy</term> of Christ and His apostles?

<margin>The sixth point</margin>
And with equal evidence, this sixth point is declared, which is: "No other such successors can be found or given on earth except for the Pope existing as the head, and the college of cardinals existing as the body of the Roman Church." Regarding this, I note first that Christ is the most sufficient head, as He proved for three hundred years and more <note>Hus refers to the first three centuries of Christianity before the Church gained official Roman state support</note>, when His church prospered; and His law is most effective for settling ecclesiastical causes, since God brought it forth for this end. For Christ, with His law, does not fail to rule the church, provided devoted priests minister that same law to the people according to the opinion of the holy Doctors <note>The influential early theologians of the Church</note>, which they produced by the instinct of the Holy Spirit—as is evident regarding Saints Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, and Ambrose, who were given to the church for doctrine after the Apostles.

<margin>The holy Doctors were more profitable to the church than many Popes.</margin>
Hence there is no doubt that Blessed Augustine was more profitable to the church than many Popes, and in doctrine perhaps more than all the cardinals currently running from the first until now. For he understood and defined the Scripture of Christ in ecclesiastical governance more... <note>original: "diffiniuit"; the text continues on the next page</note>

<summary>Jan Hus argues that the Pope and Cardinals lose their status as successors to the Apostles if they live in worldly pomp rather than spiritual service. He asserts that Christ is the sufficient head of the Church and that the early Church Fathers like Augustine provided more guidance for the faithful than many modern Popes.</summary>

->### CHAPTER XV<-

...[defi]ned the Catholic matter, by purging and correcting heretical errors from the church. How then were those four Doctors <note>The four "Great Doctors" of the Western Church: Saints Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Gregory the Great</note> not true Vicars of the Apostles and their manifest successors? Indeed, they were truer and more upright before the people than the modern Pope with his Cardinals, who shine before the people neither with a holy life nor with doctrine. Whence I boldly assert that in whatever point these four holy Doctors agree, the Pope with the Cardinals cannot lawfully define the opposite as a matter of faith for the people. And it is the same regarding other saints, such as John Chrysostom, John of Damascus, and Dionysius the Areopagite <margin>The Greek Doctors</margin>, who, taught by the Holy Spirit, illuminated Christ's church with knowledge and character.

And he argues against the first point principally thus: God is almighty, therefore God can grant other true successors of the apostles than the Pope and Cardinals; therefore, other true successors of the Apostles can be found or given who are not the Pope or Cardinals; therefore, that point is false. The first consequence <note>The logical progression of the argument</note> is proved. For if God cannot grant other true successors than the Pope and Cardinals, it follows that the power of Caesar <note>original: "Cæfaris"; referring to secular imperial authority</note>—a man, not God—in instituting the Pope and Cardinals, would limit the power of God. This consequence is false, and the reasoning is proved. For the Emperor Constantine <margin>Constantine instituted the Pope</margin> <note>Hus refers to the "Donation of Constantine," a document long believed to be the legal basis for the Pope’s temporal power, though later proven to be a forgery.</note> instituted the Pope after three hundred years. For the Roman Pontiff was a companion to other pontiffs until the donation of Caesar, by whose authority he began to rule as head. Whence the Decree <note>original: "Decretum"; specifically the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundational collection of canon law used in the Middle Ages</note>, 97th Distinction—which we cannot deny out of shame <note>original: "quod non poffumus præ uerecundia negare"</note>—speaks thus: "The Emperor Constantine, on the fourth day of his baptism, conferred a privilege upon the Pontiff of the Roman church, so that in the whole world the Pontiffs should have him as their head, just as judges have a king." In which privilege, among other things, it is read: "We grant to him power and vigor, and imperial honor, decreeing that [he should] princi[pally rule]..."

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus’s argument from page 116. Having discussed how the "Donation of Constantine" and other imperial grants are human inventions, Hus now addresses the counter-argument that the Pope’s "primacy" (his supreme rank) comes directly from God. He interprets the writings of early Church figures and legal decrees to argue that true "primacy" is a matter of humble service and spiritual virtue, rather than worldly power or wealth.</meta>

### CHAPTER XV

...stated. From which it follows that the Pope is established in such excellence not by an Emperor or by man, but immediately by God. And the same is evident, secondly, from the submission of kingdoms. And fourthly, from the testimony of the Doctors <note>The recognized authoritative theologians of the Church</note> speaking about the power of the Pope.

<margin>Anacletus explains.</margin>

Regarding the first point, it must be assumed that the Pope <note>Hus refers here to a decree attributed to Anacletus, an early Pope (c. 80 AD), though these decrees were part of the "False Decretals" used in medieval law</note> understood the "holy Roman Church" not as a stone or wooden basilica <note>A church building</note>, but as Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and the others who had inhabited that place. Therefore, in the same Decree, it says that Peter and Paul were companions in the city of Rome; hence, it is significantly said that he "obtained primacy," as must be assumed. 

Secondly, that he speaks of the primacy of men in the eyes of God, arising from the first-fruits of virtues and the building up of the Church, and not about a primacy of temporal riches or human glory—a primacy which the apostles of Christ rejected. And it is clear that the following argument is invalid: "The Roman Church obtained primacy not from the Apostles, but from the Lord himself. Therefore every Roman Pontiff ought to excel in worldly glory or rule in a secular manner." Rather, it follows from the Decree that the Roman Pontiff is bound to serve that people, not by dominating them or by suspending <term>Suspending: A form of ecclesiastical censure or punishment where a person is barred from their religious duties or the sacraments</term> them, but by praying effectively for them, just as the Decree alleges Paul did in Romans 1.

<margin>The Pope ought to serve the faithful, not dominate them.</margin>

"Although," he says, "the prayer of all the saints is poured out before the Lord for everyone, yet with these words the most blessed Paul promises the Romans with his own handwriting, saying: 'For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make mention of you always in my prayers.'" 

From this Decree, it appears that Pope Anacletus did not wish to assert that he himself ought to dominate everyone else in a civil manner, or hold primacy in terms of lordship over all other persons of the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth</note>. For by seeking his own glory in such a way, as is said in John 5, he would have the most evident sign of the Antichrist. Indeed, Boniface VIII, in his decree *Unam sanctam* <note>original: "extrauagatione Vnam sanctam"; a famous papal bull from 1302 that claimed absolute authority over every human creature</note>, did not dare to assert that expressly, because then only...

## CHAPTER XVI.

The aforementioned Doctors further assert that certain members of the Bohemian clergy, holding the Pope and the college of cardinals in low regard, do not wish to consent to this. They desire to have only Holy Scripture as their judge in such matters, which they interpret (and wish to be interpreted) according to their own heads <note>original: "secundum capita sua." Meaning according to their own private judgment or whims.</note>, ignoring the interpretation of the community of the wise in the church. Nor do they heed Holy Scripture in Deuteronomy 17: "If you see that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous for you—between blood and blood, cause and cause, leprosy and non-leprosy—and you see the words of the judges vary within your gates, rise up..."

# CHAPTER XVI

->S<-

Pilate and the soldiers, even with the crowd crying out "Crucify, crucify him," condemned Christ the Lord. In truth, they erred gravely because it was not love but hatred, not truth but lies that drove them, and an ignorance of God’s law led them astray.

<margin>The Pope can err.</margin>
And a similar deception can occur with the Pope and the Cardinals, even with our own <term>doctors</term> <note>Hus refers here to the university professors and theologians who supported the official Church position against him</note> joined to them, such that they might condemn some truth. For if the Apostles chosen by Christ, who had received the Holy Spirit, fell into <term>heresy</term> <note>Hus cites the authority of Saint Augustine and the Venerable Bede to argue that even the original Apostles were not instantly perfect in their theological understanding</note> according to the blessed Augustine and Bede, how have the Pope and Cardinals received a greater "first-fruit" of the Spirit such that they are incapable of wandering in the same way or even more so? There is no doubt that the Pope and Cardinals must be obeyed, provided they teach the truth according to the law of God, as the authority says: *They shall judge for you with a judgment of truth, and you shall do whatever they say and teach you according to His law.* <note>original: "Iudicabunt tibi iudicij ueritatem, & facies quodcũq; dixerint..." A reference to Deuteronomy 17:11</note> But if the <term>Rabbis</term>—that is, "Masters" or the "Great Ones," as <term>Lyra</term> <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a Franciscan teacher whose literal commentaries on the Bible were highly influential in the Middle Ages</note> explains—whether they be Popes or Cardinals, command or teach something contrary to the truth, even if the entire Roman <term>Curia</term> <note>The administrative and judicial body of the Roman Catholic Church</note> stands with them, the faithful person must not obey once they have recognized the truth. For God says: *You shall not follow a crowd to do evil.* <note>Exodus 23:2</note>

<margin>Daniel, Nicodemus, and the thief obeyed the Scripture.</margin>
Daniel, Nicodemus, and the thief hanging on the cross put this into practice; they refused to consent to the crowds in the condemnation of the truth, just as the Scripture describes. For Daniel condemned the sentence of the wicked priests of the children of Israel by freeing Susanna and passing judgment on the senior elders from whom iniquity had originated (Daniel 13). <note>Hus refers to the story of Susanna and the Elders, found in the Greek additions to the Book of Daniel, where a young Daniel exposes the corruption of senior religious judges</note> Similarly, Nicodemus acted in the council of the <term>pontiffs</term> <note>The high priests</note> and Pharisees. Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd that does not know the law is cursed"—then Nicodemus said to them: "Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him...?"

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...before he does so: O blessed Nicodemus, you gave such great power 
<margin>The Law is the judge</margin> to the law of God; you bore witness to the law, that it is the judge of man. Behold, our <term>doctors</term> <note>Referring to the university theologians and Church authorities opposing Hus</note> in their sayings judge it to be an "inconvenience" that our side wants to have the law as judge—the law which judges most justly, and which judges no differently than God, the most just judge. You say: *Does our law judge a man, unless it first hears from him?* <note>original: "Nunquid lex nostra iudicat hominem, nisi audierit ab ipso..." A reference to John 7:51</note> as if he were saying, it is because the law judges justly.

To that judge, Christ sent the <term>pontiffs</term> <note>High priests</note>, the Pharisees, the Scribes, and the Jews, who were accusing Christ of sin because he did not keep the Sabbath and called God his father, saying: *Search the scriptures, for they are what bear witness of me* (John 5). Did Christ not want, therefore, for the scripture to judge the Jews who did not believe in Christ? Certainly, he did. How then do the doctors wish that scripture not be the judge? They want themselves to be believed; they want whatever they condemn to be condemned, and whatever they approve to be approved. Indeed, this is what they sought and petitioned for in the <term>praetorium</term> <note>The Roman judgment hall; Hus is likening the Church's legal proceedings to the trial of Jesus</note>; for this they sought signatures from the masters who would contradict us. But the counsel of the Pharisees, scribes, and high priests was scattered because the faithful had contradicted them, refusing to consent unless they heard proof from the law, which contains all believable truth. If the high priests, Pharisees, priests, and elders of the people had known this law, they would not have condemned Christ; but they condemned him and blasphemed. The thief was more learned than they, who hanging on the cross bore witness to Christ, saying: *This man has done nothing wrong* (Luke 23).

And regarding the primary intention of the doctors, as I see it—by which they intend that the Pope must be the judge of all causes, and that whoever does not obey him should die a physical death—the doctors should be ashamed of their **ape-like** <note>original: "simiali." Hus uses this term to suggest the doctors are merely mimicking authority or acting with a distorted, sub-human lack of reason</note> and cruel similarity [to the persecutors of old], especially since Christ Jesus our Lord, the High Priest of both testaments, did not wish to [rule] civilly...

He intended that Peter should not corporally kill the stubborn one who does not obey the church, but avoid him just as one would a public tax collector or a pagan. 

What pretext is there then for arguing by a "similarity" <note>An "argument by analogy" used by theologians to claim that because the Old Testament prescribed death for certain sins, the Church can do the same</note>, that because in the Old Law the disobedient were to be killed, it must be so in the Law of Grace? <margin>Heretics are not to be immediately put to death.</margin>

<header>CHAPTER XVI</header>

The spiritual headship of the church consists principally in Christ; in this church, it is not this Pope, but Christ who is the High Priest. It is He who presides over the place—that is, the Basilica or the apostolic dignity—and He who rules the church, his bride.

But if a life contrary to Christ is seen in the Pope—manifested in pride, greed, impatience, ambition, in the exaltation of his own power, and in the weighing of his own law above the Law of Christ—then the "abomination of desolation" <note>A biblical reference to a desecrating presence in a holy place. Hus is citing Matthew 24:15, though he references chapter 13 here.</note> of Christ's virtues is seen to stand in the holy place where it ought not to stand, as Christ says in Matthew 13. Therefore, if faithful souls were to look at the spiritual state of the church on both sides—seeing how one father of a household <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> used to preside in it, who would graciously welcome by inviting, feed by refreshing, and defend by helping all those of his household; but now finds one of an entirely opposite condition presiding in that same house, it is no wonder if many are desolated. It is as if a traveler wished to stay with a true father of a household of magnificent generosity, piety, approachability, and entirely virtuous conduct, but afterward finds a monstrous beast who tyrannizes the guests hungrily, deceitfully, cruelly, arrogantly, and treacherously. The traveler entering the house, seeing such a person sitting in the chair of the pious father of the household, would be amazed, troubled, and desolated in no small measure by the sight. Thus can the "abomination of desolation" be understood, according to that passage in Zechariah 11: *Take up again the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit the abandoned, nor seek the scattered, nor heal the broken, nor nourish that which stands; but he will eat the flesh of the fat ones and tear off their hoofs. O shepherd and idol who leaves the flock!* <note>original: "o pastor, & idolum derelinquens gregem." Hus uses this prophecy to describe a corrupt Pope who consumes the wealth of the church instead of caring for the people.</note>

<margin>When the Pope is a true successor of Peter, and when he is not.</margin>
Therefore, if this description of an "idol" and the abandonment of the flock is found in a Pope, how can the future claim of the <term>doctors</term> <note>Theologians from the University of Prague who supported the Papal position.</note> be verified concerning any such Pope: that he is the high priest, the true and manifest successor of Peter, presiding over the church, the bride of Christ? For it does not follow that...

Then, regarding the saying of the Blessed Jerome, "This is the faith of the most blessed pope," which is cited in the canon law <note>original: "xxij. q. j." refers to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of Church laws.</note>, it is said that he spoke *reputatively* <note>Meaning he used the word as a formal title of honor or reputation, rather than an absolute statement of the man's personal holiness.</note>, based on the apostolic works of Pope Damasus. This is similar to how he wrote to Blessed Augustine in his letters, saying: *To the truly holy Lord and most blessed Pope Augustine.* In the same way, the saints speak "reputatively" of prelates, even when they see them deviating from the footsteps of Christ, saying that such men are to be condemned as members of the devil. But woe to those who, seeing in a pope works directly contrary to Christ, still call him "most holy father." For in Isaiah 5 it is said: *Woe to you who call evil good.* Such people, through their lying flattery, deceive both themselves and the one they flatter. For it is said in Isaiah 3: *My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps; the Lord stands to judge.*

<margin>How the Pope and Cardinals are venerated.</margin>
For if those learned in the Law of God would boldly tell the truth to the Pope and the Cardinals, and not stroke them with flattery because of fear or for the sake of promotion to benefices <note>A "benefice" was a church office that provided a guaranteed income; Hus is accusing the clergy of being "yes-men" to secure well-paying jobs.</note>, perhaps the leaders would eventually recognize themselves for who they are, and would not permit themselves to be venerated as gods. But because both sides sin in this—the first group hypocritically rejoicing in being honored and called "blessed," and the second group lying and tickling their ears with flattery—therefore both sides will necessarily be cast down headlong. For Isaiah 9 says: *And there will be those who call this people blessed, deceiving them, and those who are called blessed will be cast headlong.*

Therefore, he can do with them as he pleases, since he can even command the angels and save men or damn whomever he wishes. A man was made Pope for money <note>This refers to the sin of simony—buying or selling sacred church offices.</note>, who was given the name **Sylvester**, but he was then cast down, and **Benedict** was restored. <margin>V.</margin>Fifth, in the year of our Lord 907, **Pope Leo** presided, against whom **Christopher** rose up.

He says secondly that Blessed Jerome speaks to the Pope in this way because he was certain of the faith about which he wrote; for in that letter, he wrote specifically what is contained in Scripture and in the **creeds of the church** <note>original: "symbolis ecclesię"</note>, as is evident to anyone wishing to read the letter. Hence he says: "This is the faith which we have learned in the Catholic Church, and which we have always held." And it is clear how Jerome’s conditional statement is to be understood: that if his confession of faith is confirmed by that Pope’s judgment, whoever might wish to challenge it would be a heretic. For he said and asserted this by reputation—not from a divine revelation or from the certainty of the faith he set forth—assuming that the Pope would confirm nothing but the truth, and would not "correct" what had long been properly held in the church.

But it would be the mark of a madman to believe that this must be applied as a general rule to every Roman pontiff, because it is certain that many of them ratified errors and heresies, for they were themselves heretics. Hence, in distinction 23, in the decree titled "In the name of the Lord" <note>original: "In nomine domini." A famous 1059 decree by Pope Nicholas II which established that only Cardinal-Bishops should elect the Pope to prevent corruption.</note>, the text relates how the Pope complains that the Apostolic See is often struck by the repeated blows of the **simoniacal heresy** <note>Simony is the crime of buying or selling church offices or spiritual favors.</note>.

<margin>Electors of the Pope.</margin> 

Therefore, wishing to provide a remedy for the future, he decreed that upon the death of a Pope, the religious Cardinals, clergy, and laity should meet to elect a suitable Pope from the bosom of that church or another, wherever one might be most suitable—always preserving the privilege of the **Emperor Henry**, so that he and his heirs should have a role in the election. Once elected, as the true Pope, he shall have the power of disposing of the goods of the church even before his consecration, following the example of Blessed Gregory. Anyone who obstructs this order is anathematized <note>Formally cursed or excommunicated.</note> as the worst sort of antichrist.
