# CHAPTER XVII

Furthermore, as a primary point by which the aforementioned doctors <note>Hus refers to the faculty of the University of Prague and the high-ranking clergy who were his theological opponents.</note> believe all their statements to be necessary or true, they assert: That the Apostolic See of the Roman Church and its Prelates must be obeyed by their subordinates in all things whatsoever, except where a "pure good" is prohibited or a "pure evil" is commanded. They focus instead on the "middle ground" <term>indifferentia<gloss>Actions that are not inherently virtuous or sinful in themselves, but become so based on circumstances.</gloss></term>, which—depending on the manner, place, time, or person—can be either good or evil, according to the words of the Savior in Matthew 23: "All things whatsoever they say to you, observe and do." They also add, following Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), an influential mystic and Church Father often cited by Hus.</note> in his letter to the monk Adam beginning "If you remain in charity, etc.": the law of obedience was placed just like the tree of the knowledge of good and evil which was in the middle of Paradise. In these matters, it is certainly not right for us to impose our own understanding over the judgment of the Masters; in these things, neither the command nor the prohibition of the Prelates is to be despised. These are his words.

In the combination of the points mentioned above, the doctors <note>The "doctors" refers to the senior theological faculty at the University of Prague who opposed Hus's reforms.</note> mix truths with falsehoods, flattery with terror; these things are all entangled in their words. "But some of the clergy," they say—noting our side here—"refuse to consent, striving as much as they can to lead the faithful people into disobedience." And thirdly, the intention of our side is that the Clergy should live sincerely according to the Gospel of Jesus Christ, with pomp, greed, and luxury cast aside. And fourthly, our side desires and preaches that the Church Militant <note>original: "militans ecclesia." The church on earth, struggling against sin and the devil.</note>—composed sincerely of the parts ordained by the Lord—should be a unified mixture: namely, of the priests of Christ purely observing His law; of the world’s nobles compelling others to the observation of Christ's ordinance; and of the common people serving both of these groups according to the Law of Christ. [...and that they claim the leader of this disobedience] is Christ JESUS, whom they have not dared to name, either because they forgot to level a new slander about the disobedience of JESUS Christ—to serve whom is to reign <note>original: "cui seruire regnare est." Therefore, regarding that saying of the Doctors, that "the Apostolic See of the Roman church and the prelates must be obeyed by their inferiors in all things," etc.

<margin>What obedience is.</margin>
We must speak now concerning obedience. It should be noted, therefore, that obedience is first understood analogically, or in a very general sense, as the compliance of any creature whatsoever with respect to the divine will, which all creatures obey. They do so either without resistance—as a stone obeys by falling or moving downward, or fire by rising, or the sun by giving light, and likewise with other creatures—or they obey with resistance, like the devil or a damned human, who must obey by suffering the punishment he deserves. And it is in this way that the Saints speak when they say that all things obey their Creator; only the sinful man does not obey—that is, he does not submit to the Creator’s command without the resistance of his own will.

<margin>Obedience as a virtue.</margin>
But then, obedience insofar as it is an act of virtue or a virtue itself is described by some in this way: "Obedience is the subjection of one's own will to the judgment of a superior in matters that are lawful and honest." Or: "Obedience is the habit of carrying out the command of a superior’s will in matters that are lawful and honest." The first description is given in terms of an *act*, while the second is given in terms of a *habit* <note>In medieval theology, an "act" is a specific deed, while a "habit" is a settled disposition or character trait to perform such deeds.</note>. From these descriptions, it follows that there is no "obedience" in matters that are unlawful, and thus the term "obedience" implies something good, just as "disobedience" implies something evil. 

But it seems to me that the first description fails in this regard: that obedience is a more general concept than "subjection." This is because obedience is attributed even to God, but subjection is not; for God "obeyed" the voice of man. For in Joshua 10, it is said: "There was not before or after so long a day, with the Lord obeying the voice of man <note>original: "obediente dño uoci hoīs." Referring to the miracle where Joshua commanded the sun to stand still and God granted the request.</note> and fighting for Israel." And yet, God the Trinity was not "subject" or "subordinate" to man as if He were an inferior. Furthermore, not all obedience is toward the judgment of a superi-

Since therefore Christ did nothing except what he ought, <margin>The greater ought to be subject to the lesser, following the example of Christ.</margin> it is clear that the greater should be subject or obedient to the lesser; for whatever the fountainhead of religion <note>original: "fons religionis," referring to Christ as the source of all Christian practice.</note> has taught as the primary authority must be held.

Hence Christ, who was of a dual nature <note>The "dual nature" refers to the orthodox Christian doctrine that Christ is simultaneously fully God and fully human.</note>, was doubly obedient. For he obeyed God the Father above all things, as being lesser than the Father according to his humanity; for he himself said in John 14: *The Father is greater than I.* Secondly, he obeyed his parents, who were, as has been said, lesser than him. And he was obedient even to others, willingly sustaining his passion <note>The "passion" refers to the suffering and crucifixion of Jesus.</note> from them; and he is obedient to true and holy Christians, supplying their needs and fulfilling their will.

And it is clear that it does not follow that "if that person obeys that one, therefore he is lesser than him." Similarly, it does not follow that "if that person serves that one, therefore he is lesser than him." For Christ obeyed another man and served him; wherefore in Isaiah 43 he says: *You have made me serve in your sins, you have presented labor to me in your iniquities; I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins; bring me to remembrance that we may be judged together.* And in Matthew 20 he says: *The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve.* And regarding him, the Apostle says in Philippians 2: *Christ emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.* And in John 13, he girded himself with a towel, put water into a basin, and washed the feet of the disciples.

Hence, he is not falsely, but truly the bishop, the <term>servant of the servants of God</term> <note>original: "servus servorum dei." While this was a formal title for the Pope, Hus uses it here to describe Christ’s ultimate humility.</note>, not only the Roman one but generally of all churches. He is the Bishop of Prague. But just as he is a servant or minister, it is not by civil exaction <note>i.e., not through legal force, taxation, or worldly power.</note>, because an exacted active life was not suited to him; just as he is the bishop of souls, not of secular riches or possessions. For the Bishop himself mounted only once the foal of a donkey, humble and mild, as Zechariah 9 testifies. And Matthew 8 says: *Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests...*

And it is also in response to counsel <note>In medieval theology, a "counsel" (consilium) is a divine recommendation—like the vow of poverty—that is virtuous but not strictly required for salvation, unlike a "command" (praeceptum).</note>, as when a person obeys the counsels of God, to which he is not bound under penalty of mortal sin. ## C H A P T E R XVIII

Having already noted some sayings regarding **Obedience**, I now wish to return to the teaching of the doctors, in which it is clear that the **Apostolic See** of the Roman church and the prelates must be obeyed by subordinates in all things whatsoever, provided that a "lesser good" is not prohibited, or a "pure evil" is not commanded, but rather things that are "middle" <note>In medieval philosophy, "middle acts" (indifferentia) are those neither strictly commanded nor forbidden by God, such as specific fasting rules or administrative tasks.</note> etc.

<margin>What the Canonists <note>Experts in Canon Law, the internal legal system of the Catholic Church.</note> babble about the Apostolic See.</margin>
Where it must be noted concerning the **Apostolic See**, about which many—and especially the **Canonists**—preach much, yet they are ignorant of what the Apostolic See actually is. For some estimate that it is specifically a wooden or stone seat in which the **Pope** is accustomed to reside bodily. Others think it is the Roman Curia <note>The administrative bureaucracy that assists the Pope in governing the Church.</note>. Others that it is the seat of **Saint Peter** in which he bodily resided. Others that it is Rome. Others that it is the power of the Pope. Others...

<sig>V iij</sig>

<header>I. H. ON THE CHURCH</header>

...which is the church or basilica of St. Peter.

But it must be noted that "Apostolic" is derived from an apostolic person, <margin>Apostle means "one sent."</margin> and an apostolic person is so called from an "Apostle." An Apostle, moreover, is said to be one sent by God. Regarding the one whom God has sent, the Savior says in John 3: "I speak the words of God." <note>original: "Verba dei loquor." Hus uses this to argue that a true representative of God must speak God's truth, not their own mandates.</note> Wherefore he also says to the disciples in John 20: "As the Father has sent me, even so I send you," <note>original: "Sicut misit me pater, & ego mittam uos"</note> namely, to the testimony of truth, to the preaching of the word of salvation, and to showing the people the way of blessedness by both life and doctrine. From this, any priest who seeks not his own glory, but the honor of God, the progress of the church, and the salvation of the people—and who does the will of God and exposes the deceits of the Antichrist by preaching the law of Christ—he possesses the signs which show that God himself sent him. Hence, regarding glory, Christ says in John 5: "I do not receive glory from men." <note>original: "Claritatem ab hominibus non accipio"</note> And in John 8: "I do not seek my own glory." Regarding the second point, he says in John 6: "I have come in my Father’s name, and you have not received me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive." Regarding the third, he says in John 6: "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Christ did the will of the Father because he sought the progress of the church and the salvation of the people. Regarding the fourth, he says in John 7: "The world hates me, because I bear witness of it, that its works are evil." And ultimately, Christ showed that he was sent by God because he did the works of the Father. Wherefore in John 10: "If I do not the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, though you do not want to believe me, believe the works." And it is evident that a priest’s holy conversation <note>In the 15th-century sense, "conversation" refers to one's entire way of life and conduct among others.</note> and fruitful labor <margin>Which priest is to be believed as sent by God.</margin> in Christ’s word show the people that he is sent by God, because he does the works of the Father. Nor should a Pope, bishop, priest, or preacher be otherwise, unless he is thus sent by God; and hence the Apostle says in Romans 10: "How shall they preach unless they are sent?" Wherefore the Blessed Augustine, in the *Sixty-Five Questions of Orosius*, speaks thus when Orosius asks: "How can we know those who are sent by God?" <margin>Sent.</margin> Augustine: "Recognize the one sent by God as the one whom not a few men..."

<summary>Hus defines the term "Apostolic" by the character of being "sent by God," arguing that a true priest or Pope is recognized not by his title, but by his holy conduct and his preaching of God's word rather than his own glory.</summary>

### CHAPTER XVIII. 151

...[whom the] praise of men, or rather flattery, has chosen, but him whom the best of life and character, and the examination of Apostolic priests, or the judgment of all the people has approved—one who does not crave to rule, and who does not give money to receive the honor of the bishop’s office. For he who hurries to rule, as one of the Fathers elegantly expressed it, should know that he is not a bishop, since he desires to rule rather than to be of service. Thus says Augustine. <note>original: "Haec August." Hus is likely referencing Augustine’s "City of God," Book 19, Chapter 19, which discusses the idea that the title of bishop should imply service (prodesse) rather than just dominance (praeesse).</note>

<margin>Who is apostolic.</margin>
<margin>A false apostolic.</margin>
Having established what an Apostle is in general, we can now understand what "Apostolic" means. For a person is called "apostolic" if they guard the way of an apostle. Just as a "true Christian" is one who imitates Christ in his character, so a "true apostolic" man is a priest who follows the doctrine of the apostles, living the life of an apostle and teaching their doctrine. From this it follows that any Pope, to the extent that he teaches the doctrine of the Apostles and carries it out in his works, is to that degree called apostolic. But if he sets aside the doctrine of the Apostles, teaching the contrary by word or deed, then he is truly called a "pseudo-apostolic" <note>A false apostle or false representative.</note> or an "apostate." Hence, in Distinction 79 <note>original: "dist. lxxix." A reference to Gratian’s "Decretum," the standard collection of Canon Law used in the medieval Church.</note>: "If anyone has been enthroned to the Apostolic See through money or human favor, or by a popular or military riot, without a concordant and canonical election, let him be held not as apostolic, but as an apostate." Since, therefore, there is a greater error in the active election when the electors are compelled by the devil to choose a person whom God rejects—which is clearly evident from his works and his neglect of the spiritual office, as he is contrary to the life of the apostles—it follows much more strongly that such a person is to be held not as apostolic, but as an apostate.

<margin>The Apostolic See is the praiseworthy life of a priest.</margin>
The Apostolic See can therefore, based on what has been said, be called the life of a priest who effectively guards the life of an apostle, just as the seat of an apostle is the life of an apostle. Wherefore Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, a highly influential 4th-century preacher and Church Father.</note> in Homily 25 says: "The throne of each apostle is that virtue in which he was more perfect than the others. However, all the virtues of Christ are, as it were, a single seat, because He alone was equally perfect in every virtue." Behold, this holy man rightly perceives that the singular life of every apostle of Christ is his seat, in which he rested here by earning merit, by reason of which...

<summary>Jan Hus defines "Apostolic" authority as something earned through the imitation of the Apostles' lives and doctrines, rather than through mere election or payment. He argues that a Pope who fails to follow these examples is not truly apostolic but is an "apostate."</summary>

## BOOK II. ON THE CHURCH

of which See he now resides in the glory of Jesus Christ, according to that passage in Matthew 19: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats.* <note>Matthew 19:28. In older translations, "seats" refers to thrones of judgment.</note> Where, according to Augustine, by "twelve seats" is understood the placement of the apostles and of any holy predestined prelates <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note>; since this placement is in a state of blessedness, it cannot fail or be destroyed by tyrants. However, the number twelve, which is the number of universality, does not signify those twelve apostles individually, since at that time [Judas] Iscariot still reigned [among them], and Paul was [still] subject to him <note>Hus is pointing out that "twelve" is a symbolic number for the whole Church leadership, as Judas was still technically an apostle while Paul was still a persecutor of Christians.</note>.

<margin>The Seat of Christ</margin>
But by the **Seat of Christ’s Majesty** is understood the establishment of the eternal kingdom, from which he can never be removed. And that Seat of Christ is his *intrinsic* seat. But his *extrinsic* seat—in which he rests, dwells, or resides through grace—is all the saints.

<margin>The Seat of Satan</margin>
Just as, on the other hand, the **seats of Satan**, in which he rests, dwells, or resides, are all the wicked. Hence in Revelation 2, the one like the Son of Man, who has a sword sharp on both sides, said to the Angel of the Church at Pergamum: *I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is.* <note>Revelation 2:12-13.</note> On this, the gloss <note>A "gloss" refers to the *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> says: "understand this to mean those in whom Satan rests; yet you hold my name, and you did not deny my faith among those where Satan dwells."

But to the main point: the **Apostolic See** is the same as the **Chair of Moses**, of which the Savior says in Matthew 23: *The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses.* Now, the Chair of Moses is not Moses himself, nor is it a high seat for Moses made of wood or stone, as if for a presiding judge. Nor is it the synagogue. Rather, that Chair is the *authority* of teaching and judging the people. This is shown by the words of Christ when he says, "Upon the chair of Moses," and follows with, "what they say"—that is, what they teach from the authority and doctrine of Moses—"do [them]."

<margin>The Apostolic See is the authority of teaching according to the law of Christ.</margin>
The **Apostolic See**, therefore, is the authority of teaching and judging according to the law of Christ, which the apostles taught. In this See should reside men who are wise and God-fearing, in whom there is truth, and who hate avarice. For so it says in Exodus 18, when Moses said to his father-in-law Jethro: "The people come to me..."

How remarkably he touches upon the Roman prelates.

Would that that **Chair** <note>original: "Cathedra"; referring to a seat of authority or a bishop’s throne.</note> now had such men! And where can they be discerned? Certainly in the Roman Curia <note>The administrative and judicial body that assists the Pope.</note>, where they preside over the **Chair of Saint Peter**—that is, they sit in the authority of the Apostles, which is the authority of judging spiritual matters and teaching the law of the Lord Jesus Christ—if only that greed, injustice, and pride were excluded, and a holy life flourished. The Savior himself testifies, saying in Matthew 23: *The scribes and Pharisees sit on the Chair of Moses; therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do, but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not.* <note>Matthew 23:2-3.</note> Behold, here he touches upon a life lacking the works of the law. For *they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on men's shoulders*—behold, indiscreet doctrine and injustice! *But they will not move them with their own finger*—behold, a luxurious life. *They do all their works to be seen by men*—behold, vain glory. For they broaden their **phylacteries** <note>original: "philacteria"; small leather boxes containing Hebrew texts worn by Jews during prayer. Hus is making a biting pun here.</note> throughout the whole world, as if they themselves were the first ones observing the law of the Lord—there is hypocrisy. They magnify the fringes with which they cover their mules. <note>High-ranking clergy were often criticized for the lavish decorations on their horses and mules.</note> They love the first places at feasts for pleasure and honor, and the first chairs in the Synagogues—that is, in the gatherings of the churches—because this one wants to be a Cardinal, that one a Patriarch, that one an Archbishop; and greetings with kneeling in the marketplace—that is, in public—and to be called by men "Rabbi"—that is, "Our Master"...

...so governing the church of Christ. Whence they also call the **Roman Curia** <note>The administrative and judicial body of the Papacy.</note> the teacher of the churches.

And granted these things as possible, they themselves are the seats—not of Christ, but of Satan—sitting according to their own life in the **Chair of pestilence** <note>original: "Cathedra pestilentiæ"; from the Latin Vulgate of Psalm 1:1, often translated as the "seat of the scornful." Concerning which the **Psalmist** <note>King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note>, speaking of Jesus Christ, says: *Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the chair of pestilence.* Where **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Hus.</note> says it is to be understood regarding our Lord Jesus Christ as the "Lordly Man" <note>original: "homine dominico"; a term Augustine used to emphasize Christ's humanity as the model for believers.</note>, who does not sit in the Chair of pestilence. 

<margin>
The Chair of pestilence.
</margin>

He did not want an earthly kingdom with pride, which is the chair of pestilence; and rightly so again, because there is almost no one who lacks the love of ruling and does not crave human glory. Pestilence is a disease spreading widely and involving all, or almost all. Although "Chair" is more suitably understood as destructive doctrine, whose speech spreads like a cancer. Thus says the Blessed Augustine, calling the Chair of pestilence the **lust for power** <note>original: "libidinem dominandi"</note> and destructive doctrine, in which Chair the Elders of the church sit, wishing to rule in a secular manner, and teaching that their own mandates and doctrines should be observed more firmly than the mandates of God.

<margin>
Those who truly sit in the chair.
</margin>

However, he truly sits in the Chair—that is, in the authority and doctrine of the law—who teaches the law and performs the mandates of the law. Whence Augustine says regarding that verse of the Psalm, *His will is in the law of the Lord*: "It is one thing to be in the law, another to be under the law. He who is in the law acts and behaves according to the law. He who is under the law is driven according to the law." 

Behold, a plain exposition of the saint. *Whoever therefore does and teaches them, he shall be great in the kingdom of heaven,* says the Savior in **Matthew** five. Therefore, he truly sits in the **Chair of Moses** or the **Chair of Peter** who, in the authority of Scripture, both lives well and teaches well, adding nothing foreign to the law. Nor does he seek profit or pride from the Chair. Conversely, he sits poorly in the Chair who teaches poorly or lives poorly, or who teaches good things but lives poorly, or who neither teaches good things nor lives well—and such, alas, are many, who seek what is their own, and not what [is of Jesus Christ]...

This is Augustine’s point, and at the end of that homily he concludes, saying: "Behold why the hireling is said to flee when he sees the wolf. Why? Because he does not care for the sheep. Why does he not care for the sheep? Because he is a hireling. What is a hireling? It is one who seeks temporal reward; he shall not dwell in the house [of the Lord] forever."

Here Augustine shows those who, being hirelings now in the church, sit in the Chair—that is, in the authority of teaching the law of God. And again, in his commentary on the Gospel of **John**, regarding that last word of John, that **Simon Peter** pulled the net full of great fish <note>Refers to the miraculous catch of 153 fish in John 21:11, often interpreted allegorically as the gathering of the elect into the Church.</note>, he says: "He is the least who undoes by his actions what he teaches with words."

And further below, finally, so that he might show that these "least" ones are reprobates—who teach good things by speaking, but undo them by living badly—he says that they will not just be "least" in eternal life, but will not be there at all. When he had said, "he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven," he immediately added: "Unless your **righteousness** <note>original: "iustitia"; Hus emphasizes that outward religious status is worthless without internal moral integrity.</note> abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees," [you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven].

# CHAPTER XVIII

<margin>What is the Chair of Moses or of Peter?</margin>
From what has already been said, it is clear that the **Chair of Moses** or the **Apostolic See** <note>original: "Sedes Apostolica"; the seat of authority of the Pope as successor to St. Peter.</note> is the authority for teaching the law of God, or the lineage of holy Popes or of the bishops succeeding them. This lineage provides—as is perceived to be for the greater honor of God, the greater utility of the Holy Church, and more wholesome for both the ruler and the subject—by not appointing the unworthy, not setting aside the humble, and not limitlessly assigning church offices through profit-seeking, blood relations <note>original: "sanguinem"; referring to nepotism, the practice of giving offices to relatives.</note>, or any private affection.

<margin>Which mandates are truly Apostolic and to be accepted.</margin>
And it is further evident which mandates are "Apostolic," as the **Lord of Lincoln** <note>Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), Bishop of Lincoln, a famous English theologian and scientist who famously refused to appoint a nephew of Pope Innocent IV to a church position.</note> says in his response to the letters of the Roman Pontiff regarding the appointment of a certain relative as a **Canon** <note>A priest serving in a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> of the church of Lincoln. He responds thus: 

> "I obey," he said, "Apostolic mandates with all filial affection, both devotedly and reverently. But to those things which oppose Apostolic mandates, I, being zealous for my Father’s honor, oppose and resist; I am bound to both by reason of my status as a son, according to the divine command. Indeed, Apostolic mandates are not—and cannot be—anything other than the Apostolic doctrines and those of our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, the Master of the Apostles." 

Thus spoke the man of Lincoln. Therefore, a faithful disciple of Christ must weigh, when an **Apostolic mandate** emanates, whether it is expressly a command of some Apostle, or of the law of Christ, or has its foundation in the law of Christ; and once that is known, he must reverently and humbly obey such a mandate. ...they love [favors] from their Superior, and for these things God is served; whoever is such a person is a **mercenary** <note>original: "mercenarius"; often translated as "hireling," referring to someone who works only for pay rather than out of love for the flock.</note>; he should not count himself among the children. For concerning such people, the Lord says: "Truly I say to you, they have received their reward." <note>Matthew 6:2</note> Thus speaks **Augustine**. 

But regarding the fact that such people sit in the **Chair**, he says in the same place, after some intervening words: "Listen to how even mercenaries are necessary. For many in the church, though they pursue earthly advantages, nevertheless preach **Christ**; and through them, the voice of **Christ** is heard, and the sheep follow not the mercenaries, but the voice of the Shepherd through the mercenary." Listen to how the mercenaries were pointed out by the Lord himself. He says: "The scribes and Pharisees sit upon the **Chair of Moses**; what they say, do; but what they do, do not do." <note>Matthew 23:2–3</note> 

What else did he say except: "Through the mercenary, hear the voice of the Shepherd"? For by sitting in the **Chair of Moses**, they teach the law of God; therefore, God teaches through them. But if they wish to teach their own things, do not listen, do not act; for surely such people seek their own interests, not those of **Jesus Christ**. Yet no mercenary has dared to say to the people of God, "I seek my own things, not those of **Jesus Christ**." 

Here **Augustine**, at the end of that homily, concludes by saying: "Behold why the mercenary is said to flee when he sees the wolf. Why? Because he has no care for the sheep. Why does he have no care for the sheep? Because he is a mercenary. What is a mercenary? It is one who seeks temporal reward; he shall not dwell in the house [of the Lord] forever." 

Here **Augustine** shows who the mercenaries currently existing in the **church** are, who sit in the **Chair**—that is, in the authority of teaching the law of God. And again, commenting on John—regarding that final word of John, "Simon Peter drew the net full of great fish" <note>John 21:11</note>—he says: "He is least who undoes by his deeds what he teaches by his words." 

And further on, finally, so that he might show that these "least ones" are the wicked—those who teach by speaking good words, which they undo by living wickedly—and that they will not be as the "least" in eternal life, but will not be there at all; when he had said, "he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven," he immediately added: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and **Pha-**" <note>The text continues on the next page: "...risees."</note>

### CHAPTER XVIII

...of the Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven." <note>original: "Pharisaeorum"; this completes the sentence from the previous page referencing Matthew 5:20.</note> Certainly, those are the scribes and Pharisees who sit in the **Chair of Moses**. And of whom he says: "What they say, do; but what they do, do not do; for they say and do not do." <note>Matthew 23:3</note> They teach with words and undermine by their conduct. This is what **Augustine** says. And he speaks similarly upon the Psalm, *Blessed are the undefiled*, regarding that verse: *Blessed are they who search his testimonies, they seek him with their whole heart.* <note>Psalm 119 (118):1-2</note>

<margin>What the Chair of Moses or of Peter is.</margin>
From what has already been said, it is clear that the **Chair of Moses** or the **Apostolic See** <note>original: "Sedes Apostolica"; the official seat or authority of the Pope.</note> is the authority for teaching the law of God, or the succession of holy Popes or bishops who follow them. This succession provides—as it feels is more excellent for the honor of God, more useful for the Holy Church, and more healthful for both the leader and the subject—not by promoting the unworthy, nor by setting aside the humble, nor by limiting an ecclesiastical office through greed, blood relations, or some private affection.

<margin>Which are truly Apostolic mandates and to be received with reverence.</margin>
And it is further clear what **Apostolic mandates** are, as the Lord of **Lincoln** <note>original: "Lynconien."; referring to Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), Bishop of Lincoln, famous for his moral independence and critiques of the papacy.</note> says in his response to the letters of the Roman Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent IV</note> concerning the appointment of a certain relative as a Canon of the church of **Lincoln**. He responds thus: "I obey Apostolic mandates," he says, "with filial affection, entirely, devotedly, and reverently. But to those things which oppose Apostolic mandates, being zealous for my Father’s honor, I oppose and resist them. To both of these I am bound by reason of my sonship, according to the divine command. For **Apostolic mandates** are not, nor can they be, anything other than the Apostolic doctrines and those of our Lord **Jesus Christ** himself, the Master of the Apostles." Thus speaks the man of **Lincoln**. 

Therefore, a faithful disciple of **Christ** ought to weigh, when an Apostolic mandate emanates, whether it is expressly a mandate of any Apostle, or of the law of **Christ**, or has its foundation in the law of **Christ**; and once that is known, he must reverently and humbly obey such a mandate. If, however, he truly recognizes that a mandate of the **Pope** opposes a mandate or counsel of **Christ**, or tends toward some evil for the church, then he must boldly re-

...to resist, lest he become a participant in the crime by his consent. <note>original: "particeps criminis ex consensu"</note> Wherefore, trusting in the Lord and in Jesus Christ—who powerfully and wisely protects those who profess His truth and rewards them with the prize of eternal glory—I resisted the **Bull of Pope Alexander V**. This bull was obtained in the year of our Lord 1409 by Lord **Zbyněk**, the Archbishop of Prague. In it, he commanded that no one (even if they were fortified by an **Apostolic** or any other kind of grant <note>A formal license or "indult" giving someone permission to do something usually restricted by canon law.</note>) should perform preachings or

<margin>The word of God must be preached everywhere, following the example of Christ.</margin>
sermons to the people, except in Cathedral, Collegiate, Parochial, or Monastic churches, or in their cemeteries. This mandate is contrary to the deeds and words of Christ and His apostles; it is not **Apostolic**. For Christ preached to the people on the sea, in the desert, in the fields, in houses, in synagogues, in villages, and in the streets. He commanded His disciples, saying in the last chapter of Mark: *Go into the whole world, preach the gospel to every creature.* <note>Mark 16:15</note> And they went forth and preached everywhere—that is, wherever the people wished to hear—with the Lord cooperating. Therefore, this mandate is to the detriment of the Church, for it binds the word of God so that it may not run freely. Thirdly, it is to the prejudice of the **chapels** <note>This refers specifically to the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, where Hus preached, which was not a parish church.</note> that were established and confirmed by the Diocesan bishops and reasonably privileged by the **Apostolic See** <note>The office or jurisdiction of the Pope.</note> for the purpose of preaching the word of the Lord within them. For no benefit is seen to arise from that mandate, but rather a deceitful and inconsistent illusion. In this matter, places designated for divine ministry and reasonably privileged for the divine word are despoiled of their lawful liberties because of private affection, or an injurious or troublesome petition, or for the sake of temporal gain. Therefore, I appealed from that mandate to **Alexander** himself, so that he might be better informed. But while I was pursuing that appeal, the Lord Pope himself died shortly thereafter.

# CHAPTER XVIII

...I appealed to **Pope John XXIII** <note>original: "ad Papam Ioannē. xxiij." Hus is referring to the Pisan Pope Baldassare Cossa, who was later deposed.</note>, who for two years granted no audience to my advocates and proxies, and in the meantime, I was further burdened by legal proceedings. Since, therefore, an appeal from one Pope to his successor did not profit me, and to appeal from a Pope to a council is a long and uncertain aid to seek in a grievance, I have ultimately appealed to the head of the church, the **Lord Jesus Christ**. For He Himself is more excellent than any Pope in deciding a case, as He cannot err, nor deny justice to one who asks rightly, nor can He damn a person without demerit according to His own established law.

<margin>Indulgences</margin>
Furthermore, I resisted the divine ordinance regarding the **indulgences** <note>Payments made to the church in exchange for the remission of temporal punishment for sin. Hus famously opposed the 1412 sale of indulgences to fund a crusade against the King of Naples.</note> made or promulgated in the year of our Lord 1412 <note>The text reads M.CCCC.II (1402), likely a printer's error for M.CCCC.XII (1412), the year of the specific indulgence controversy Hus refers to.</note> by the Bulls of **Pope John XXIII**, about which enough has been said elsewhere. For a Pope can command nothing lawfully except for the destruction of malice and the building up of the church; this should be held universally. The **Apostle** <note>Refers to St. Paul.</note> testifies to this in 2 Corinthians 10, saying: *The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty in God for the destruction of strongholds, by which we demolish counsels and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.* And in the last chapter of 2 Corinthians, he says: *Lest I should act more harshly according to the power which the Lord has given me for building up, and not for destruction.* <note>2 Corinthians 10:4-5 and 13:10</note> 
<margin>What a Pope may lawfully command.</margin>
Wherefore, the **Bishop of Lincoln** <note>original: "Lynconiēñ." Refers to Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous English scholar and bishop known for challenging papal abuses.</note> writes in a letter to the Pope: "The Apostolic See cannot create a schism, for to it has been handed a power of every kind by the holy Lord of the holy ones, Jesus Christ—as the Apostle testifies—for building up, and not for destruction." And further down: "Nor," he says, "can your discretion decree anything harsh against me because of this, because all my speech or action in this matter is neither a contradiction nor a rebellion, but a filial duty owed to Father and Mother—that is, the honoring of Christ and the Church, because it is the observation of a divine mandate."

Briefly summarizing, I say that the holiness of the **Apostolic See** <note>The authority of the Pope/Rome.</note> can only act toward building up and not toward destruction; for this is the **fullness of power** <note>original: "plenitudo potestatis" — a technical legal term for the Pope's supreme authority.</note>: to be able to do all things for the purpose of building up. 
<margin>Appeal from the Pope to Christ.</margin>
However, these things which they call **provisions** <note>The practice where the Pope appointed his own candidates to church offices (benefices), often for a fee, bypassing local authorities.</note> are not for building up, but for manifest destruction; therefore, the most blessed Apostolic See cannot perform them. These are the words of the Bishop of Lincoln.

# THE CHURCH BY JAN HUS

...because he appealed to the tribunal of Christ against the Pope. Whence the *Cestrensis* <note>original: "Cestreñ." Refers to Ranulf Higden, a monk of Chester and author of the *Polychronicon*.</note> narrates in his seventh book how, upon the death of **Robert of Lincoln** <note>Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), a famous Bishop of Lincoln who challenged papal abuses.</note>, a voice was heard in the Papal court saying: "Come, you wretch, to judgment." And on the following morning, the Pope <note>Innocent IV, whom Grosseteste had opposed regarding the appointment of the Pope's nephew to a canonry.</note> was found dead, as if struck in the side by the tip of a staff. Although the Bishop of Lincoln shone with the most brilliant miracles, he was nonetheless not permitted into the **Catalog of Saints** by the court.

<margin>The Pope is capable of the most serious error.</margin>
And it is clear that a Pope can err, and all the more seriously in cases where his sin would be multiplied more abundantly, more intensely, and more insurmountably, as **Bernard** <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, in his treatise *De Consideratione* addressed to Pope Eugenius III.</note> says in his book to Pope Eugenius. It is more *abundantly* sinful if it spreads through all of Christendom; more *intensely*, if it concerns the withdrawal of spiritual goods regarding the care of souls; and *insurmountably*, if no one dares to contradict him—partly because of his alliance with the **secular arm** <note>The power of the state or civil government used to enforce church decrees.</note>, partly because of the cloaked censures thundered against the "sons of obedience," and partly because of the ecclesiastical promotions and dignities he provides for his accomplices. Hence, just as a Papal office that benefits the church deserves more merit, so a Papal office corrupted in a man who abuses his position, infecting the church more widely, deserves greater condemnation.

<margin>Signs by which a failure of the Pope is noted.</margin>
Now, a sign of the Pope's failure is if, having set aside the law of God and the devout professions of the Gospel, he attends to human traditions—a point on which Bernard rebuked Eugenius. 

The **second sign** is if the Pope and ecclesiastical superiors, abandoning the lifestyle of Christ, are entangled in the world in a secular manner. 

The **third sign** is if he appoints merchants of the world into the ministry of Christ and strives primarily to maintain a secular life, while the poor churches are burdened. 

The **fourth sign** is if, through his own command or the placement of unfit persons in pastoral care, he deprives souls that should be saved of the word of God. 

Hence, considering this, the **Bishop of Lincoln** <note>Robert Grosseteste.</note> refused to admit a certain relative of the Pope as a canon in the church of Lincoln, making among other things a sound argument. "After the sin of **Lucifer**," he said, "which will be the same at the end of time during the reign of the son of perdition, the **Antichrist**, whom the Lord JESUS will kill with the spirit of his mouth. Nor is there, nor can there be, any other kind of behavior so adverse or contrary...

### CHAPTER XVIII

...contrary to apostolic or evangelical doctrine, and so hateful, detestable, and abominable to the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and so destructive to the human race, as to kill and destroy souls that ought to be quickened and saved by the office and ministry of pastoral care, through the deprivation of that pastoral ministry. 

<margin>It is supremely contrary to the Gospel to shear the sheep and not feed them.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the argument of Jan Hus, building upon his citations of Robert Grosseteste. Having established that the neglect of souls is a supreme sin, Hus now directs this critique toward the contemporary Papacy and its administrative systems.</meta>

# JAN HUS ON THE CHURCH

...these two sins are more serious, insofar as they are opposed to greater goods. And since God himself is the primary cause of those goods, it follows that the slayers and destroyers of the sheep are worse than others, just as the slaying and destruction of the sheep are themselves worse sins. It is clear, then, that the worst ministers of Antichrist and Satan are those who kill souls.

<margin>The Pope harms the church through the distribution of benefices.</margin>
From these points, it is held that to rebel against one who goes astray is nearly the same as obeying Christ the Lord. This problem arises most especially from "provisions" <note>Ecclesiastical appointments made by the Pope before a position was even vacant.</note> which savor of personal favoritism. Therefore, I call the world to witness that the Papal distribution of benefices <note>original: "beneficiorum"; church offices that provided a guaranteed income.</note> sows hirelings <note>original: "mercenarios"; those who serve only for the wage rather than for the spiritual care of the people.</note> far too widely in the church. On the part of the Popes, it gives occasion for them to boast of their delegated power, to over-value worldly dignity, and to affect a pretended holiness. Furthermore, those doctors who expect a worldly reward from the Pope, or who serve his power out of a slave-like fear—and who thus claim his power is incomprehensible, that he is incapable of sin, that he cannot be corrected, or that he may lawfully do whatever he pleases—these are the false prophets and false apostles of Antichrist.

<margin>What is the Apostolic See?</margin>
From what has been said, it is now clear that the Apostolic See is the authority of judging and teaching the law of Christ. Or, in a second sense, it is the lineage of holy Popes succeeding one another, as was previously stated. It is in this way that the Apostolic See is understood in the Decree <note>Hus refers here to the "Decretum Gratiani," the collection of canon law.</note> under the section titled *Sacrosancta* <note>original: "Distinct. xxij. Sacrosancta"</note>, where Pope Anacletus says: "But this Apostolic See, the head and hinge, as was aforesaid, was established by the Lord and not by another; and just as a door is governed by a hinge, so by the authority of this holy Apostolic See, all other churches are ruled, the Lord so disposing." This Pope intended to imply that he himself was the "head and hinge"—the head in presiding and the hinge in ruling. But he has a weak enough argument to prove his intention. For he argues by a comparison, saying: "Just as a door is held by a hinge, so by the authority of this holy Apostolic See, all churches are ruled." It would be enough to argue that the Pope, along with his "hinges," <note>original: "cardinibus"; Hus is making a biting pun here. ### CHAPTER XIX

...the distinction of Bernard in his letter to Adam the Monk <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) wrote Letter 7 to a monk named Adam who had left his monastery. Bernard uses this letter to discuss when a monk—or any Christian—is required to obey a superior.</note> concerning pure good and pure evil. Therefore, it should be noted that after Blessed Bernard shows that one should not obey anyone in matters of evil, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, to do evil at anyone’s command is clearly not obedience, but rather disobedience."

<margin>Pure goods and pure evils</margin>
Truly, it must be observed that some things are pure goods and some are pure evils. In these matters, no obedience is owed to men, because those [pure goods] are not to be abandoned even when they are forbidden, <note>The OCR text "omittenda sunt" (must be omitted) likely contains a missing "non" (not) from the original source text of Bernard, which argues that pure goods must *not* be abandoned even if a superior forbids them.</note> nor are those [pure evils] to be committed even when they are commanded. Furthermore, between these two categories are certain "middle things" <note>Also known as *adiaphora*, these are actions that are morally neutral in themselves, such as whether to eat certain foods or wear certain clothes.</note> which, according to the manner, place, time, or person, can be both evil and good. And in these middle things, the law of obedience is established, just like the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil which was in the middle of Paradise. In these matters, it is certainly not right for us to prefer our own judgment to the decision of the masters. In these things, neither the command nor the prohibition of the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> should be despised.

Further down: Faith, hope, and charity are pure goods and other things of this sort; they can neither be forbidden nor neglected. <margin>Pure evils</margin> Pure evils are theft, sacrilege, adultery, and other such things, which certainly can neither be commanded well nor carried out; they cannot be allowed, nor can they be done. No man’s prohibition has the power to oppose the [divine] commands, and no man's command can override what is forbidden [by God]. Next, there are the "middle things," which in themselves are known to be neither good nor evil. <margin>Middle things</margin> These can be commanded or forbidden indifferently, both for good and for bad reasons; however, subjects must never obey them in a bad way. Examples of these things include fasting, keeping vigils, reading, and other such activities.

It should be known, however, that certain middle things pass beyond the status of being neutral or bad. For example, while marriage is something one may or may not choose to enter, once it is entered, it is not permitted to be dissolved. Therefore, what was clearly a "middle thing" before the wedding takes on the force of a "pure good" for those already married. Likewise, for a person living in the world to possess property is a "middle thing," because it is also permitted *not* to possess it. But for a monk, because he is not permitted to possess property [due to his vows], it is a "pure evil." So says Bernard.

He argues that human authorities must be obeyed only in "middle things," while divine law overrides human commands regarding pure goods and evils.</summary>

<margin>a neutral work</margin> It should also be noted, regarding the sense of those speaking about human acts, that a work is called **Neutral** <note>original: "Neutrum"</note> among them which, by its primary intention, expresses neither a moral good nor the evil of a vice, such as building or weaving.

<margin>Works good or evil in kind.</margin> Moreover, works are said to be **good or evil in kind** <note>original: "de genere." These are actions that are generally considered good or bad based on their typical nature, before specific circumstances are considered.</note> which express the substance or nature of a work that is morally good or evil, yet do not imply the circumstances that by themselves establish the nature of such acts in the category of virtue or vice, such as giving alms and killing a man. For both of these can be done as well as they are ill, according to the difference of the cause or the intention of the worker. For to give alms for the sake of vainglory is an evil, just as killing a man by the authority of God, lest he infect the church, is a good. <note>Hus follows the medieval theological tradition which argued that even an act like killing—normally an evil—could be virtuous if commanded by God or performed for the common good (such as capital punishment), while a normally virtuous act like almsgiving is ruined by a bad intention.</note> Some, however, are composite works, which are called **simply** <note>original: "simpliciter," meaning inherently or without qualification.</note> good or evil morally, such as committing adultery and stealing with respect to vice, and charitably loving God and neighbor with respect to virtue.

Briefly, then, some act is **simply good**, such as charitably loving God. Another is **simply evil**, such as hating God. Likewise, something is **good in kind**, which, namely, inclines a person more toward judging it to be good than judging it to be evil, such as fasting or giving alms. Something is **evil in kind**, which, namely, inclines a person more toward judging it to be evil than judging it to be good, although it can be done well, as in the case of killing a man. <margin>A neutral work</margin> But a **neutral work** is called a work that no more inclines a person toward judging it to be good than evil, nor vice versa, such as weaving, eating, plowing, or running. Therefore, a simply good work holds the first rank, a work good in kind holds a sort of middle rank, and a neutral work holds the lowest rank. An example of these three: Loving God, fasting, and weaving. Similarly in their opposites: for a simply evil work is like hating God, and an evil in kind is like killing a man. But the third, namely the neutral, is not given as an evil,

<meta>catchword: evil,</meta>

### CHAPTER XIX

...[neutral], <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the discussion on "neutral" acts from the previous page.</note> because then it would not be neutral. For it is called neutral because it leans no more toward virtue than toward vice, or vice versa.

<margin>A twofold work: virtuous or vicious.</margin>
Furthermore, it should be noted that the immediate division of human works is that they are either virtuous or vicious. This is evident because if a man is in a state of vice and does anything, then he acts viciously. And if he is virtuous and does anything, then he acts virtuously. For just as vice—which is called a crime or a mortal sin—universally infects the acts of a man, so virtue vivifies all the acts of a virtuous man to such an extent that one existing in grace is said to merit and pray even while sleeping or in whatever else he is doing, as the holy doctors say, especially the blessed Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and others. 

And that saying is founded on that word of Jesus Christ our Savior, which he spoke in the sixth chapter of Luke: <note>Hus cites Luke 6, though the passage regarding the "simple eye" is typically found in Luke 11:34 or Matthew 6:22.</note> "If your eye be simple, your whole body will be bright." That is, if the intention <term>intentio</term> <note>In medieval theology, the "intention" is the specific goal or motive that directs a person's will toward an action.</note> is good in grace toward the work, then your whole body—that is, the collection of all your works—will be bright because it is clean before God. But if your eye—that is, your intention—is evil, criminal, and defiled by vice, your whole body—namely of your works—will be dark, that is, vicious. 

Hence the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, commands, saying: "Do all things for the glory of God," in the first chapter of Second Corinthians <note>original: "secunda Corinthiorum primo." This citation actually refers to 1 Corinthians 10:31.</note>. And elsewhere in the last chapter of First Corinthians: "Let all your things be done in charity." Therefore, the whole manner of living charitably is virtuous, and the whole manner of living of a man without charity is vicious. From this it is clear that just as no one can be neutral regarding virtue or vice, since one must either be in the grace of Almighty God or outside of grace, so no manner of life <note>original: "conversatio," referring to one's conduct or way of living.</note> of a man can be neutral. Therefore, in virtuous things one must obey a superior, but in vicious commands one must boldly resist.

<margin>Human commands are not to be cared for as much as God's.</margin>
With these things noted above, every faithful Christian ought to take care lest he believe that if the Roman Pontiff or a Prelate commands anything, it must be done as if it were a command of God. Just as if he...

[...by taking] <note>original: "accipiendo," completing the word from the previous page's catchword</note> his sword to arm yourself against your own throat, would you have acquiesced? If you could have prohibited this for others, would it not also be counted as the crime of homicide? Come then, see that perhaps under the pretext of obedience you have not served something more serious. Thus says Bernard. And he brings forward many testimonies of Scripture and concludes: "You therefore, against all these and other innumerable testimonies of truth in this manner, thought that anyone should be obeyed. O hateful perversity! The virtue of obedience, which always battles for the truth, is being girded against the truth." Thus says Bernard.

<margin>Five conditions of obedience.</margin>
Wherefore Bernard himself, in a sermon on the Advent of the Lord, sets down **five conditions** that make obedience right. **First**, when the work is holy, because one must not obey against God. **Second**, when it is voluntary. **Third**, when it is pure according to a holy intention, following the teaching of the Savior in Matthew 6: *“If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light.”* **Fourth**, when it is discerning <term>discretum</term> <note>In medieval theology, "discretion" is the ability to perceive the correct middle ground and avoid extremes.</note>, since excess or deficiency corrupts it. And **fifth**, when it is firm, persevering until the proper end.

<margin>Nothing but good should be commanded.</margin>
From this it is clear that a subject who considers an undiscerning command of a Superior <term>Praepositus</term> <note>A 'Superior' or 'Provost'—anyone in a position of authority over another in the church hierarchy.</note>—which is known, or ought to be known, to lead to the detriment of the church by distracting from the worship of God and the progress of the salvation of souls—ought to resist that Superior. For such resistance is true obedience, performed not only toward God according to the law of **fraternal correction** <term>fraterna correptio</term> <note>The Christian duty to privately and kindly correct a fellow believer or superior who is erring, based on Matthew 18:15.</note>, but also toward the Superior himself. This is because no Superior ought to command anything except what is good. Therefore, since a subject is bound by obedience to "the good" in a general sense by a Superior, it follows that he obeys him by resisting in this way, just as he should, because he does what is good by turning away from evil. From this it is clear that a subject who obeys his Prelate in evil is not excused from sin. For the Savior says in Matthew 15: *“If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.”* This means if the blind—that is, the ignorant or evil Prelate—provides leadership to the blind—that is, the ignorant or evil subject—by commanding...

<note>original: "Denunciamus uobis in nomine dñi nostri Iesu Christi, ut subtrahatis uos ab omni fratre ambulante inordinate & non secundum traditionem quā acceperunt a nobis..."</note>
And below:
> For when we were with you, we charged you that if anyone does not wish to work, neither let him eat.
<note>original: "Nam cum essemus apud uos denunciabamus uobis, quoniam si quis non uult operari, non manducet."</note>
And it is clear how subjects ought to reasonably judge the commands and works of their Superiors <note term="Superior">Latin: "Praepositi"; those placed in authority over others.</note>, because otherwise they would be in danger of eternal death; nor could they judge with discernment concerning them—in what they ought to believe them, in what they ought to follow them, and in what things they ought to reasonably obey them according to the law of the Lord. For our best Teacher, the Lord, forewarned us: "Beware of false prophets" in Matthew 7. And "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees" <note>The "leaven" refers to the corrupting influence of their hypocrisy or false teaching.</note> in Matthew 16. And Matthew 24 says:
> Do not believe, do not go out, and do not do according to their works
<note>original: "Nolite credere, nolite exire, & secundum opa eorum nolite facere"</note>
in Matthew 23. He even encouraged the priests and the crowds to judge concerning his own works, saying in John 8:
> Which of you convicts me of sin?
<note>original: "Quis ex uobis arguet me de peccato?"</note>
And in John 10:
> And if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works.
<note>original: "Et si mihi non uultis credere, operibus credite."</note>
And what an evil it is for the Church of **Christ**, that our Superiors demand more that their own approvals and disapprovals be believed in all their judgments, than they demand that the faith of Holy Scripture be believed—which is the Catholic <note>The word "Catholic" here refers to the universal, orthodox Christian faith as defined by the scriptures.</note> faith. And they punish more for a transgression of their own... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

### One is not to be obedient to the church or its prelates in all things, even in neutral works, which are neither good nor evil. Likewise, Excommunication cannot take away the execution of Christ's mandates. CHAPTER XX.

<margin>"To be obeyed" and "ought to obey" mean the same thing.</margin>
Furthermore, so that the Doctors <note term="Doctors">Specifically the eight theologians of the University of Prague who opposed Hus and defended the absolute authority of the Pope and the Church hierarchy.</note> might be better understood in their twofold statement when they say: "The Roman church and its prelates are to be obeyed in all things by subordinates," etc. And again: "Therefore they are to be obeyed and complied with." I assume, according to the rules of true grammar, that this phrase "is to be obeyed" carries the same weight as the phrase "ought to obey." And further, that this word "ought" implies a debt of obligation to obedience under penalty of mortal sin <note term="Mortal sin">In Catholic theology, a grave sin that destroys the relationship with God and leads to spiritual death if not confessed.</note>. This assumption is clear from the Doctors' citation of that saying of the Savior in Matthew 23: "All things whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do." <note>original: "Oīa quæcunq; dixerint uobis seruate & facite."</note> For this word of the Lord is a command. 

Secondly, this assumption is clear from the words of the Doctors when they say: "But certain of the clergy in the kingdom of Bohemia refuse to consent, striving, as much as in them lies, to lead the faithful people into disobedience toward their prelates, and to irreverence for the papal, episcopal, priestly, and clerical dignities." Now it is well known that the disobedience and irreverence which the Doctors imply would be a mortal sin. 

Thirdly, this assumption is clear from the citation of Saint Augustine, where he says: "If you have not been obedient to the father"—understand here not the physical father, but the spiritual father—"you have lost all virtues." <note>original: "Obediens patri non fueris... oēs uirtutes perdidisti."</note> Now it is clear that...

<summary>Hus begins Chapter 20 by arguing that the "Doctors" of the Church wrongly demand absolute obedience. He asserts that the obligation to obey prelates is only valid when their commands align with God's law and do not lead to mortal sin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus's argument from Chapter 20. <page-num>177</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER XX</header>

...it is that a virtuous man cannot lose all his virtues except through mortal sin <note>original: "peccatum mortale"</note>. And thus, by that authority, disobedience is weighed as a crime.

<margin>No one should be excommunicated except for mortal sin.</margin>
Therefore, this statement of the Doctors <note term="Doctors">The eight conservative theologians of the University of Prague who were Hus’s primary intellectual opponents.</note>—based on the assumption that the Roman Church and the Prelates are to be obeyed in all things by their subordinates, etc.—is only valid insofar as it means one "ought to obey" under the penalty of mortal sin. Hence, they are now shouting in this sense: that I am disobedient to the Roman Church, and because of this, they excommunicate me. Yet it is clear from both the law of God and the Canon law that no one should be excommunicated except for a mortal sin, as I have stated elsewhere.

<margin>The Pope is not to be obeyed in all things.</margin>
Maintaining this assumption, I put forward this conclusion: No Apostolic See of the Roman Church—that is, no Pope together with the Cardinals (as the Doctors conceive it) and the Prelates—is to be obeyed by subordinates in all things that are neither "purely evil" nor "purely good." This is proven as follows: No king, marquess, duke, baron, knight, citizen, or peasant is bound under penalty of mortal sin to obey the Roman Church and its Prelates [if they command him] not to possess property or to enter into marriage. These things—namely, possessing property and entering into marriage—are neither purely good nor purely evil for such persons; therefore, the conclusion follows. The logic is clear and the secondary point is evident from the Blessed *Bernard* in his letter to the Monk *Adam*, when he says: "It must be known that there are intermediate <note>These are "neutral" actions, neither commanded nor forbidden by God's law, often called *adiaphora*.</note> things which often take on the character of pure goods or pure evils. For while marriage is permitted to be entered or not, once it is done, it is not merely permitted [but a duty]. Therefore, what was clearly a neutral matter before the wedding takes on the force of a 'pure good' for those who are married. Likewise, to possess property is a neutral matter for a secular man, since it is also permitted for him not to possess it; but for a monk, because he is not permitted to possess it, it is a 'pure evil.'" So says Bernard. The major premise is proven thus: The Roman Church is not permitted to command, under penalty of mortal sin, that a king, marquess, duke, baron, knight, citizen, or peasant must enter into marriage or must not possess property; therefore, none of the aforementioned people are bound to obey such a command under the penalty of mortal sin.

<margin>The Church cannot bind anyone beyond the counsels of Christ.</margin>
The question regarding matters beyond the counsels <note term="counsels">Hus refers to the "evangelical counsels" (poverty, chastity, and obedience), which in Catholic theology are considered paths to perfection for those who choose them, rather than requirements for all Christians.</note> is well known, and the preceding point is clear: because it is not permitted for the Roman Church to exalt its own commandment above the counsel of Christ. But by commanding that a king, marquess, duke, baron, or knight should possess nothing of his own, the Roman Church would be exalting its own commandment above Christ's counsel. This is the first counsel among the twelve principal evangelical counsels—namely, voluntary poverty <note>original: "uolūtaría paupertas"</note> consisting in the renunciation of property, which implies a state of need. Christ counsels this but does not command it, saying to a certain young prince in Matthew 19: <insert>original: "Si uis perfectus esse, uade & uende omnía quæ habes, & da pauperibus, & sequere me."</insert> "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and follow me." Similarly, if the Roman Church were to command that a king, marquess, or other secular person enter into marriage, it would be commanding against Christ’s counsel; how then would it not be acting against Christ? For the observance of virginal chastity until death is the third evangelical counsel of Christ, concerning which he says in Matthew 19: "There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." Christ does not command this but counsels it, so that whoever it suits may hold to it willingly, saying: "He who can take it, let him take it."

Therefore, it would be a great presumption for the Roman Church to restrict someone under the penalty of mortal sin <note>original: "peccatum mortale"</note> beyond the counsels of its own Lord. For this would be to impose unbearable burdens on the shoulders of men, as the Savior says in Matthew 23—burdens which the scribes and Pharisees, sitting in the chair of Moses, do not carry themselves but impose upon others. Whence the Apostle of Christ [Paul], who beheld the secrets of God which the Roman Church has not seen, did not dare to command anyone to marry, nor to remain in continence. Therefore, in 1 Corinthians 7, he says: "Each one has his own gift from God, one in this way, and another in that." The Apostle wished to command nothing except what the Lord commanded through him, and thus what was useful for the one obeying. For many things are counsels for some that are not counsels for us, due to our frailty or ignorance. Just as one might marry in the Lord without mortal sin, even though it would be better for him <note>The text ends mid-sentence; "for him" is the translation of the catchword "sibi".</note>

<margin>When the Church should be obeyed regarding fasts and prayers</margin>
Likewise, in acts that are good by their nature, such as fasting and prayer (which are not **pure evils**), the Roman Church or the Prelates <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who has authority over others.</note> are not to be obeyed except in a measure balanced by reason. This is evident because it might happen that a subordinate continues prayer and fasting to such an extent that he fails, harming both himself and the Church. But this must be avoided both by the one giving the command and the one following it. Therefore, the preceding premise is clearly true. For it is certain that it would be a "tempting of God" <note>To "tempt God" in this medieval context means to recklessly put oneself in danger—such as through extreme fasting—expecting a miracle to prevent the natural consequences of one's actions.</note> to obey a Prelate, or to vow to him, that I would never eat or drink more than a certain amount, or never have more than a certain amount of clothing or covering—and so on regarding other poorly conceived counsels. 

And it would be even greater folly for a prelate to bind a community to such a singular degree of austerity. Since, according to the diversity of times, of sickness and health, of youth and old age, of heat and cold, such things must vary in the same person—and much more so in a diverse community, where different "means" must be adapted to different persons. For according to Aristotle in the second book of his *Ethics*, the "middle way" <note>Aristotle’s "Golden Mean" is the desirable middle between two extremes, one of excess and the other of deficiency.</note> is not the same for everyone. For the "middle" amount of food proportioned for Milo <note>original: "Miloni" — Milo of Croton was a legendary ancient Greek wrestler famous for his immense strength and his ability to eat an entire ox in a single day.</note>—who wanted to eat an entire ox in a day—would not be the proportional "middle" for just any youth, or an elderly person, or someone healthy or sick.

He uses Aristotle's concept of the "Golden Mean" to demonstrate that a single rule cannot fit the physical needs of every person in a community.</summary>

<margin>
Christ did not wish to constrain his disciples to fasting.

And for this reason, the Savior excused his disciples in such a way when they were accused of not fasting. For in Matthew 9, it is said: *The disciples of John came to Jesus, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?"* <note>original: "Quare nos & pharisæi ieiunamus frequenter, discipuli autem tui non ieiunant?"</note> The Savior responded to these critics—who had joined themselves with the Pharisees in rebuking Christ—speaking on behalf of his disciples: *Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.* <note>The "wedding guests" or "children of the bridegroom" (filii sponsi) refers to the disciples; Christ is the "bridegroom."</note> *No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear results. Neither is new wine put into old wineskins; otherwise, the skins burst, the wine is spilled, and the skins are destroyed. Instead, they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.*

Here, the Savior excuses his disciples from the observance of fasting. First, because he himself, as the bridegroom of the Church, granted a dispensation to his "children" for that time. Second, because that physical fasting was not suitable for them at that time, as Lyra <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349) was a Franciscan scholar whose literal commentary on the Bible was a standard reference for medieval theologians.</note> says. Hence the Bridegroom says: *Can the wedding guests mourn?*—that is, be saddened by afflicting themselves with fasting—as if he were saying "no," since fasting is not appropriate for them now. *But the days will come*—namely, the days of the Passion—*when the bridegroom will be taken from them* through death, as far as his physical presence is concerned, *and then they will fast*—that is, with the fasting of sorrow. This is according to John 16: *You will weep and lament,* and then they will fast, specifically when such a fast becomes appropriate for them.

Then, through a double example <note>The examples of the unshrunk cloth and the new wine in old skins.</note>, the Savior proves that physical fasting was not suitable for them then. In Luke 5, "observances" are also mentioned, where it says: *Why do the disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?* To whom he said: *Can you make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?*—as if to say, beyond the will of the bridegroom, you cannot lawfully make his children fast.

<margin>When obedience is meritorious.</margin>
And from this it follows that no obedience shown to a superior is of any use for merit, except insofar as it inclines one toward obedience to the commands and counsels of the Lord Jesus Christ. This is clear, because obedience owed or given to Christ is in itself the basis of merit; as it increases or decreases, so does the merit itself. Hence, nothing is more religious than obedience rendered to God, as the **Decretum** <note>The *Decretum Gratiani* is a collection of Canon law compiled in the 12th century; it served as the main textbook for church lawyers in Hus's time.</note> teaches in Part 2, Case 8, Question 1, in the chapter beginning "Sciendum." There it is noted that the prophet Samuel says in **1 Samuel 15** <note>original: "pri. Regum. xv." In the Latin Vulgate used in the Middle Ages, 1 and 2 Samuel were called 1 and 2 Kings.</note>: "Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to submit is like a crime." Obedience alone, says the *Decretum*, is the virtue that possesses the merit of faith, without which anyone is proven to be an unbeliever, even if they seem to be a believer. In sacrifices, it says, the flesh of another is slaughtered, but through obedience, one’s own will is slaughtered; from this it is clearer than light that the text speaks of obedience owed to God. For in 1 Samuel 15, Samuel says to Saul: "Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you from being king." And Saul said to Samuel: "I have sinned, because I have transgressed the word of the Lord and your words, fearing the people and obeying their voice." And it is clear how much the Prelates of the people blaspheme when they claim this kind of obedience for themselves based on Scripture or the law of the church.

It is clear, secondly, regarding the authority of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Hus and many other reformers.</note>, which the doctors cite for themselves from Sermon 86, where he says: "If you fast days and nights, if you offer prayer, if you are in sackcloth or ashes, or if you do anything else except what is commanded in the law, and you seem wise to yourself, but have not been obedient to your father—understand here not your physical father, but your spiritual father—you have lost all your virtues." This is clear because he who does not obey God, the spiritual father, has lost all virtues. And from this Augustine adds: "Therefore obedience is worth more than all other moral virtues." Thus, the proof offered by the doctors, attempting to deduce their own intended meaning from this authority <note>Hus is arguing that the "spiritual father" Augustine mentions is God, whereas the church hierarchy (the "doctors") falsely claims Augustine meant that people must obey the clergy above all else.</note>, is far-fetched.
