# LXII. ON THE CHURCH

<margin>
Excommunication ought not to hinder the execution of Christ's commands.
</margin>
In the face of a pretended excommunication, whether threatened or already imposed, a Christian must carry out the commands of Christ. This is evident from the conclusion of the Blessed Peter and the other Apostles in Acts 5: "We must obey God rather than men." <note>original: "Obedire oportet magis deo quam hominibus"</note> Consequently, it follows from this that a priest of Christ, who lives according to His law, possesses knowledge of the Scriptures, and has a desire to build up the people, must preach, notwithstanding any pretended excommunication. This is clear because preaching the word of God is a command given to priests. As the Apostle Peter testifies in Acts 10: "He commanded us," he said, "to preach to the people and to testify." And in Matthew 10, Jesus sent these twelve, commanding them and saying: "Go not into the way of the Gentiles." And further: "As you go, preach, saying, the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The same is evident in Luke 9 and 10.

<margin>
Augustine. It is the duty of priests to teach.
</margin>
This is also clear through Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> in the prologue of his sermons, where he says: "There are few priests who preach the word of God justly, but there are many who remain silent to their own damnation—some out of ignorance, as they refuse to be taught, and others out of negligence, as they despise the word of God. But neither the former nor the latter can be excused from the fault of silence, since those who do not know how to preach ought not to be in authority, nor should those who do know how to preach remain silent, even if they are not in positions of power." Thus he speaks.

<margin>
Jerome
</margin>
Likewise, through St. Jerome <note>Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate Latin Bible.</note> regarding the text of Ezekiel 3: "If, when I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him, nor speak to turn him from his wicked way so that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand." There, Jerome says: "A priest is bound to preach; let him see to it that human fear does not make him silent. It is a great danger to keep silent the words of God for a threefold reason: namely, because of fear, because of laziness, or because of flattery." Likewise, through Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD). His work "Pastoral Care" was the definitive guide for the medieval clergy.</note> in his *Pastoral Care*, chapter 15, and in Distinction 43: "Let the ruler [be...]," where he proves very solemnly through many authorities of Scripture. Among other things, he says: "For it is written that the sound may be heard when he enters the sanctuary <note>A reference to Exodus 28:33-35, describing the bells on the High Priest's robe that must ring so he does not die when entering the Holy Place.</note> in the sight of the Lord, so that he does not die." <meta>This page transitions from the general obligations of the priesthood (discussed on page 184) to a specific critique of how church authorities and "doctors"—university-trained theologians—interpret biblical commands regarding obedience to the hierarchy. # JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH

Now we must briefly address the authorities that the doctors have brought forward to strengthen the requirement for human obedience. For first, they say that the Roman Church and its Prelates must be obeyed by those below them in all things, and so on, according to the sentence of the Savior in Matthew 23: "All things whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do." Here I marvel why the doctors have so openly cut off the Savior’s words; for they did not include the preceding phrase, "The scribes and Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses" <note>This refers to the "Cathedra Moysi," the seat of authority for those who teach the Law of God; Hus implies the authority comes from the Law, not the person.</note>, nor did they add what follows: "but do not do according to their works." Instead, they only presented the middle portion, saying: "All things whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do."

<margin>
Prelates are indignant if their evils are made public.
</margin>

It seems to me they did this because the Pope and other prelates of the church do not wish to be compared to scribes and Pharisees, and if anything is said regarding their evil works, they are indignant. On the other side, the doctors and masters flatter such men, and thus "they will heap up for themselves masters with itching ears, turning away their hearing from the truth" <note>original: "prurientes auribus a ueritate auditum auertentes." A reference to 2 Timothy 4:3, describing people who seek teachers who only tell them what they want to hear.</note>, and the masters respond with flattery. Therefore, the Apostle’s prophecy is fulfilled in both; for in 2 Timothy 4, the Apostle adjures Timothy, saying: "I testify before God and Jesus Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by His coming and His kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and teaching. For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up for themselves masters with itching ears, and will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but will turn toward fables."

It is no wonder, then, that the Prelates welcome the sayings of the aforementioned doctors with gratitude, because they have smeared all those sayings with the oil of flattery, and have included no word of correction to suppress their malice. But a Master, a Bishop, and a most just Judge will come, who will most strictly weigh both the fawning of the doctors and the malice of the prelates. It is He who said: "The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on the chair of Moses. All things, therefore, whatsoever they shall say to you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do."

<summary>Jan Hus accuses church theologians of selectively quoting Matthew 23 to demand absolute obedience to the Pope while hiding the biblical warning to avoid the "works" of corrupt leaders. He argues that this flattery fulfills St. Paul's prophecy about teachers who turn away from the truth to please their listeners.</summary>

# CHAPTER XXI

they do. Truly, that master <note>Hus refers to Christ as the "Master" of the prelates.</note> did not flatter the malice of the prelates; rather, he spoke the truth of the doctors, taught his faithful, and refuted the scribes sitting in the chair because of their evil works. He spoke and taught the truth—truth because it was from above the chair of Moses (mentioned above in Chapter 18), which signifies the authority of judging and teaching the law of God. Of this chair, Moses said in Exodus 18: "They come to me so that I may judge between them and show them the precepts of God and his laws." Therefore, observe all things whatsoever they shall say to you—<gloss>the interlinear gloss adds: "those things pertaining to the Chair"</gloss>—observe them, namely in your heart, and do them, in your works. But do not do according to their works. <gloss>The interlinear gloss adds: "hold to the doctrine, not to their life,"</gloss> for they say and do not do.

<margin>
Prelates say and do not do.
</margin>

Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching and critiques of clerical corruption.</note> says: "They preach the faith, yet they act unfaithfully; they give peace to others, yet they themselves have no fear; they cry out the truth, yet they love a lie; they chastise greed, yet they love desire." Augustine <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD), a cornerstone of Western theology.</note> says the same as above in Chapter 18: "By sitting in the chair of Moses, they teach the law of God; therefore, God teaches through them. But if they wish to teach their own things, do not listen to them, and do not do them."

It is clear, therefore, that Christ's saying and mandate are most true. It is also plain that he does not command us to observe and do *all* the precepts of those sitting in Moses's chair; otherwise, he would not have said afterward, "For they bind heavy and insupportable burdens," which consequently are burdens that ought not to be carried. This is also clear in the previous chapter, regarding how he excused his disciples for eating with unwashed hands and for their conduct regarding fasting, despite the mandates of the authorities.

Regarding the authority of Augustine, which the doctors immediately attach here, it was discussed near the end of the preceding chapter. <meta>This page continues the discussion in Chapter 21 of Jan Hus’s *De Ecclesia*. Having previously established that Christians should obey the "Chair of Moses" (divine law) rather than the personal whims of corrupt prelates, Hus now examines "neutral" or "indifferent" actions—tasks that are neither explicitly commanded nor forbidden by God—and how the duty of obedience applies to them.</meta>

# ON THE CHURCH

And in these neutral matters <note>Hus uses the term *media* (middle things), referring to actions that are morally indifferent, neither inherently good nor evil until context is added.</note>, a law of obedience is placed, just as it was with the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which was in the middle of Paradise. In these matters, it is certainly not right for our own judgment to dictate a sentence over the teachers. In these things, neither the command nor the prohibition of prelates should be despised at all. Here it should be noted that the adverb of comparison, "as if" <note>original: *tanquam*</note>, suggests a certain similarity, but not an absolute one. For in Genesis 2, regarding the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the law was established by God, who can neither deceive nor be deceived. And this law was established under penalty of death; for God said to Adam: "Do not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for in whatever day you eat from it, you shall die." Therefore, in that case, we must weigh the commander, weigh the command, and weigh the condition of the person who must obey. The commander is God, who cannot err. The command is very useful. And the man was one who heard God Himself commanding. Therefore, to eat from the tree of knowledge of good and evil after a negative command was pure evil.

Alongside this, suppose that a prelate named Peter commands his subject John to gather strawberries <note>In medieval theological debates, gathering strawberries (*fraga*) was a standard example used to describe a "neutral" act—something trivial that only becomes a matter of "obedience" because a superior commanded it.</note>. Let it be asked whether the one commanding in this case can err, how useful that work is to the one obeying, and whether the one obeying is as prepared for that work as Adam was for God's command. It is clear that in all three aspects, there is no equal similarity. For the prelate can err, the work is not as useful, and it remains a fact that the person obeying is not as naturally disposed to that work as Adam was to the Lord's command.

<margin>
Neutral work <note>original: *Opus medium*. In Scholastic philosophy, these are "indifferent" acts like walking or picking up a straw, which only gain moral character through intention or command.</note>
</margin>

Therefore, Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic often quoted by Hus regarding the limits of obedience.</note> says that a "neutral work" is that which, according to manner, place, time, or person, can be both good and evil. Here this saint lists the circumstances involving the commander, the work itself, and the one obeying. Hence, when he says it is a neutral work "according to manner," he hints at the due measure of reason—meaning the commander must not deviate from divine counsels. For if a prelate were to command his subject Peter, a priest learned in the law of God, to feed sows on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>, and God for that same day co[mmanded]... <note>Text breaks off mid-sentence; the argument likely continues that divine duty overrides a trivial or degrading command from a superior.</note>

<summary>Jan Hus argues that while obedience to church leaders is generally required in neutral matters, a prelate's authority is not absolute like God's. He distinguishes between God's perfect command to Adam and the fallible, sometimes trivial, commands of human prelates.</summary>

he might support himself, performing a work of supererogation <note>A "work of supererogation" refers to a good deed that goes beyond what God strictly requires as a minimum for salvation.</note> that is incompatible with that act. In such a case, Peter the priest is bound to obey God in His counsel more than the prelate in his command. This is evident, for the one to whom every subordinate is more bound in obedience is more worthy of reverence, and the enjoined act is more useful. 

<margin>God’s counsel should be placed above man’s command.</margin>

Now, the act enjoined by the prelate—namely, to feed the sows on the Lord’s Day—is indifferent regarding merit; however, the act enjoined by God possesses in itself the quality of merit. Wherefore, I would wish that St. Bernard would respond to this case: if St. Benedict had commanded him to feed the sows, and at the same time God had counseled him to provide for the salvation of souls in the church to those seeking counsel, I estimate that the authority of the Counselor, and the greater utility of the counsel compared to St. Benedict's command, would have compelled Bernard to obey the divine counsel rather than Benedict’s command, for the honor of God and the salvation of those seeking counsel.

And from this it seems to follow that we are more bound to any divine counsel than to an incompatible human command. Secondly, it seems to follow that no one is bound to obey a private command except insofar as it encourages a divine counsel or command. And it is clear that within the "manner" of obedience is implied the due measure of reason and the quality of the command, which both the one obeying and the commander ought to weigh. For what reason would there be for the command of a stupid and fat bishop <note>original: "stolidi & pinguis Episcopi"</note> to make a priest feed sows and leave without pasture the sheep of Christ, whom He redeemed with His own blood?

<margin>The circumstance of place must be weighed in a command.</margin>

Similarly, the circumstance of place must be weighed; for if a prelate should command a subordinate to appear in a place of enemies who are plotting the subordinate’s death, the subordinate is not bound to obey. Wherefore Pope Clement V, concerning sentences and the matter of things judged <note>original: "de Senten. & re iud." refers to a section of Canon Law</note> in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of canon law named after Pope Clement V.</note>, in the decree *Pastoralis*, says: 
> For who would dare, or by what reason is anyone bound to dare to undergo the judgment of such a consistory <note>A formal council or court of the church.</note>, to place oneself in the bosom of enemies, and to offer oneself voluntarily to a death to be inflicted by violent injury, and not by justice?

This indeed...

<meta>This page continues Hus’s argument from Chapter 21 regarding the limits of obedience. He argues that if a person is summoned to a trial where the judges are biased or the location is outside their home province, natural and canon law provide the right to refuse, as such a trial is fundamentally unjust.</meta>

# JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH

### Page 190

...is rightly feared, this is customarily avoided, human reason flees from this, and nature abhors this. Therefore, let him who would think that such a summons <note>original: "citationem"; a formal legal call to appear before a court.</note> binds the person summoned lose all hope. Nor should the power of defense, which springs from natural law, be taken away, since even the Emperor is not permitted to remove those rights which exist by natural law.

<margin>The words of Pope Nicholas.</margin>
Likewise, Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael: <note>Refers to a letter from Pope Nicholas I to the Byzantine Emperor Michael III, preserved in the Decretum Gratiani, the standard textbook of medieval Church law.</note> "Because suspect and hostile judges ought not to be allowed, as reason itself dictates and is proven by many examples. For what more pleasing or agreeable gift can one give to an enemy than if he commits to him, for the purpose of attack, the person he perhaps wished to harm?" Which, accordingly, the Sixth Chapter of the Canons of the Synod of Constantinople is known to prohibit. In the same chapter, Pope Gelasius, a most powerful fighter against heretics, says: "I ask," he says, "where the judgment they pretend could be conducted, and whether before those same people so that they are simultaneously enemies, witnesses, and judges? But human affairs ought not to be committed to such a judgment. But if human judgments—where the judges are the same as the enemies—ought not to be committed to a trial, how much less divine—that is, ecclesiastical—matters? Let him who is wise understand." 

And indeed, from this, the pious Emperor Justinian is known to have promulgated in his laws, <note>Justinian was the 6th-century Byzantine emperor who codified Roman Law, which deeply influenced Church law.</note> saying: "Let it be permitted to him who considers a judge suspect to him, before the lawsuit begins, to refuse him, so that recourse may be had to another." For it is in a way natural to decline the snares of judges and to wish to flee the judgment of enemies. Thus Saint John "Golden-Mouth" <note>original: "Ioannes os aureum"; better known as John Chrysostom, a famous early Church Father and preacher.</note> refused to enter the assembly of the Council gathered against him. 

Thus far that text, where Gratian <note>The 12th-century jurist who compiled the "Decretum," the foundational text of Canon Law.</note> concludes: "The accused is by no means to be led outside his province." Wherefore Pope Fabian says: "For let the case always be conducted where the crime is committed; and he who has not proven what he charged shall himself suffer the punishment he intended for the other."

Likewise, Pope Stephan says: "The license of accusing shall not proceed beyond the boundaries of the provinces, but every accusation shall be heard within the province." The same is clear from the Roman Synod, in the chapter "No one" <note>original: "Nemi" (likely for "Nemo").</note>...

<summary>Jan Hus uses a variety of legal authorities, including Popes and Emperors, to argue that an accused person has a natural right to a fair trial. He asserts that no one should be forced to appear before a biased judge or outside their own home region (province).</summary>

# CHAPTER XXI

<margin>No one should be summoned to the papal court.</margin>
"No one." <note>original: "ca. Neminem"; likely a reference to a specific legal canon beginning with this word.</note> What appearance <note>original: "color"; used here in the legal sense of a pretext or justification.</note> or reason for obedience is there, when a person is summoned from three hundred miles away—someone unknown to the Pope and denounced by enemies—to travel so anxiously toward Rome among enemies? He comes before judges and witnesses who are his enemies; he consumes the resources of the poor on expensive travel, or if he lacks funds, he travels miserably in thirst and hunger. And what is the gain of such an ordeal?

Certainly, it results in the neglect of the labor commanded by God regarding his own salvation and the salvation of others. In that place, he will not be taught how to believe well, but how to litigate <note>original: "litigare"; to engage in legal disputes.</note>, which is not permitted for a servant of God. There, he will be stripped of his possessions in the consistory <note>The formal assembly of the Pope and his cardinals.</note>; his holy character will grow cold; he will be driven to impatience through oppression; and if he has nothing to give, he will be condemned, even if justice is on his side. And what is more grievous: he will be compelled to adore the Pope as if he were God, on bended knees.

<margin>The Pope must be adored in Rome.</margin>
Blessed, therefore, be God who said in Genesis 18: "I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I will know." <note>Hus emphasizes that God "descends" to investigate local matters personally rather than summoning people to a distant throne.</note> Blessed be the Son of God who descended from heaven to "seek and to save that which was lost," as it says in Luke 19. He went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every infirmity. But when he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep having no shepherd (Matthew 9).

Blessed be Christ himself who commanded Peter in Matthew 18, saying: "If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone." For this reason, the Pope will find no precedent for such summons <note>original: "citationes"</note> except by doing the opposite of how Christ visited people. If the Popes would only weigh that law of Christ in Matthew 7: "Whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets," I believe they would not reasonably want to summon people and force them to undertake such a dangerous and unknown journey. Why, then, would they press others without a clear and rational cause? Why do they not consider the exemplary life of Christ the High Priest <note>original: "Pontificis"; Hus pointedly uses the title usually reserved for the Pope to describe Christ.</note>, who piously visited those wandering and oppressed by the devil...

<margin>
One who wishes to reprove another ought to be blameless.
</margin>
In this, a Vicar of Peter should note **First**: that when he wishes to reprove a brother, he must first keep himself blameless, since charity <note>In the sense of Christian love and care</note> must begin with oneself. How then can a Prelate <term>Prelate: a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</term> who is completely soaked in the heresy of Simony <term>Simony: the corrupt practice of buying or selling church offices or spiritual things</term>, in pride, in lust, and in greed, lawfully reprove a brother? Or how will he be able to condemn someone to death, when the Savior says in John 8: "He among you who is without sin, let him be the first to throw a stone at her." Truly, if this law of Christ were weighed carefully, a Prelate would rarely be found in these times who could lawfully correct someone or condemn them for heretical depravity.

He should note **Second**: that the Savior commands, saying: "Go." Here he commands that judges ought to visit their subjects in order to correct them in the places where the crime is said to have been committed—as the canon laws also declare. For Christ did this, and similarly the Apostles. Christ will also do this at the final judgment, as he alone foretells in Matthew 25. **Third**: a Vicar of Peter or a Prelate should note that he ought to be prudent, diligent, and intent in his manner of reproving, so that he does not excommunicate before the end of the third warning. **Fourth**: he should take note of the multitude of faithful witnesses who can attest to the brother's crime. And **Fifth**: he should "tell the church" as the greater authority. For thus the Lord commanded Peter: "Tell the church."

<margin>
Why the author refused to appear in Rome.
</margin>
From what has just been said, I conclude that the alleged excommunication does not affect me, nor does it bind me. This is because the hostile judges and witnesses reside in Rome, and the judge is a primary party in the case. For me, it is a long distance, surrounded on all sides by German <note>original: "Teutonicis"; Hus refers here to his ongoing conflicts with German scholars and clergy who opposed his reforms</note> enemies; I see no fruit in appearing, but rather the neglect of the people regarding the word of God. I hope that Christ has fortified me, just as he said in Matthew 10.

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...by the sword, as is clear regarding the laymen Jan, Martin, and Stascon, who, by contradicting the lying disciples of the Antichrist, fell by the sword <note>original: "Ioanne, Martino & Stascone." These three men—Jan, Martin, and Stascon—were young artisans executed in Prague in July 1412 for publicly protesting the sale of indulgences. Hus viewed them as the first martyrs of his movement</note>. Others, however, offering their necks for the sake of the truth, were martyrized, captured, imprisoned, and slaughtered, and yet they did not deny the truth of Christ—priests as well as laymen and women. But those who joined them deceitfully went away, for, terrified by the censures <note>Censures were ecclesiastical punishments, such as excommunication or interdict</note> of the Antichrist and by imprisonments, they turned to the opposite way. Yet the Lord continues to multiply the children of the Church, who are patient in suffering and announce the truth of Christ the Lord. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has hidden the way of truth from the wise and prudent and revealed it to simple laypeople and humble priests <note>original: "paruulis sacerdotibus." Hus often contrasts the "little" or "lowly" priests with the wealthy, powerful "prelates"</note>, who choose to obey God rather than men. These are the ones who, keeping the life of Christ before their eyes, obey their prelates in acts that are good by nature <note>original: "actibus bonis de genere." In medieval philosophy, this refers to acts that are inherently good, such as prayer or charity</note> and in neutral acts <note>original: "actibus neutris." These are "indifferent" acts—things neither commanded nor forbidden by God, like walking or sitting—where a superior might traditionally claim authority</note>, but only to the extent that those acts, limited by circumstances, can be reasonably traced back to the edification of imitating Jesus Christ.

<margin>A virtuous act is regulated by eight circumstances.</margin>
For they truly understand that eight circumstances rectify an act so that it may be virtuous, as shown in this verse: *Who, what, where, how much, how many, why, how, when.*

**Who**, therefore, pertains to the person who must obey. 
**What**, namely, what he must do when commanded. 
**Where**, because in one place it is fitting to obey in an act that is good by nature or neutral, but not in another or everywhere. 
**How much**, namely, how much he must obey; for he is only bound to the extent that something edifying is commanded which can be traced to the commandment or counsel of Jesus Christ. For no one is bound to obey his own private superior infinitely—as the foolish babble when they say that the Pope’s power extends to commanding infinitely, and that every individual Christian must obey him to that extent.

**How many**, namely, how many acts he can lawfully do when it is not necessary, if a subject [is responding] to the command of a priest imposing penance...

### CHAPTER XXI.

...gives two groschen or pence, or fasts three days a week. That he should give as many groschen or fast as many days as the **ignorant priest** <note>original: "Idiota." In this context, Hus uses the term to refer to unlearned or worldly clerics who lack spiritual understanding.</note> prescribes or limits—unless he satisfies the purse of the confessor, who requires that he give as much for the **construction of the church of St. Peter** <note>This refers to the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, which was largely funded by the sale of indulgences—a practice Hus and later reformers fiercely opposed.</note> as if he were actually there in person, and as much to the **Papal treasury** <note>original: "cameram Pape."</note> as he would have spent on the journey—all such things are taxes invented by the devil.

The faithful person must also weigh the circumstance of the **end** <note>In medieval philosophy, the "end" (finis) refers to the purpose or intention behind an action.</note>, namely, *why* or for what purpose he ought to obey in a given act. 
<margin>The end is the measure of the things that lead to that end.</margin>
If it leads to the honor of God and the direct benefit of the Church, then the end is good. If, however, another end is pretended, then it goes against the word of the Apostle: *Whatever you do, do it in the name of Jesus Christ.* For the end measures all the means that are performed for its sake. Hence **Aristotle** concludes in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "ij. de anima."</note> saying: "It is therefore just that all things be named after their end," so that if the end is good, the means to that end are also good.

Another circumstance is also added when it is asked: **How?** For it is not enough to perform an act that is "good by nature" <note>original: "bonū de genere." An act like fasting or giving alms that is inherently virtuous.</note>; it is also required that it be done *well*. Nothing is done well by a person unless they are in a state of **charity** <note>original: "charitate." This refers to "caritas," the theological virtue of divine love or selfless grace, rather than simple modern "charity" or almsgiving.</note>. Thus the Apostle says: *Let all your deeds be done in charity.* The Apostle proves that nothing is done well without charity in the first letter to the **Corinthians**, chapter 13, saying: *If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.* 

The reason for this is that the branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, as the Savior says in **John 15**: *You cannot bear fruit unless you remain in me*—namely, through charity. Whence it is commonly said (as a certain philosopher once phrased it) that **God is a rewarder of adverbs, not of nouns.** <note>This famous scholastic maxim means that God judges the *manner* in which an act is done (the adverb, e.g., "done lovingly") rather than just the *thing* done (the noun, e.g., "a fast").</note> It is clear, then, that for true obedience, grace or charity is required. All other circumstances are folded into that one adverb, "how," because the person obeying must execute the commanded work charitably, humbly, prudently, joyfully, bravely, and readily.

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus's systematic analysis of the conditions required for valid obedience to church authorities. Having previously discussed the "end" or purpose of an action, he now moves to the final condition: "When." This leads into a complex logical paradox intended to show the limits of papal authority.</meta>

<page-num>198</page-num>
<header>JAN HUS - ON THE CHURCH</header>

The final condition is **When**, namely, it is appropriate to carry out the commanded work, as was stated before regarding time; for without doubt there are many good, neutral, or general acts which it is not expedient to command at any given time, and consequently, it is not expedient to obey them at just any time.

<margin>It is argued.</margin> 
But it is further argued for this point as follows: suppose that the Pope enjoins any cleric subject to him, by virtue of holy obedience and under the pretext of **absolution from punishment and guilt** <note>original: "absolutionis a pœna & culpa." This refers to a plenary indulgence, which Hus famously argued was being abused by the papacy to raise funds.</note>, or some other spiritual benefit, that he should meet the first person who is fully obedient to the Pope. And suppose he enjoins any Layman in a similar form that he should meet the first person who is **disobedient to the Pope** <note>original: "Papæ inobedienti."</note>, and let this injunction be made under the gravest **anathema** <note>A formal curse or sentence of excommunication used by the Church against those who disobeyed its mandates.</note>. 

And suppose also that every Cleric or Layman subject to this Pope was at first fully obedient to him, and that every Cleric meets only one Layman first, and vice versa. It seems a contradiction follows. Let us take **Peter** the Cleric and **Paul** the layman as the ones first meeting each other, and I ask: Is Peter at the moment of meeting obedient to the Pope? If so, then in this case one must say that Paul, at that same moment, is disobedient to the Pope; because since he first meets Peter, who is fully obedient to the Pope, and yet he was commanded to meet the first person who is *disobedient* to the Pope, it follows that Paul incurs the mark of disobedience. 

And thus if Peter, in this case, is disobedient to the Pope at the moment of meeting, then one must concede that Paul is obedient, and consequently Peter is too; for before the meeting both were obedient, and Peter does not become disobedient simply by meeting him, but rather his obedience is confirmed according to what has been said. 

Nor is it valid to deny the possibility of this case for such reasons. First, because the command is either neutral or possible. Second, because a **Prelate** <note>A high-ranking church official, like a bishop or the Pope.</note> can command something simply impossible and entirely irrational; therefore, by the same reasoning or even more so, he can command this. Thus, no response remains except the truth: that because of his commanding, a cleric or layman incurs neither more nor less punishment or reward. Because it is necessary...

# CHAPTER XXI

...a command which is to be obeyed must first be reasonable in the sight of God. And then it should be carried out, even if no human authority were to command it under the law of obedience, since otherwise a person would become disobedient to reason. And it is clear that, just as in this case one does not wait for a full remission of sins or a formal curse <note>original: "anathema."</note>, so it is generally the case in the judgment of the people: it matters not, except insofar as one has deserved it before God. For this logical objection must be resolved. Similarly, suppose that **Peter the Prior** has two groups of twelve cloistered monks, all of whom are obedient to him. He commands the more steadfast group of twelve not to speak with the other group, except perhaps to bring a disobedient person back to obedience. It is clear that the second group of twelve should not speak with the rest, except to confirm an obedient person in obedience to Peter. Now, suppose **Paul** from the first group begins to speak with **Linus** from the second group, both attempting to maintain obedience in this act, so that immediately before that conversation each was properly obedient to Peter—then a contradiction will be revealed. <note>Hus uses these convoluted "what-if" scenarios, common in medieval university logic, to demonstrate that if obedience is based solely on a human superior's word rather than divine truth, one can be trapped in a logical impossibility where an act is simultaneously obedient and disobedient.</note>

<margin>A prelate is to be charitably corrected when he commands wrongly.</margin>
Also, as **Bernard [of Clairvaux]** says in his letter to the monk **Adam**, neutral matters <note>original: "media." In scholastic theology, these are "indifferent things" (adiaphora) that are not specifically commanded or forbidden by God’s law, such as specific fasting rules or administrative tasks.</note> can be commanded or forbidden indifferently, both for good and for ill. Therefore, when a **Superior** <note>original: "Præpositus."</note> commands or forbids wrongly, the subordinate—once he realizes the superior is commanding or forbidding wrongly—ought to rebuke him according to the **law of charity** as a brother, since by commanding or forbidding in such a way, the superior sins against God and against his brother.

This is clear from that rule of Jesus Christ in the eighteenth chapter of **Matthew**: *If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone.* Nor does it matter that one who is more excellent in virtue rebukes one who is lower in morals, even if the latter is **superior in status** <note>original: "superior ad statum." This is a central and controversial point of Hus's theology: that spiritual character and "virtue" take precedence over official church rank. He argues that a humble but virtuous person has the right to correct a corrupt Pope.</note>; for otherwise that law of Christ would perish, which ordains that any Christian prelate, when he has sinned, must be corrected by another. For this law says universally: *If your brother sins against you, rebuke him.* Hence if—to speak of the impossible—**Christ** were to sin, since He is our brother according to the second chapter of **Hebrews**, He would have to be corrected by the Church. Hence He hinted at this when He said to the crowds in the eighth chapter of **John**: *Which of you convicts me of sin?* For this reason, the Church appropriately sings in...

The final condition is **When**; specifically, it is appropriate to carry out a commanded work at the proper time, as was said before regarding time. This is because, without doubt, there are many good acts—both in their nature and neutral ones—which it is not expedient to command at just any time, and consequently, it is not expedient to obey them at just any time.

But the argument for that point continues like this: suppose that the Pope enjoins any cleric subject to him, by virtue of holy obedience and under the promise of absolution from **punishment and guilt** <note>original: "a pœna & culpa" — a theological term referring to the full remission of both the temporal punishment and the eternal guilt of sin, often associated with plenary indulgences.</note> or some other spiritual support, that he should encounter the first person who is fully obedient to the Pope. And thus if *Peter*, in this case, were disobedient to the Pope at the instant of the encounter, then one would have to grant that *Paul* is obedient, and consequently *Peter* too, because before the encounter both were obedient, and *Peter* does not become disobedient because of the encounter, but rather his obedience is confirmed according to what has been said.

Second, because a **Prelate** <note>A high-ranking church official, like a bishop or abbot.</note> can command something simply impossible and entirely irrational; therefore, by the same token or even more so, he can command this. Thus, no response remains except the truth: that because of his commanding, the cleric or layman incurs neither more nor less punishment or reward. Because it is necessary...

# CHAPTER XXI

...a command that is to be obeyed must first be reasonable in the eyes of God. And then it would be carried out, even if no one under human obedience commanded it, since otherwise a person would become disobedient to reason. And it is clear that, just as in this case there is no need to wait for a full remission of sins or an **anathema** <note>A formal curse or excommunication from the Church.</note>, so generally it is not so in the judgment of the people, except in so far as one has deserved it before God. For it is necessary that this logical objection be resolved. 

Similarly, suppose that **Peter the Prior** <note>The head of a religious house or a high-ranking monk.</note> has two groups of twelve cloistered monks, all of whom are obedient to him. He commands the more steadfast group of twelve not to speak with the other group, except perhaps to bring a disobedient monk back to obedience. And it is clear that the second group of twelve should not speak with the first, except by the command of Peter to confirm obedience. Now, suppose **Paul** of the first group begins to speak with **Linus** of the second group, both of them intending to maintain obedience in this act, so that immediately before that conversation both were properly obedient to Peter—a contradiction will then become apparent.

<margin>A Prelate is to be corrected charitably when he commands wrongly.</margin>
Likewise, as **Bernard** <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic whose writings were often cited by Hus to support church reform.</note> says in his letter to the monk **Adam**, neutral matters <note>original: "media" — literally "middle things," referring to actions that are neither inherently good nor inherently evil, but depend on circumstances.</note> can be commanded or forbidden both well and poorly. Therefore, when a **Prelate** <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> commands or forbids poorly, the subordinate—once he realizes the superior is commanding or forbidding wrongly—ought to correct him according to the law of **charity** <note>original: "charitas" — the Christian theological concept of selfless love for God and neighbor.</note> as a brother, since by so commanding or forbidding, the superior sins against God and against his brother. 

This is clear through that rule of Jesus Christ in the eighteenth chapter of Matthew: *“If your brother sins against you, go and point out the fault between you and him alone.”* Nor does it stand in the way that one who is more excellent in virtue corrects one who is lower in morals, even if the latter is superior in status. Otherwise, this law of Christ would perish, which ordains that any Christian Prelate, when he has sinned, is to be corrected by another. For this law speaks universally: *“If your brother sins against you, correct him.”* Thus, if—by some impossibility—Christ had sinned, since He is our brother according to the second chapter of Hebrews, He would have to be corrected by the Church. Hence He hinted at this, saying to the crowds in the eighth chapter of John: *“Which of you convicts me of sin?”* Therefore, the Church appropriately sings in the person of

in the person of our Savior: "My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I saddened you? <margin>A superior can be corrected by an inferior, even the Pope.</margin>
It is clear, therefore, that every wayfarer <note>original: *viator*; a theological term for a living person journeying toward heaven, as opposed to a "comprehensor" who has already reached the destination.</note> who sins ought to be corrected by a brother; otherwise, the law of Christ would be lacking in providing a remedy against the stain on his bride <note>The "bride" refers to the Church.</note>. Therefore, it is treacherous <note>original: *perfidum*</note> to assert that a person of a superior status cannot be corrected in their behavior by an inferior subordinate. Thus, in certain cases, a son may lawfully correct a father, a daughter a mother, a subject a Prelate, and a disciple a master, according to the rule of charity.

But an objection is raised against this: that the Pope holds the place of the Lord Jesus Christ on earth; but it was not permitted for anyone to correct Him, as is clear from Matthew 16, where Peter is called "Satan" because of his attempt to correct Christ; therefore, it is not permitted to correct His representative. But this argument is quite lame, as it would require one to say that every Vicar of Christ is as impeccable <note>Sinless or unable to err.</note> as Christ Himself. On the contrary, it follows that neither the Pope nor anyone else should be corrected or set right *insofar as* he follows Christ as the head. But if a Bishop or a confessor, while holding the place of Christ, attempts an act of lust upon a virgin or a chaste wife, should she not vehemently rebuke him as an Antichrist and a treacherous enemy of her soul? For in that illicit act, he does not hold the place of Christ, but rather that of the Antichrist and the devil, most wickedly tempting the woman. And it is clear that the saying of Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux.</note> which the doctors cite—namely, that in these "middle matters" <note>original: *mediis*; actions that are morally neutral or "indifferent," neither commanded nor forbidden by God's law.</note> it is certainly not our place to prescribe our own sense over the judgment of the Masters—must be understood as applying to the Prelates in all things where neither a command nor a prohibition is to be despised, provided the circumstances are suited to the act of due obedience.

If, therefore, the superior would be glad in the first case, why should he not be even more glad in the second? If he accepts a guardian in the first, why not in the second?

<margin>How the saying of Augustine—that subordinates should not judge their superiors—is to be understood.</margin>
Nor does that saying of Blessed Augustine in *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* stand in the way: "What kind of people those who command ought to be is not to be discussed by subordinates." This is true and clear in the sense that they should not rashly discuss what kind of people [superiors] ought to be; however, reason teaches them that [superiors] ought to be good and should not live wickedly. And if they do live badly, subordinates, observing this, must guard against their evil works. Hence Augustine says: "If one must obey human authority, it is even more necessary to be subject to divine teaching." I will speak briefly. First, discussing this: that the following **logical deduction** <note>original: *consequentia*; in medieval logic, this refers to the necessary connection between a premise and a conclusion.</note> of the Doctors is very bad. Because the proceedings against **Jan Hus** were received by the community of the Clergy in Prague, and they obeyed them, therefore they must be obeyed. <margin>Learning a deduction from the high priests and Pharisees.</margin>
Perhaps they learned that deduction from the High Priests, the scribes, and the Pharisees, who formed a similar deduction. For in **John 18**, when Pilate said to them: 
> What accusation do you bring against this man? 

They responded and spoke, forming this deduction: 
> If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you. 

And **John 19** sets down this causal reason when Pilate said: 
> I find no case in him. [They said:] We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God. 

In the first deduction of the Jews, the Doctors implied that they themselves did not err, saying: *If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you*, that is: because this man is an evildoer, therefore we handed him over to you. Similarly, our Doctors imply in their deduction that the community of the Clergy in Prague cannot err; otherwise, if it could err, then their deduction would not be valid. And because that community can err in accepting proceedings—just as it errs in initiating them and maliciously executing them—therefore the deduction of the doctors is not good.

And I wonder at that enormous **tail** <note>original: *cauda*; Hus uses this term to mock a supplemental clause or "appendix" the Doctors added to their argument to shield themselves from criticism.</note> of the Doctors, by which they wish to cover the shame of that statement, when this "tail" is added: *Nor is it for the Clergy in Prague to judge whether the excommunication of Master Jan Hus be just or unjust.* If indeed those proceedings must be obeyed

He now focuses on a logical contradiction in the Doctors' defense: they claim they lack the authority to judge the justice of his excommunication, yet they simultaneously declare it just through their obedience.</meta>

### CHAPTER XXII

...regarding excommunication; therefore, they must be obeyed so that they are just, and not so that they are unjust. And because the Clergy, along with the Doctors, obey them and have accepted them, they therefore obey them as if they were just, and accepted them as just; and consequently, the Doctors together with the Clergy have judged that the **proceedings** <note>original: *processus*; the legal actions and sentences carried out by the ecclesiastical court.</note> are just. And yet their **tail** <note>original: *cauda*; Hus refers to a specific concluding clause or "add-on" in the Doctors' formal statement.</note> says that it is not for the Clergy in Prague to judge whether the excommunication of **Master Jan Hus** is just or unjust—and thus a manifest contradiction is confirmed. The Clergy in Prague shout, confirm, and assert that the excommunication of Master Jan Hus is just; therefore, the Clergy in Prague judge that this excommunication is just, while the "tail" of the Doctors says that it is not for the Clergy in Prague to judge whether that sentence is just or unjust. It is most clearly evident that this "tail" contradicts the actions and judgment of the Clergy in Prague.

Likewise, if it is not for the Clergy in Prague to judge whether that excommunication is just or unjust, and yet the Clergy approve it and act according to the proceedings, then the Clergy in Prague do not know if they act justly or unjustly, nor can they hope that they act justly. For judgment must precede hope.

Likewise, the Doctors themselves judge that the excommunication of Master Jan Hus is just. This is evident because they judge that the proceedings must be obeyed—and not as if they were unjust, therefore as if they were just. And consequently, the Doctors judge that the excommunication commanded in the proceedings is just.

Likewise, the Doctors say that the proceedings must be obeyed, especially because in them a pure good is not prohibited, nor is a pure evil commanded, but only **indifferent matters** <term>indifferent matters (media): in medieval theology, these are actions that are neither inherently good nor inherently evil in themselves, where obedience to a superior is generally required.</term>, in which one must obey according to Gospel doctrine and according to **Blessed Bernard**. <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a highly influential Cistercian abbot and mystic whose writings on obedience were frequently cited by both sides of the Hus controversy.</note> Therefore, the Doctors judge that the things commanded in the proceedings are just, among which is the excommunication of Jan Hus. Therefore, the Doctors themselves judge that the excommunication of Jan Hus is just. And since they themselves are the Clergy in Prague, that "tail" refutes the Doctors themselves. Likewise, they themselves judge that the excommunication which [is commanded] in the proceedings...

...is commanded, it is a middle ground between a pure good and a pure evil. When it is commanded according to the proper manner, place, time, and person, it then passes into a pure good, because it is an instruction from the Pope or the Prelates. Therefore, the Doctors who judge the **excommunication** <note>original: *excommunicatione*; the formal expulsion of a person from the religious community.</note> in this way judge it to be just. And yet, because of their **tail** <note>original: *cauda*; Hus's term for the concluding clause of the Prague faculty's document.</note> they ought not to judge that it is just. In doing so, they do what they ought not; indeed, they know not what they do. For they claim it is not for the clergy in Prague to judge whether the excommunication of Jan Hus is just, yet they simultaneously judge that it *is* just. It is laughable how the Doctors of Law agreed to that "tail"—those who judge the **Decrees, Decretals, and legal proceedings** <note>original: *Decreta, decretales, & processus*; the body of Canon Law and the specific legal actions taken against Hus.</note> to see if they are just, or if they were issued justly. They are duty-bound to provide a rational explanation of the Decrees and Decretals and to discern whether proceedings are just or unjust. According to the requirements of the law, they should advise others whether such proceedings ought to be admitted and upheld, or whether they should be rejected, or if it is permitted to appeal against them. It is clear that both sets of Doctors have irrationally blocked their own power of rational judgment.

However, as to how the proceedings thundered against me are null and erroneous, the venerable Master **John of Jesenice** <note>Jan z Jesenice (d. 1420), a brilliant lawyer and Hus's legal representative who studied at Bologna.</note>, Doctor of Canon Law from the University of Bologna, has made this clear in the schools through a public determination. And because, as I said, proceedings of this kind principally command excommunication, suspension, and interdict, I shall speak briefly about them.

What excommunication is.
</margin>

<header>CHAPTER XXII</header>

...participation. This is what the **Apostle** <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> wishes for the Corinthians, saying at the end of 2 Corinthians: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the **fellowship** <note>original: *communicatio*; translated here as fellowship or participation to reflect the communal sense.</note> of the Holy Spirit be with you all." And this fellowship is the **communion of saints** <note>original: *communio sanctorum*; the spiritual union of all members of the Christian Church, living and dead.</note>, who are the mystical body of Christ, of which Christ is the head; this is the communion we believe in when we say: "I believe in the communion of saints."

<margin>Second: of the sacraments.</margin>
The second fellowship or communion is the participation in the sacraments. As it says in Ephesians 4: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." Yet it is understood specifically as the participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. In 1 Corinthians 10: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the fellowship of the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord? Since there is **one bread** <note>original: *uerus panis*; though the OCR reads *uerus* (true), Hus is quoting the Vulgate's *unus* (one) to emphasize unity.</note>, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread and the one cup."

<margin>Third: of prayers.</margin>
The third fellowship or communion is the participation in **suffrages** <note>original: *suffragiorum*; the collective prayers, intercessions, and good works of the Church which benefit its members.</note>. In this, the righteous man glories in the Lord in the Psalm: "I am a companion of all who fear You, and of those who keep Your commandments."

And besides this three-fold fellowship, there is a fellowship consisting of the social interaction of Christians, both good and bad; whereas the first three belong only to good men, people of the world think more about this fourth kind.

Secondly, it should be noted that I am speaking here of **Excommunication** in a way that corresponds to the four types of fellowship just mentioned. First, it is a separation from the participation in divine grace which makes one pleasing to God. Second, it is a separation from the worthy participation in the sacraments. Third, it is a separation from the participation in the prayers that prepare one for eternal life—this is the opposite of the three-fold communion. And fourthly, it is a public exclusion from the social interaction of Christians by the decree of a spiritual or secular judge.

<margin>Excommunication is not incurred except on account of mortal sin.</margin>
From these points, it follows first that excommunication from the first three types never happens, nor can it happen, except through **mortal sin** <note>original: *peccatum mortale*; a grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note>. This is evident because...

<summary>Jan Hus defines four levels of "communion" (spiritual grace, sacraments, collective prayer, and social interaction) and their corresponding forms of excommunication. He argues that true spiritual excommunication—separation from God's grace—can only be caused by the individual's own mortal sin, not by a legal decree.</summary>

->I. H. ON THE CHURCH<-

...because no one is ever separated from the **communion of saints**, which is the participation in the grace of God, and of the sacraments and the **suffrages** <note>original: *suffragiorum*; collective prayers or intercessory acts of the Church</note> that prepare one for life, except through mortal sin. It is this alone that divides or separates a person from this kind of communion, just as it separates them from God himself. Nor can it even happen except through mortal sin, because as long as a person is in a state of grace, they are a participant in the threefold communion mentioned above, according to their present righteousness. And since God is a most just judge, He cannot harm a person regarding this kind of participation except by that person's own lack of merit; therefore, the conclusion is true. 

Second, it follows that no judge can ever excommunicate someone in this way, unless that person has first excommunicated themselves through a crime. Third, it follows that no judge should excommunicate anyone except on account of a crime, or mortal sin. And this is clear in the **Decretum** <note>original: *xj. q. iij.*; a reference to the 11th Case, Question 3 of the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard collection of canon law</note>, where it is said: "Let no Bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion under **anathema** <note>The most severe form of excommunication, involving formal exclusion from the Christian community</note> without a certain and manifest cause of sin. Because anathema is the condemnation of eternal death, and it should not be imposed except for a mortal crime, and on one who could not be corrected otherwise." And in the same source (24, q. 3, c. *His ita respondetur*), it is said: "Before God, it is not the sentence of the priests that is sought, but the life of the accused. For a sentence is of no consequence to someone whom the stain of sin has not infected."

Also, **Lyra** <note>Nicholas of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a highly influential Franciscan biblical commentator</note> says on the end of Hosea 4: "Let Israel go, you Judah, because of their malice, for their banquet is separated," that is, excommunicated. And in the Decretum (2, q. 1, *Multi*): "No one should be excommunicated except for a crime," according to **Augustine**.

<margin>Greater and lesser excommunication.</margin>

It is commonly said, however, that excommunication is twofold: namely, **Major** and **Minor**, as found in the laws regarding the sentence of excommunication. There it is held that **minor excommunication** removes one from the receiving of the **Sacraments**. **Major excommunication**, however, separates one from the **communion of the faithful**. Minor excommunication is the separation through [mortal] sin...

# CHAPTER XXII

<margin>Unjust excommunication is meritorious for a person.</margin>
...mortal [sin] from the participation in spiritual goods, by which a person makes themselves unworthy through a crime to obtain a share of grace; and no one can inflict that excommunication upon a person who persists in the grace of God.

**Greater excommunication** is the separation which the Prelates of the church proclaim against a person as a public sinner, through which they exclude them from the company of Christians and from participation in the **Sacraments**. And it is this excommunication that they now mark me with in their legal proceedings and denunciations, excluding me from all human participation. But blessed be God, who did not give such power to that excommunication that it could take away virtue or righteousness from a just man while he suffers humbly, nor can it inflict sin upon him. 

Rather, while he sustains it patiently, it serves to purify him, as a saw does to iron or fire to gold, and it serves to increase the reward of blessedness, as the Lord says in Luke 6: *Blessed shall you be when men hate you, and when they shall separate you, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of Man's sake. Rejoice in that day and be glad; for behold, your reward is great in heaven: for according to these things did their fathers to the prophets.* <note>original: *Lucæ, vj.*; a reference to the Beatitudes in the Gospel of Luke, verses 22-23</note>

<margin>Excommunication ought to be a medicine.</margin>
Now, this excommunication ought to be **medicinal**, that is, it ought to be a remedy for healing a person in spirit, and for leading them back into the fold of Christ, and ordained toward eternal life as the ultimate end. Whence **Blessed Augustine** in his *Homily on Penance*, and it is held in the Law <note>original: *ij. q. j. Multi*; referring to the *Decretum Gratiani*, Case 2, Question 1</note>: "Excommunication ought not to be mortal, but medicinal." 

And also in the chapter *Cum medicinalis*, regarding the sentence of excommunication, in the **Sixth Book of Decretals** <note>original: *li. vj.*; the *Liber Sextus*, a major collection of Canon Law published in 1298</note>: For a notorious sinner, on account of a crime, after a triple warning or public citation, if he refuses to be corrected, should be avoided in communication, according to the Savior's precept in Matthew 18, where he said to Peter: *If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone; if he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take one or two others with you, so that in the mouth of two or three...* <note>original: *Matth. xviij.*; a reference to Matthew 18:15-16</note>

# CHAPTER XXII

<margin>Judges often excommunicate themselves.</margin>
[...excommu]nicates another for the sake of worldly gain, primarily for his own honor, or to avenge a personal injury, or knowingly without the cause of a crime, that person actually excommunicates himself. For a judge ought only to excommunicate one whom God has already excommunicated on account of a crime that the judge knows the person has committed. This should only happen after a triple warning, and out of charity for the honor of God, for the salvation of the man being excommunicated, and for the benefit of others—so that they might fear and not be infected by his sin. This is just as Paul did in the last chapter of 1 Corinthians <note>original: *j. Corinth. ult.*; likely referring to 1 Corinthians 5:5-7</note>, where he commanded the people to purge out the public fornicator <note>A reference to the "incestuous man" in the church at Corinth whom Paul ordered to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so his spirit might be saved</note> so that he would not infect them, and so that his spirit might be saved. 

If these things were weighed carefully, a faithful person would recognize how many Prelates, Clergy, and Laymen are excommunicated by God, for this applies to all who turn aside from the commands of the Lord. Indeed, how many excommunicate themselves while they bring or proclaim a sentence of excommunication against others! This is especially true of the clergy, who pray almost daily during Prime <note>The first of the "canonical hours," or scheduled daily prayer services for monks and priests</note> saying: *Cursed are those who turn aside from your commands* <note>original: *Maledicti qui declinant a mandatis tuis*; from Psalm 119:21. Hus is pointing out the irony of priests reciting this psalm while they themselves are disobeying God</note>. 

This is a brief summary of excommunication, concerning which a solemn position was made by that pious Christian of holy memory, a great zealot and searcher of the law of Christ, Master Frederick Epinge, Bachelor of Canon Law, when he treated the first article: *No Prelate should excommunicate anyone unless he first knows that person to be excommunicated by God* <note>original: *Nullus Prælatus debet aliquem excommunicare, nisi prius sciat ipsum esse excommunicatum a deo*</note>, a subject about which I have also written elsewhere. And if you do not wish to believe this, go learn from the wall in Bethlehem <note>The Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, where Hus preached. He famously had the walls of the chapel painted with texts and images contrasting the lives of the Popes with the life of Christ and the teachings of the Church Fathers</note>; there you will find how excommunication does not harm the just person, but benefits him, and why even a just man ought to fear an unjust "Pilatic" <term>Pilaticam: excommunication carried out for political or worldly reasons, named after Pontius Pilate</term> excommunication. 

Wherefore, we respond to why this should be so for several reasons: Second, because of the danger to the one who excommunicates unjustly. Third, because of the harm to the brothers which could arise from the foolish application of church censures. Fourth, so that those who retreat from the truth are not scandalized. Fifth, so that people do not injure the excommunicated person by blaspheming them. Sixth, lest through impatience the victim fall from merit or turn away from justice. Other causes are explained more fully and pertinently elsewhere.

...to be said. For the wicked excommunicated Christ, as well as the man born blind, as is clear in John 9. <note>original: *Ioan. ix.*</note> And a distinction could also be made regarding its opposite, which is "communion in evil," about which Ephesians 5 <note>original: *ad Ephes. v.*</note> says: *Do not communicate in the unfruitful works of darkness.* <note>original: *Nolite communicare operibus infructuosis tenebrarum*</note> And in 2 John: *Whoever says "welcome" to him communicates in his wicked works.* <note>original: *Qui dixerit ei aue communicat operibus eius malignis.*</note> And Ecclesiasticus 13: *What communion has a holy person with a dog?* <note>original: *Quæ communicatio sancto ad canem?*</note>—as if to say, none. Hence, in Revelation 18 <note>original: *Apocalyp. xviij.*</note>, John says: *And I heard another voice from heaven saying, "Come out of her, my people, so that you do not participate in her sins and do not receive her plagues, for her sins have reached even to heaven."* <note>original: *Exite de illa popule meus...*</note> Let us pray the Lord that He may deign to keep us in His communion and guard us from that which is unlawful.

### What suspension is, what an ecclesiastical interdict is, and when and how they should be applied. Also, the author complains about his own unjust excommunication and the imposition of an interdict, etc. CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>
What suspension and ecclesiastical interdict are.
</margin>
Now we must speak of suspension. Here it should be noted that "to suspend" <term>suspensio: a legal penalty in the Church where a cleric is temporarily forbidden from exercising his orders or office</term> in this context means to prohibit someone from their ministry or from some benefit because of a crime. Thus, what the ancient decrees call "suspending," the new laws and decretals <term>decretales: letters of the Pope that possess the authority of law in the Catholic Church</term> call "interdicting" <term>interdictum: a censure that prohibits the faithful from participating in certain holy rites or receiving sacraments</term>. In such cases, they call it an ecclesiastical "suspension from office" or "from an ecclesiastical benefit," or an ecclesiastical "interdict" against performing the office of the Church.

<margin>
The Pope can suspend no one unless God has suspended them first.
</margin>
Given the definition of suspension just stated, it must be noted that just as it belongs properly to God to be the first to excommunicate a man, so it is with suspension. Therefore, it is impossible for a Pope or a Bishop to justly suspend anyone unless God has first suspended them. Just as it is impossible...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 23 of Jan Hus's treatise. Hus is expanding on the idea that human censures—like excommunication or suspension—carry no spiritual weight unless they are first enacted by God. He argues that even the Pope's thoughts are subject to divine cause, and provides several biblical examples of God "suspending" unworthy priests and leaders from their duties.</meta>

### CHAPTER XXIII

Ee iii
<meta>catchword: Item</meta>

It is impossible for the Pope to think anything justly, unless God causes that thought first. Whence the Apostle rightly says in 2 Corinthians 3: <note>original: *ij. Corinth, iij.*</note> *that we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.* <note>original: *q non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid ex nobis tanquam ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex deo est.*</note> And the supreme Bishop himself says in John 15: <note>original: *Ioan. xv.*</note> *Without me you can do nothing.* <note>original: *Sine me nihil potestis facere.*</note> From this it is clear that a <term>suspension</term> <note>An ecclesiastical penalty where a cleric is forbidden from performing their religious duties or receiving income from their office.</note> decreed by a prelate is valid only insofar as Almighty God makes it so. 

God’s active suspension extends to priests, kings, and all who remain alive, whom He removes from office or withdraws from life through divine vengeance. Thus, He suspended a certain man from the dignity of the priesthood, as is written in Hosea 4: <note>original: *Oseæ .iiij.*</note>

> Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you so that you do not perform the office of priest for me. <note>original: *Quia tu scientiam repulisti, ideo te repellam ne sacerdotio fungaris mihi.*</note>

And in Isaiah 1:

> Do not offer sacrifice further in vain. <note>original: *Ne offeratis ultra sacrificium frustra.*</note>

And in Malachi 1:

> I have no pleasure in you, and I will not receive a gift from your hand. <note>original: *Non est mihi uoluntas in uobis, & munus non accipiam de manu uestra.*</note>

And the Apostle of Christ suspends all who exist in a state of crime from the ministry of the body and blood of Christ, saying in 1 Corinthians 11: <note>original: *Pri. Corin. xj.*</note>

> Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. <note>original: *Quicunque manducauerit panem uel calicem biberit domini indigne, erit reus corporis & sanguinis domini.*</note>

Likewise, in 1 Samuel 2, <note>original: *pri. Regum .ij.* — The Vulgate Bible counts 1 and 2 Samuel as 1 and 2 Kings.</note> one reads of the grave suspension of Heli <note>The High Priest Eli.</note> and his lineage, because he corrected his sons improperly. Whence God said to Heli:

> Why have you kicked away my victims and my gifts which I commanded to be offered in the temple? And why have you honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the firstfruits of every sacrifice of my people Israel? Therefore the Lord of Israel says: I spoke clearly, saying that your house and the house of your father should minister before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me; but whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him, and those who despise me shall be held ignoble. Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house.

And further below:

> And this shall be a sign to you, that which is to come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they shall both die, and I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall act according to my heart and my soul.

Regum. xv." — In the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note> concerning Saul, who spared the enemies of his God beyond God's command: *Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you so that you are not king.* <note>original: "pro eo q̄ abíecístí sermonem domíní, abíecít te domínus ne sís rex."</note>

<margin>Multiple types of suspension.</margin>
And it is clear how suspension varies, because there is one kind of suspension from <term>office</term> <note>The performance of spiritual duties.</note> and another from <term>benefice</term> <note>The land, property, or income attached to a church office.</note>, or from some other good, from which a sinner is justly suspended on account of a crime. Likewise, there is a suspension *de facto* <note>meaning "in practice" or "by actual deed"</note> and a suspension *de jure* <note>meaning "by law" or "by right"</note>, along with other subdivisions. Now, suspension by law, as has been said, must principally originate from and be regulated by God. However, God sometimes causes suspension *de facto* through good ministers, and sometimes through evil ministers. But God Himself, through His own power, suspends every criminal Prelate from his office or ministry while he is actually in a state of crime. For by the very fact that he falls into <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave sin that, in medieval theology, separates the soul from God's grace.</note>, he sins in whatever he does; and consequently, he is prohibited by God from acting in such a way, and consequently is suspended by God from that office.

Whence in the forty-ninth Psalm <note>Psalm 50 in modern English Bibles, following the Hebrew numbering rather than the Latin Vulgate's 49.</note>, the prophet says: *But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant in your mouth? For you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion. Your mouth abounded in malice, and your tongue framed deceits; sitting against your brother you spoke, and against your mother's son you placed a scandal.* <note>original: "Peccatorí autẽ díxít deus, quare tu enarras íustícías meas... aduersus fílíum matrís tuæ ponebas scandalũ."</note> Where God enumerates the

<margin>God suspends sinners on account of these sins.</margin>
sins on account of which He suspends a sinner from the narration of His covenant, which is the law of truth. The first sin is disobedience to God; the second is the rejection of His words; the third is theft; the fourth is adultery; the fifth is malice of the mouth, which is divided into lying, blasphemy, false testimony, perjury, deceit, detraction, vain talk, cursing, foul talk, and so forth. The sixth sin is on account of the <term>scandal of Christ</term> <note>In this context, a "scandal" is a stumbling block or an action that leads others into sin or away from the faith.</note>. ### CHAPTER XXIII

->...suspended by God from the proclamation of His covenant.<-

Therefore, let the faithful soul take note of this aforementioned suspension from the office of proclaiming God’s <term>covenant</term> <note>In this context, "testament" or "covenant" refers to the Holy Scriptures and the duty to preach them.</note>, and consider the three examples mentioned above to see if our own Prelates and Clergy are currently suspended by the Lord. First, if they reject the knowledge of scripture and the duty to evangelize, they are then suspended by the Lord, as we read regarding a lesser case in the fourth chapter of Hosea: <note>Hosea 4:6: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I also reject you from being a priest for me."</note>. For our Prelates have, in every respect, greater material and forms for preaching, as well as more reasons why they should preach more than the priests of the Old Law; yet they perform this duty less. Therefore, since there is a greater reason for them to act, and the same Lord is present—who, by the demands of His justice, cannot ultimately withhold punishment for a greater crime—it is clear that our Prelates, if they are of this sort, are more severely suspended. They are all the more guilty because they ought to stand firm for the law of Christ even more fervently during the times of the <term>Antichrist</term> <note>Hus often identified the corruption in the Church hierarchy as a sign of the end times or the influence of the Antichrist.</note>.

<margin>To what extent a Prelate is bound to his subjects.</margin>
Regarding the second suspension, which the Lord inflicted upon Eli, let the faithful note whether our Prelates either fail to punish their spiritual children, or punish them more culpably than Eli’s natural sons were punished by him. <note>Eli was the High Priest whose sons, Hophni and Phinehas, corrupted the tabernacle; Eli failed to restrain them and was punished by God (1 Samuel 2-4).</note> In order to discern the greatness of that guilt, the faithful should note two things: First, that a Prelate is more strictly bound to a spiritual son than he is bound by reason to a natural son. Second, that a punishment inflicted for the sake of extorting money—whereby sin is essentially sold—is far more detestable than a punishment that is simply withheld out of natural love, as Eli seems to have spared his sons.

Regarding the third suspension, which applies to both prelates and kings as well as other secular princes, let the faithful note that these leaders defer more to the public enemies of the Lord for the sake of private gain than Saul deferred to <term>Amalek</term> <note>The Amalekites were enemies of Israel; Saul was commanded to destroy them but kept their King and the best livestock for himself, leading to his rejection by God.</note> out of greed for temporal goods. If this is the case, there is no doubt that the same God, who cannot bypass His own justice, will punish these offenders more severely. Whence, there is an evident sign of the gravity of the punishment:
