# CHAPTER XXIII

<margin>Woe to the moderns</margin>
...are heavily rebuked. Woe, therefore, to the modern spiritual and secular princes who practice lewdness <note>original: "luxuriam". In this context, it refers specifically to sexual immorality and excess.</note> themselves, giving a bad example to their subjects, and who do not correct those under them—or if they do correct them, they do it out of greed. Such men are without a doubt suspended from their office by the Lord. For it is written in the Papal law, in the third book of the Decretals <note>The Decretals of Gregory IX, a primary collection of Canon Law used in the Middle Ages.</note>, in the chapter "On the life and conduct of the Clergy," under the heading: *We command your fraternity* <note>original: "Fraternitati tuæ mandamus"</note>, that you should take care to diligently warn the clergy of our jurisdiction who, being in the <term>Subdiaconate</term> <note>The lowest of the "major orders" in the church hierarchy; from this rank upward, celibacy was strictly required.</note> or above, keep fornicating women, that they must remove them from their company and never admit them again. But if they despise this and refuse to comply, you are to suspend them from their ecclesiastical <term>benefices</term> <note>A "benefice" was a church office, such as a parish or a cathedral post, that provided a steady income to the holder.</note> until they have made worthy satisfaction; and if they presume to keep the women while under suspension, you must take care to remove them from those same benefices forever.

<margin>A Bishop must be suspended from office if he does not restrain fornicators.</margin>
<margin>Consider these things, O priests who keep concubines.</margin>
Therefore, because the fault lies not in the law itself but in the superiors who should put it into practice, we know that under the same title the Pope says: "As for those Prelates who presume to keep such men in their iniquities, especially under the pretext of money or some other temporal benefit, we will that they be subject to the same punishment." And in the eighty-second <term>Distinction</term> <note>A division within the "Decretum Gratiani," the foundation of medieval Canon Law.</note>, under the authority of Blessed Gregory, it is said: "If any Bishop consents to the fornication of his clergy—by not attacking it with the authority of his office, whether through prayer or public outcry—he must be suspended from his own office." This suspension, according to the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio (c. 1250–1313), a famous commentator on Canon Law known as "The Archdeacon."</note>, ought to be perpetual and equivalent to deposition <note>Removal from office.</note>, because of the difficulty of gathering enough Bishops to formally depose such a Bishop, or a Bishop who has thus <term>simoniacally</term> <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling spiritual things, named after Simon Magus in the Book of Acts.</note> sold, or continues to sell, justice. And because a Metropolitan <note>A high-ranking bishop with authority over others, such as an Archbishop.</note>, such as the Roman Pontiff, might be sluggish toward his own Cardinals in the execution of this holy institution, the laws have ordained a third remedy for this confusion: namely, that the Mass of a priest should not be heard by anyone who knows for a fact that the priest is a fornicator, nor should the goods of the church be administered to him to fuel his crime. For in the thirty-second Distinction, in the chapter *No one* <note>original: "Nullus"</note>, Pope Nicholas speaks thus: "No one should hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows without doubt maintains a concubine," etc. Regarding this, Alexander II speaks in the same Distinction: "By this decree we command that no one should hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows without doubt [keeps] a concubine..."

From these things, when the state of the church is examined, it is gathered that from the Pope down to the lowest priest, few are excluded at any given time from suspension, except for the one who irreproachably follows the Lord Jesus Christ. ### CHAPTER XXIII

...material things, which will not endure after the day of judgment. And woe to me if I keep silent, not attacking avarice, or the manifest luxury of the Clergy. For in Distinction 84 <note>original: "dist. lxxxiiij". Nor is one free from the suspicion of secret complicity who ceases to oppose a manifest crime. In the same place: "For what does it profit a man not to be defiled by his own error, if he provides consent to one who errs?" In the same place: "He is seen to consent to the one who errs who does not step forward to cut away what ought to be corrected." Hence Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational author for medieval theology.</note>, in chapter 15 of his *Pastoral Care*, bringing forward that passage from the prophet in Lamentations 2 <note>original: "Threnor. ij."</note>: "Thy prophets have seen false and foolish things for thee, and they have not laid open thy iniquity, to provoke thee to penance," speaks thus: "For in sacred speech, those are sometimes called prophets who, while they judge present things to be fleeting, make manifest those things which are to come. The divine word reproves them for seeing false things because, while they fear to correct faults, they soothe the delinquent with a hollow promise of security, because they in no way open up the iniquity of the sinners. Because they remain silent from the voice of rebuke, for the 'key of opening' is the speech of correction. Because by rebuking, it uncovers the fault which even he who committed it often does not know." Thus says he. And it is held in Distinction 42: "Let the ruler be..." <note>original: "Sit rector". A specific canon regarding the character of a church leader.</note> And would that our doctors <note>Teachers and high-ranking theologians.</note> would take notice of these things, for then they would not stroke the life of the Prelates <note>To "stroke" or "palpate" here means to flatter or handle gently rather than correcting.</note>, nor would they be unfaithful in opening up their iniquity to them, so as to provoke them to penance. Let them see for themselves in how many ways one person consents to the crime of another. For he consents who cooperates, who defends, who gives counsel and authorizes, and he who does not threaten or rebuke.

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus's argument in Chapter XXIII of *De Ecclesia*. He is explaining how the corrupt hierarchy (which he terms "Antichrist") uses ecclesiastical punishments to silence those who expose clerical sins. This page specifically contrasts the "interdict" and "fulminations" used by the church of his time with the mercy shown by Christ.</meta>

# I. H. ON THE CHURCH

...has constantly resisted, they place an **interdict** <term>interdictum: a legal strike where a community is prohibited from receiving sacraments or holding church services</term> among the people, forbidding the performance of divine offices, the administration of the Sacraments, and even burial—even for men however just—so that through that devised **aggravation** <note>In canon law, an "aggravation" was a formal intensifying of an ecclesiastical penalty.</note> they may obtain their own will. It is an evident sign when such censures proceed from the Antichrist—which they call **Fulminations** <note>original: "Fulminationes". These were formal "thunderbolt" condemnations or public pronouncements of excommunication.</note> in their legal processes—while they are struck against those who preach the law of Christ and argue against the wickedness of the Clergy.

<margin>Disobedience to Prelates is punished more severely than disobedience to God.</margin>
The second sign is that those censures are multiplied more on account of disobedience shown to them [the prelates] than on account of disobedience shown to God, and thus more for their own injury than for the injury of our God. For in that way the ancient enemy, practiced in malice, proceeds: he exalts the obedience of the Antichrist above the obedience of Christ, and thus usurps **excommunication** <note>Hus argues that the church leaders have "stolen" the power of excommunication to use for their own ends rather than for God's purposes.</note> for disobedience to himself, which Christ instituted for disobedience shown to God. 

Moreover, he proceeds in this way: First he defames the disciple of Christ, then he accuses him, then cites him, excommunicates him, suspends him, and if he cannot hand him over to prison or to death, then he invokes the **secular arm** <term>brachium seculare: the use of civil authorities (kings or lords) to carry out physical punishments the church was technically forbidden to perform</term>; and not even being able to conquer in this way, he heaps up an interdict through malice. Most principally, however, he proceeds thus against those who lay bare the wickedness of the Antichrist, who has especially usurped the Clergy for himself. Whence he extends those censures for the sake of his Clergy, as for those litigating in the greed for **Benefices** <term>beneficia: church offices that provided an income</term>, and when the people have not given the tithe according to their wish, or if a prince of the Clergy has arrested or seized **temporalities** <note>original: "temporalia". Secular property or assets owned by the church.</note>, or if some cleric—even a most wicked thief or otherwise criminal—has been captured and held in custody by secular authorities, or if a priest has been wounded to the point of bloodshed, or even when the people have lawfully withdrawn obedience from those very Prelates at some time.

<margin>Christ did not impose an interdict as his vicars do</margin>
Christ, however, the Supreme Pontiff, even when that prophet was detained—than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women <note>A reference to John the Baptist.</note>—did not impose an interdict, not even when Herod beheaded him. <meta>This page continues the argument from page 227, where Jan Hus (I.H.) distinguishes between the righteous punishments of God and the self-serving "fulminations" and interdicts of the corrupt ecclesiastical hierarchy. ->### CHAPTER XXIII<-

He [Christ] delivered this doctrine to his members, saying in Matthew 5: "Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the good and the bad, and sends rain on the just and the unjust." Following this doctrine in word and deed, the first Vicar of Christ, the Roman Pontiff, in 1 Peter 2, teaches the faithful, saying: "In this you were called, because Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that we should follow his footsteps; he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; who, when he was cursed, did not curse back, and when he suffered, did not threaten." And Paul, traveling the same path, says in Romans 12: "Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse." This same doctrine was followed by other saints, who, in the midst of their own persecution, did not "hurl thunderbolts" <note>original: "fulminabant" — the formal act of pronouncing an ecclesiastical curse or excommunication.</note> of excommunication or suspension, nor did they impose an **interdict** <term>interdictum: a legal strike where a community is prohibited from receiving sacraments or holding church services</term>; rather, when heavier persecution came, they applied themselves all the more to divine ministries.

For Pope Hadrian IV, who began his reign in the year of our Lord 1154, placed all of Rome under interdict because of the wounding of a single Cardinal. Oh, how "patient" this Pope was! Yet not like Christ, Peter, or Paul, or the apostle Andrew. Afterward, Alexander III, in the year of our Lord 1159, interdicted the kingdom of England (found in the chapter "It is not for us" concerning *Espousals*). Pope Celestine III, who began in 1082 <note>The text lists 1082 ("M. lxxxij"), though Celestine III actually reigned from 1191–1198. Afterward, Innocent III, who began in the year of our Lord 1199, published the interdict through many **decretals** <term>decretales: papal letters that formulated church law</term>, such as in the chapter "In the Lateran Council" regarding prebends in book 3 of the Decretals. <meta>This page continues Jan Hus's critique of the "interdict," a practice where the institutional Church would suspend all religious services and sacraments in a specific geographic area as a form of collective punishment. Hus argues that this practice lacks any biblical foundation and harms the spiritual well-being of the innocent.</meta>

# JAN HUS: ON THE CHURCH

...ty, such interdicts are multiplied.

<margin>There is no underlying reason why a general interdict should be imposed.</margin>
Therefore, I always ask for the foundation or the logic behind a **general interdict** <term>interdictum: a legal sanction that prohibited a community from participating in certain sacraments and religious rites</term>, whereby the righteous—without any fault of their own—are deprived of the Sacraments, such as Communion, confession, and the rest, and sometimes even infants are deprived of baptism. Similarly, why is the ministry of God among righteous men diminished through an interdict because of one man? It would be quite a marvel if service were taken away from an earthly king by all his good servants simply because of one servant who was opposed to him. It would be even more absurd if, because of one who was a good and faithful servant of the king, a **Vassal** <note>In the feudal system, a noble who held land in exchange for service; here, Hus uses it to represent an underling attempting to manipulate a higher authority.</note> wishing to bend that servant to his own will, were to forbid all the king's servants from performing their ministry for the king himself. How then can a Pope or Bishop so thoughtlessly, without Scripture or revelation, so easily forbid the ministry to Christ the King?

<margin>Evil, not good, results from the interdict.</margin>
For once a general interdict is placed on a city or diocese, sin is not diminished, but increased. For burial is denied to the righteous, contrary to the Scripture in Ecclesiasticus 7: "Do not withhold grace from the dead." <note>original: "Mortuo non prohibeas gratiam."</note> For who doubts that it is a work of mercy to bury the righteous dead? For in Tobit 12, the angel Raphael spoke to Tobit in this way: "When you prayed with tears and buried the dead, and left your dinner, and hid the dead in your house, and buried them by night, I offered your prayer to the Lord." Who also doubts that hearing confession, giving counsel for salvation, and preaching the word of God are works of mercy? Likewise, providing the Sacrament of the Eucharist to a devoted people and performing baptisms. What logic, then, is there to withdraw these from the people of God without any merit of their own?

Hence, the Blessed Augustine writes to Bishop Maximus (as found in Canon Law, Case 23, Question 4): "If," he says, "you have an opinion on this matter based on certain logic or explored through the testimony of the Scriptures, please deign to teach us how a son may be rightly **anathematized** <term>anathema: a formal curse by the Church, excommunicating a person</term> for the sin of his father, or a wife for that of her husband, or a servant for his master's, or anyone in the house—including one not yet born—if they should be born at the time when the entire house is bound by an anathema, such that the **washing of rebirth** <note>Hus is referring to baptism (original: "lavacrum regenerationis").</note> cannot help them in the danger of death; for this was a bodily punishment which we read some...

# CHAPTER XXIII

Those who despise God, along with all those who shared in that same impiety, perished among the saints. ### CHAPTER XXIII 225

...even if the bodies of innumerable martyrs are killed for God—and this is seen as a literal statement. If innocents are dragged from the church, and if the bodies of martyrs perish, it is no loss; but it is said that common homicide exists there. Likewise, the **gloss** <term>gloss: a standard marginal commentary used to interpret legal or biblical texts</term> says: He commits a graver sin through whose fault the soul of a child departs from this life without baptism, than he who might kill many innocents by removing them from the church. <note>original: "Grauius peccat cuius culpa anima pueri de hac uita sine baptismo decesserit..." This reflects the medieval belief that dying without baptism prevented entry into heaven, making the denial of sacraments a spiritual "murder."</note>

<margin>Note the malice of the clergy.</margin>
But alas, the Clergy, blinded by malice, does not heed all these things. For the sake of a small non-payment of money—sometimes even by a poor man who is unable to pay—they deprive the people of the sacraments of the church through an **interdict**, <term>interdict: a legal punishment that prohibited an entire town or region from receiving most sacraments</term> as has been said. Christ did not teach thus; He especially taught the Clergy not to contend in judgment, saying in Luke 6: "To him who strikes you on one cheek, offer the other also; and from him who takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who asks of you, and from him who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back." <note>Luke 6:29-30</note> But the impatient Clergy, hearing that most wholesome doctrine of Christ, will laugh it to scorn. Nor is it a wonder, for the Savior says afterward in Matthew 7: "Everyone who hears these words and does not do them is like a foolish man who built his house upon the sand." <note>Matthew 7:26</note> Who, I ask, is a more foolish man than the Clergyman who, grounding himself in the filth of the world, holds the life and doctrine of Christ in derision? For the Clergy is now so ruined that they hate those who frequently preach and name the Lord Christ; and when anyone alleges Christ on his own behalf, immediately with wide and rancorous mouths they say, "Are you Christ?" and in the manner of the Pharisees, they defile and excommunicate those who confess Christ.

<margin>The unjust excommunication of the author.</margin>
Therefore, because I preached Christ and His Gospel, and exposed the **Antichrist**, <note>Hus frequently used the term "Antichrist" to describe the corrupt institutional structures of the church rather than a single individual.</note> wishing that the Clergy would live according to the law of Christ, the Prelates first arranged—together with Lord **Suico** <note>Suico: Zbyňek Zajíc of Hasenburk (c. 1376–1411), the Archbishop of Prague who initially supported but later fiercely opposed Hus.</note> of Prague, the Archbishop—a **Bull** <term>Bull: an official decree issued by a Pope</term> from **Pope Alexander**, <note>Alexander V, whose 1409 bull prohibited preaching in private chapels like the Bethlehem Chapel.</note> so that the word of God might not be preached to the people in Chapels. From this Bull I appealed, and I was never able to obtain a hearing. Consequently, having been summoned, I did not appear for reasonable causes; because of this, they ordained an excommunication through **Michael de Causis**, <note>Michael de Causis: a former priest from Prague who became a primary accuser and prosecutor of Hus at the Council of Constance.</note> after an agreement had been made, and just recently they procured in...

<header>ON THE CHURCH</header>

...interdict, by which the common people of Christ are burdened <term>angariantur: to be pressed into service or forced into a hardship</term> without fault.

I would wish, therefore, that the doctors who say that in legal proceedings a "pure good" is not prohibited, nor is a "pure evil" commanded, but only "middle things" <note>original: "sed sola media." In medieval philosophy, "middle things" (adiaphora) are actions that are neither inherently good nor bad but can be commanded by an authority.</note>, would prove these claims. And first, let them prove that an interdict so general is a "middle thing" between a pure good and a pure evil—an act that deprives the innocent of the sacraments and burial, hinders divine service, and brings about no good, except scandals, detractions, and hatreds. And how will the doctors be able to show that this is lawful: to excommunicate the people of God from the sacraments, from burial, and from divine services? Regarding this, as has been said, the most powerful doctor of the church, the Blessed Augustine, rebuked Bishop Auxilius. The proof of these doctors—combined from a hypocritical cloaking and the cleverness of peasants—would not satisfy Augustine as a rational argument when the doctors say:

<margin>The style of the Roman Curia.</margin>
"But according to the style of the church and the Roman Curia, customary and observed." Behold the hypocritical cloaking before the fathers of our fathers! Behold the cleverness of peasants: let only "middle things" be commanded there. O Doctors, of which church is that "style"? Is it by chance the Apostolic one? Tell us, which Apostle's style is that, or which saint's after the Apostles? Is it perhaps Christ's style, the style of the head of the Holy Church, in whose style every useful truth for the church is contained?

But I ask, where is this saying contained? "Every place, city, fortified town, village, or borough, whether exempt or not exempt, to which the same Lord Jan Hus shall go, and for as long as he remains there and makes a stay, and for three natural days continuously following his departure from there... in these writings we subject to such an ecclesiastical interdict, and we wish for divine services to cease in them." <note>This is a direct quote from the papal decree issued against Hus. It essentially turned him into a spiritual "miasma," where his presence alone would cause a town to be stripped of its religious rights.</note> Perhaps that style is founded on this: "It is necessary always to pray, and not to lose heart" (Luke 18). Or there: "Praise God, all you nations." And there: "In every place, praise the Lord." # CHAPTER XXIII

<sig>Gg ij</sig>

...because of this formal decree <note>original: "fulminationem"; a "fulmination" was the official public pronouncement of a church penalty like an interdict or excommunication.</note>, will divine services cease for you? Will Christ, the just advocate, not intercede with God the Father for his faithful members? Or will the angelic choir not cry out: *Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of Hosts* <note>original: "Sabaoth"; a Hebrew term for "armies" or "heavenly hosts" used in the liturgy.</note>? Will that voice cease, of which John speaks in Revelation chapter 5:

> I heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and the living creatures and the elders, and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: "Worthy is the one who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing, and every creature which is in heaven, and which is on the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and those which are in them."

Nor do the doctors say that this is irrelevant, for all rational creatures—according to the style <note>The "style" refers to the established legal formulas and bureaucratic procedures of the Roman administrative offices.</note> of the Roman Curia—are subject to the command of that Curia. For every human creature is subject to the Roman Pontiff, as the style of his own law says in the *Extravagantes* <note>The *Extravagantes* were collections of papal decrees that circulated "outside" the main body of established canon law at the time.</note> of Boniface VIII.

<margin>Every rational creature is subject to the Roman Pontiff.</margin>
> Furthermore, we declare, say, and define that to be subject to the Roman Pontiff is absolutely necessary for the salvation of every human creature.

Similarly, the angelic creature is subject to the Roman Pontiff himself, as the style of the Curia says in a Bull of Pope Clement:

> We command the angels of Paradise that they lead the soul of that person—having been fully absolved from purgatory—into the glory of paradise.

Since, therefore, according to that style of the Curia, every rational creature—both angelic and human—is subject to the Roman Pontiff’s command; and since the style in the legal proceedings of that same Curia says that to whatever place (whether exempt from local jurisdiction or not) Jan Hus turns, and for as long as he remains there, we subject that place to an ecclesiastical interdict <note>An interdict was a collective punishment that prohibited all public worship and sacraments in a specific geographic area.</note>; it follows that if—which is entirely possible by the absolute power of God—Jan Hus through death turns toward the heavenly Jerusalem, that place too must be subjected to the ecclesiastical interdict.

<margin>The Pope places an interdict on heaven.</margin>
But blessed be God Almighty, who has commanded that the angels, with all the saints in that same heavenly Jerusalem, shall not be subject to such an interdict.

## ON THE CHURCH

<meta>catchword: remainder</meta>

Blessed also be Christ, the Supreme Roman Pontiff <note>original: "Summus Romanus Pontifex"; Hus is intentionally applying the Pope's highest title to Christ to argue that the true leadership of the Church is divine, not human.</note>, who gave grace to his faithful so that even when no Roman Pontiff exists for a certain time, they are able—under the leadership of Christ the Lord—to reach the heavenly homeland.

<margin>Agnes, the woman Pope.</margin>
For who would say that, during the time when Agnes <note>Commonly known in history as "Pope Joan," a legendary female figure believed in the Middle Ages to have reigned as Pope between Leo IV and Benedict III.</note> was the woman holding the papacy (only in appearance) for two years and five months, no human being could be saved? Or again, who would say that in the interval after a Pope’s death—between the death of the Pope and the election of a successor—none of the people dying at that time could be saved? Blessed also be almighty God, who ordains that his militant church <term>militant church: the community of Christians currently living on earth, "soldiering" for the faith</term> lives in such a way that she is not "decapitated" or dead simply because a Pope has died. This is because her life depends not on the Pope, but on Christ the head. Even when a Pope is a fool or has become a heretic, the militant church remains the faithful bride of the Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>Three Popes at one time.</margin>
Blessed also be the Lord, who, being the one head of the church, preserves her in unity so effectively that even when there is a "triple-headed" monster <note>original: "tripertito uocato capite"; a reference to the Western Schism where three rival men claimed to be the true Pope simultaneously.</note> of Popes, the bride of the Lord Jesus Christ remains one. For currently, Balthazar, called John XXIII, is in Rome; Angelo Correr, called Gregory XII, is in Rimini; and Peter de Luna, called Benedict, is in Aragon. Why does not one of them, who is called the "most holy father," compel the others and their followers—out of the "fullness of power"—to submit to his jurisdiction? After all, does the "style" <term>style: the official legal language and bureaucratic procedures of the papal administration</term> of the Roman Curia not say that he possesses the fullness of power over every human being on earth?

It is, therefore, a sufficiently weak foundation and proof to claim that something must be held as unbreakably true just because it follows the "style" of the Roman Curia. For in the *Sixth Book of Constitutions* <note>original: "libro sexto"; referring to the *Liber Sextus*, a collection of canon law published by Boniface VIII in 1298.</note>, a rule is given regarding two people who receive letters from the Pope for the same provision <note>A "provision" was a papal appointment to a church office.</note> on the same day. The one to whom the Pope granted a canonry <term>canonry: a position or office within a cathedral or collegiate church</term> is to be preferred over the one to whom he did not grant a canonry, provided the executor was ignorant of who first petitioned for it. But if they are equal in "grace" <note>In this legal context, "grace" refers to the formal favor or grant bestowed by the Pope.</note> according to the form of the papal "style," then the one who presented the letter first will have the stronger right to the Prebend <term>prebend: the portion of the church's revenues granted to a canon as a stipend</term>. And thirdly, if they are equal in all three of these things, then the Canons to whom the appointment belongs, or the majority of them, are bound to elect...

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus's critique of the Roman Curia's legalism. He argues that human-made legal traditions ("style") often contradict divine judgment and that "tradition" alone is not a valid excuse for sin or error, especially when it deviates from the example of Christ or the Apostles.</meta>

### CHAPTER XXIII

...the remainder being devoid of the fruit of grace. This is the case unless it clearly appears from the wording of the Papal letters that the Pope intended to provide for both individuals. However, this three-part maxim of the Curia's "style" <term>style: "stylus Curiæ," referring to the established legal procedures, formulas, and bureaucratic customs of the Roman court</term> seems to be a principle directed against Christ. For, assuming—as happens in the majority of cases—that the person preferred for a canonry <term>canonry: an office or position within a cathedral or collegiate church</term>, whether at the time of presentation, or during the granting of grace, or thirdly in the election by the Chapter, is more unworthy in the eyes of God than the other candidate, then according to this "style" maxim, judgment is being made against the judgment of Christ. From this it follows that such a maxim of style is against conscience, and consequently against Christ. What kind of proof is it, then, to say: "the customary and observed style of the Roman Curia allows or asserts this, therefore it is in harmony with the law of Christ and must be accepted by Catholics"?

<margin>Not everything the Roman style does is immediately right.</margin>

Furthermore, that rustic sophistry which the doctors <term>doctors: the high-ranking academic theologians and legal experts of the university</term> put forward—namely, that "before the fathers of our fathers, it was so believed or observed"—would be enough to conclude that these same doctors should believe and observe the erroneous customs of the pagans and Jews. Indeed, it would imply they ought to worship Baal, just as the Bohemians <note>original: "Boemi"; Hus refers to the Slavic people of Bohemia (the modern-day Czech Republic) and their pre-Christian history.</note> did while they were still pagans. They have against them that passage in Ezekiel 20: 
> *Walk ye not in the statutes of your fathers, neither observe their judgments.* 

What a shameless proof from the doctors: "it was believed, observed, or held before the fathers of our fathers, therefore it must be believed, observed, and held by us." For foolish men make such tasteless arguments to find excuses for their sins. He who speaks in Psalm 105 <note>Psalm 106 in modern Bibles; original: "Peccauimus dñe cum patribus noſtris..."</note> is not of their number: 
> *We have sinned, O Lord, with our fathers; we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they were not mindful of the multitude of your mercies.* 

<margin>Fathers of fathers</margin> 
And if the doctors should happen to say that by the phrase "fathers of fathers" they mean the holy prophets, the Apostles, or the later saints, then they should have explicitly cited the scriptures of those individuals. Against such scripture, it would not be lawful for anyone to rebel. If they did this, their persistence would cease—that persistence which shatters their own sophistry or reasoning when they claim that in legal proceedings, according to the customary and observed style of the church and the Roman Curia before the fathers of our fathers, it is commanded...

# THE CHURCH

Blessed also be Christ, the Highest Roman Pontiff <note>original: "Summus Romanus Pontifex." Hus provocatively applies the Pope's highest title to Christ himself.</note>, who gave grace to his faithful, so that even when no Roman Pontiff exists for a given time, they are able to reach the heavenly homeland, led by Christ the Lord.

<meta>This page continues Jan Hus's critique of the legal and administrative practices of the Roman Curia. # ON THE CHURCH

<margin>It is perverse that divine things should cease in the presence of an evil person.</margin>
In that place, [the Curia] sits as the only intermediary between pure goods and pure evils. For which of the holy fathers, prophets, apostles, or other saints ever commanded that wherever a man—even the most wicked—should turn, the divine offices should cease? For Christ, seeing the most disobedient Judas, his own betrayer, did not cease from divine matters at his great supper. On the contrary, while Judas himself was present, Christ performed the divine rites and gave him his most holy and divine body to eat. He also more steadfastly warned his disciples to watch and pray with him, lest they enter into temptation because of the violent assault of the scribes, Pharisees, and high priests.

<margin>Neither Christ nor the saints could support the interdict.</margin>
Nor did the most pious High Priest <note>Referring to Christ as the ultimate High Priest.</note> cease from his most divine prayer while being blasphemed and crucified, but instead prayed for his crucifiers, saying:
> Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. 
Luke 23. Therefore, praying with a cry and with tears, he was heard for his reverence, as noted in Hebrews 5. Hence his true and manifest <term>Vicars</term> <note>A term usually applied to the Pope ("Vicar of Christ"), but Hus here applies it to the Apostles and saints who truly follow Christ's example.</note>, the Apostles and other saints, imitated him in this; and first among them was Stephen, who says in the sixth chapter of Acts: 
> Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them, for they know not what they do.
And it is a wonder why an <term>interdict</term> <note>A legal punishment by the Church that suspends all public worship and most sacraments in a specific territory or for a specific group.</note> is not declared on account of the Jews who deny Christ is God (and thus do not follow his whole law), or on account of manifest <term>Simoniacs</term> <note>Those who buy or sell church offices or spiritual things; named after Simon Magus.</note>, who are the chief heretics, cursed, excommunicated, suspended, and interdicted by the writings of the holy Apostles and other saints, and are alienated from the holy priesthood.

<margin>The simoniacal trade of the clergy.</margin>
The reason is that those Simoniacs sell and buy excommunications, suspensions, and interdicts. They nourish and defend their <term>Simony</term> with these things as if they were the most powerful weapons. Nor is proof necessary, since this simoniacal commerce is evident to the eye, even to the peasants who are distressed, vexed, oppressed, and despoiled by these very Simoniacs. For the <term>Gehizite heresy</term> <note>A synonym for Simony, named after Gehazi, the servant of Elisha who took illicit payment for a miracle (2 Kings 5).</note> has grown so strong that men, even against their will, are driven into this kind of crime—not slowly, but persistently and conveniently for the sake of trade. And all commerce of this kind springs from the <term>style</term> of the Roman <term>Curia</term> <note>The "Stylus Curiae" refers to the established legal procedures and bureaucratic customs of the Papal administration.</note>, which otherwise...

<summary>Hus argues that the "interdict"—the suspension of church services as a legal punishment—is un-Christian, noting that Christ prayed for his enemies even during the crucifixion. He claims the practice is used by corrupt officials to extort money, a practice he labels "the Gehizite heresy."</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Master Jan Hus’s most famous work, De Ecclesia (On the Church). Following his critique of the interdict, he turns his attention to the financial corruption of the Roman Curia and the legal battles in Prague over the "45 Articles" of John Wycliffe, which Hus refused to condemn unconditionally. The page ends with a colophon noting the work's completion in 1413 and its eventual printing in 1520.</meta>

# CHAPTER XXIII

The Curia of the Bishops subordinates its subjects in a style that is both <term>Simoniacal</term> <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments.</note> and **Gehazite**. <note>original: "Giezitico"; a reference to Gehazi, the servant of the prophet Elisha who was cursed with leprosy for taking illicit payment (2 Kings 5). In the Middle Ages, it was a common synonym for greed and corruption in the church.</note> This is evident in the letters dimissory <note>Official documents by which a bishop released a candidate for ordination to another bishop.</note>, in confirmations, absolutions, admissions, and in other things invented for the sake of draining money.

Now one should speak regarding the condemnation of the forty-five articles. <note>These were forty-five propositions drawn from the works of the English reformer John Wycliffe, which the authorities in Prague and Rome demanded Hus condemn as heretical.</note> But I say briefly that up to this day, the doctors of the <term>Town Hall</term> <note>original: "praetorium"; referring to the Old Town Hall of Prague, where the university faculty and city officials debated the condemnation of Wycliffe’s ideas.</note> have not proved that any one of them is heretical, or erroneous, or scandalous. 

But I wonder why the doctors do not now teach in the Town Hall that the article regarding the taking away of temporal goods is not practiced—specifically this one: *Temporal lords can, at their own discretion, take away temporal goods from ecclesiastics who are habitually delinquent.* Now they remain silent along with the Pontiffs and Pharisees, nor do they gather at the Town Hall to condemn that article; yet while practicing it, what they feared has certainly come upon them, and will come upon them in the future: For they will lose their temporal goods, but may God grant that they preserve their souls. 

The doctors were saying that once the condemnation of the articles was made, then there would be peace and concord. But their prophecy has turned into the opposite quality. For those condemning were rejoicing, while those paying the taxes <note>original: "census"; annual payments or rents.</note> are mourning. They condemned this article: *Tithes are pure alms.* <note>Hus argued that tithes were not a mandatory tax by divine law but a form of charity that could be withheld if the priest was corrupt.</note> And many coming to the Town Hall asked that their taxes, which are alms, should not be taken away. But certain lords of the Town Hall responded, saying: "Behold, you previously condemned the idea that tithes are pure alms, and now you say that they are alms; thus you attempt to act against the condemnation." And so much for the present, leaving other matters to be deferred for the future.

---

### HERE ENDS THE TREATISE OF MASTER 
### JOHN HUS, which he collected in the year of the Lord 1413. 
### And it was publicly pronounced in the City of Prague.

->of August, in the year 1520.<-

### CHAPTER XXII

The causes and cases of the Bishops are called into doubt, being conducted in the style of the book of **Simon de Gleichen**. <note>original: "Symonis de Gleichen"; likely a corruption of "Simony" (the buying/selling of church offices) or a reference to a specific contemporary figure associated with financial corruption.</note> This is plain to see in those continuous letters dimissory, <note>official documents by which a bishop released a candidate to another jurisdiction.</note> and first of all in the sale of absolutions, the division of benefices, and other schemes invented for the sake of draining money.

Now, concerning confessions, it is evident that the **sacramental jurisdiction** <term>Sacramentalis dicio: the legal and spiritual authority to grant or withhold the sacraments.</term> is not open to all; it is not available to the poor, nor to certain people among the barbarians or foreigners—it is even closed to them. And let those who do not teach such doctrine to the people know that it is not only a matter of the removal of persons, but also many other things. These are things that the temporal lords could use to justify withholding their support to stop such oppression of the church members and to slow the church's greed: specifically, in the exchange of **Pensions and Prebends** <note>Fixed portions of the church's revenue given to a clergyman.</note> which they aggressively seek for their own promotion. They do not fear to act this way, lest their lords should quickly perish to them, and they do not care how much they pollute themselves.

Beyond these, there are many other ways in which certain men seem to become detestable and contemptible in their offices and jurisdictions. This is because they do not follow the proper modes, but rather turn the laws and the writings of piety into the opposite of their intended quality. For even when they grant pardons or grant permission for many things to be done in houses, they take away a great deal, and they extort **tithes**. <note>A tax of one-tenth of one's income or produce paid to the church.</note> Many give judgment in exchange for money so that they do not have to give that same money to certain people who are entitled to alms. Instead, they claim that they owe these alms to "lords of detraction" which were not previously granted. Because of this, the "Time of Tithes" is called an "unconquered whip" <note>original: "lora... invicta"</note> due to its extortion, and likewise, legal condemnations are extorted. As for the flocks [the congregations], the rest is deferred to the future.
